Patience Instructions
A 5 or 10 minute activity where the aim is to use your knowledge of the glossary key terms to make
one continuous link, matching key word with definition.

 1. Shuffle the cards.

 2. Place 5 starter cards on the desk in a vertical row. Place the rest of the card in a pile, face down on
    the desk.

 3. Look at the 5 starter cards and link any that match. Replace any starter cards to ensure that there
    are always 5 in a row.

 4. Turn over the top card from the pile. Does it link? If yes, place it and look for any further links. If
    no, place it to the side.

 5. Repeat step 4 until all cards link.


Remember to maintain your central 5 for as long as possible.



An Alternative

 1. Split the class into 3 teams (number of teams depends on class size).

 2. Each team appoints a team leader who collects a set of cards and gives one to each member of their
    team. Any spares are placed face up on the desk.

Properties of Matter
 Aim: to observe and compare the properties of the three states of matter.


Equipment:
                                                        Safety Information
• Balloon filled with air
                                                        Latex balloons – possible allergen.
• Balloon filled with water
                                                        Check with students and offer an
• Balloon filled with (set) plaster                     alternative


Method:
Step 1: Taking care not to burst any of the balloons,
try to twist or bend each one. Can you change its
shape? Record your observations.

Step 2: With one hand, hold the balloon where it has
been tied and gently push the contents away with
the other. Can you compress the contents? (Again,
take care not to burst any of the balloons.) Record
your observations.

Step 3: Hold a balloon in each hand and compare
their densities. Then swap one balloon and compare
again. Keep comparing until you have decided which balloons are dense and which are not. Record your
observations.

Step 4: Holding the balloon where it is tied, hold it just above the desk, then let go. Do the contents
move and flow inside the balloon at all? Record your observations.

Step 5: Compare the balloons in any other ways you can think of and record your observations in the
blank rows on the table.




                                                Page 1 of 4
                                                                                       Properties of Matter

Result table

                          Solid                       Liquid                   Gas
Can it change shape?

Can it be compressed?

It is dense (heavy)

Does it flow?




Questions
 1. Describe each state of matter in a short paragraph, using the observations you have recorded in
    your table.

 2. Draw the particle arrangement for each state of matter: solid, liquid and gas.

 3. Using your particle diagram, explain why:

   a. A gas can be compressed

   b. A liquid can flow

   c. A solid is dense


 Extra Challenge
 Mix a tablespoon of cornflour with a few drops of water in a beaker. Stir until you have a smooth
 paste. What do you notice about the mixture when you stir and stop stirring? Does the mixture have
 properties like a solid, liquid or a gas? How would you classify this substance?

Answers
Result table

                          Solid                      Liquid                    Gas
Can it change shape?                 NO                        YES                      YES

Can it be compressed?                NO                        NO                       YES

It is dense (heavy)                  YES                   IN BETWEEN                    NO

Does it flow?                        NO                        YES                      YES


Questions
 1. Describe each state of matter in a short paragraph, using the observations you have recorded in
    your table.

    A solid object has a fixed shape and volume, it cannot be compressed and does not flow. Solid
    objects are usually a high density.

    A liquid object has a fixed volume but can change shape as it flows. It cannot be compressed and
    is usually a medium density.

    A gas object does not have a fixed shape or volume. It can flow and be compressed easily. Gas
    objects are not very dense.

 2. Draw the particle arrangement for each state of matter: solid, liquid and gas.




            SOLID                                 LIQUID                                  GAS

 3. Using your particle diagram, explain why:

   a. A gas can be compressed

   As a gas is compressed, the particles move closer together and the spaces between particles
   becomes smaller.
                                                                                        Properties of Matter
    b. A liquid can flow

   The particles are arranged closely together, but not tightly packed and so they can move and slide
   past one another.

    c. A solid is dense

   Since the particles are arranged so close together, with very little space in between, there is a lot
   of mass in the volume.


 Extra Challenge
 Mix a tablespoon of cornflour with a few drops of water in a beaker. Stir until you have a smooth
 paste. What do you notice about the mixture when you stir and stop stirring? Does the mixture have
 properties like a solid, liquid or a gas? How would you classify this substance?


The cornflour, when mixed with water, forms a non-Newtonian substance and can exhibit properties
of two states, depending on the pressure and force applied.

When the mixture is under pressure and being stirred, it exhibits properties of a solid, becoming hard
and holding its shape.

When the mixture is not being stirred it exhibits properties of a liquid, becoming ‘runny’ and flowing
(becoming less viscous).

EXTRA WORKSHEET 2:                           Making salt
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                         LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL                          VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


All the salt produced in Australia is made by using sunlight to evaporate water
from ponds of salt water. Seawater contains about 3.4% of total salts, of which
2.7% is sodium chloride. Sodium chloride is the salt that makes up almost all
of the table salt you buy. The main constituents of seawater are shown in the
table.
       Component                        Percentage (%)
 sodium chloride                               2.68
 magnesium sulfate                             0.22
 calcium sulfate                               0.12
 magnesium chloride                            0.32
 potassium chloride                            0.07
 other salts                                   0.01
 water                                        96.58


The process
Salt water is pumped from the sea into a nearby field consisting of a series of
shallow ponds. In the first pond, the action of the sun and the wind evaporates
some of the water, making the water more concentrated in dissolved salts.
The concentrated salt water is now called brine. As the concentration of the
brine increases, so does its density. The density of the brine is measured
regularly by scientists. Substances such as calcium carbonate crystallise and
settle to the bottom of this first pond.




Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2351 7   Page 1
 When the brine has reached a particular density it is pumped into the next
pond. There it is left to evaporate further. As it evaporates, crystals of gypsum
(calcium sulfate) form and settle to the bottom. The brine is then pumped into
the next pond. Here the remaining water is allowed to evaporate for a long
time. Sodium chloride crystals form and settle to the bottom of the pond. This
is the salt that the producers want to sell. Once most of the sodium chloride
has crystallised, the water is pumped out of this pond and discarded. More
brine is pumped into the pond.




Salt is made by moving sea water through a series of ponds and letting the water
evaporate


The layer of sodium chloride salt is normally harvested once a year. During
harvest, the pond is drained and machines lift the layer of salt from the pond
floor.

Excess brine is removed from the solid salt by a centrifuge. This spins the
brine off, leaving the salt crystals damp but otherwise clean. The remaining
moisture is driven off by heating to just above 110°C to produce dry salt
crystals.

Crushing and sieving to specific size ranges are the final steps in producing
the various salt grades. Sizes vary depending on the use, ranging from very
coarse salt used for pickling and presentation of oysters in restaurant meals,
right down to micro-fine salt used in making butter. In between there is a wide
variety of particle sizes that cater for all needs, from food ingredients to
pharmaceuticals, textiles, stockfeed and swimming pool additives.

Separating a Liquid Solute from a Solution. Distillation
Last lesson we used ___________ to separate a soluble SOLID from a solution.
If the solute is a LIQUID we need to use distillation. This uses both evaporation
and condensation.
This system relies on the fact that different liquids have different temperatures
that they boil at.
   a.  The mixture is heated till the boiling point of ONLY one liquid is reached.
      The thermometer allows the temperature to be monitored.
   b. The gas that has been produced rises up and moves into the central tube
      of the condenser. The condenser has a water jacket with cool water
      flowing through it. This cools the gas back to liquid.
   c. This liquid pours into a collecting beaker.




We call the liquid in the collecting beaker the DISTILLATE.

separate the alcohol and water. Alcohol boils at just over 80 degrees Celsius.
 Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. A mixture of water and alcohol is placed in

Separating iron filings from sand
Magnets are used for recycling because they can attract certain types of
metals from the recycling pile.
The metals that magnets attract are iron, nickel, and cobalt. It can also attract
steel because steel has iron in it!
In your investigation, you will use a similar idea in removing iron filings from
sand.

Aim
To investigate how a magnet can extract iron filings from sand and to calculate
the percentage of iron in the mixture.
You will need:
       eye protection
       a bar magnet
       a small plastic bag
       a mixture of iron filings and sand
       a top pan balance
       a calculator
       two small plastic containers
       paper weighing boat.

Method

   1. Measure the mass of the plastic container and record it on the table on
        page 2.
   2. Set the top pan balance to ‘zero’ with the container still on it. If you are
        unsure how to do this ask your teacher.
   3. Weigh out approximately 10 g of the sand and iron filing mixture and
        record the exact mass to 2 decimal points.
   4. Remove the plastic container from the top pan balance.
   5. Put the bar magnet into the small plastic bag and work it through the
        sand and iron filings.
   6. Taking care not to get the iron filings on your fingers, place the iron
        filings removed from the mixture into the other small plastic container.
   7. Repeat steps 5 and 6 until you have removed as many of the iron filings
        from the mixture as you can.
   8. Measure the mass of the sand without the iron filings and record your
        result in the table.

searchText: ﻿Separating mixtures Sedimentation and Decantation These processes can be used to separate an insoluble solid from a mixture of the solid and water. If the insoluble solid is heavy enough it will settle to the bottom of the vessel (sedimentation ) and form a sediment. The clearer water can then be separated from the solid sediment by pouring the liquid off (decantation) This process has a disadvantage in that the process of sedimentation can be very slow. Filtration Filtration can be used to separate an insoluble solid from a mixture of the solid and water. For example, a mixture of sand and water can be separated by filtration. In the filtration process, the mixture is poured through a folded filter paper supported in a filter funnel. The liquid passes through the small holes in the filter paper but the solid is trapped on the filter paper. The liquid that passes through the filter paper is called the filtrate and the solid trapped on the paper is called the residue. Evaporation The change of a liquid to a gas (or vapour) is called evaporation. Evaporation can be used to separate a dissolved solid from its solvent. For example, salt can be obtained from sea water by the process of evaporation. In this process, the solvent is evaporated and the solute is left behind in the container. Distillation

searchText:
Separation of Rock Salt
 Aim: To obtain pure salt from rock salt.

Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Sample of rock salt
                                                         Hot water – risk of scalds and burns
• Pestle and mortar
                                                         Wear goggles,     take   care   when
• Two 250cm³ beakers                                     heating
• Stirring rod                                           Glassware – risk of cuts if broken
• Filter funnel                                          Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
                                                         immediately
• Filter papers
                                                         Bunsen burner – risk of burns
• Tripod
                                                         Place under cold running water for 10 minutes
• Heatproof mat
                                                         and inform teacher
• Bunsen burner

• Evaporating basin




Method:
Step 1: Carefully grind up the rock salt in the pestle and mortar.

Step 2: Stir the ground rock salt into a beaker of water to dissolve it.

Step 3: Carefully filter the solution through the filter paper in the funnel, into the second beaker.

Step 4: Transfer approximately 10ml of the filtered solution into the evaporating basin and set on the
tripod over the Bunsen burner.



                                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                                                         Separation of Rock Salt


Step 5: Heat the water until it is gently boiling and the water begins to evaporate off.

Step 6: When crystals begin to form on the sides of the basin, turn off the Bunsen burner – you now
have a saturated solution.

Step 7: Leave the equipment to cool and then move the basin to a warm place to evaporate more slowly
(overnight).



                    Rock salt is a mixture of sand and salt. It is also sometimes called grit salt and
                    is used on roads during winter. The sand and salt compounds have different
                    properties and so they can be separated.


Questions:
 1. In step 2, water is acting as a solvent. What is a solvent?

 2. Explain how the salt water solution is separated from the sand in step 3.

 3. Draw a clearly labelled diagram to show the particles of sand and salt in step 3.

 4. What is meant by a saturated solution, as described in step 6?

 5. Explain, in terms of energy and particle arrangement, what evaporation is.




                                                 Page 2 of 3
                                                                                        Separation of Rock Salt



Answers:
1. In step 2, water is acting as a solvent. What is a solvent?
   A solvent is a substance able to dissolve other substances.

2. Explain how the salt water solution is separated from the sand in step 3.
   The sand grains are insoluble (unable to dissolve) and so they cannot pass through the porous
   filter paper with the water and are left in the filter funnel.

3. Draw a clearly labelled diagram to show the particles of sand and salt in step 3.




4. What is meant by a saturated solution, as described in step 6?
   As much salt as possible is dissolved - no more salt can be dissolved.

5. Explain, in terms of energy and particle arrangement, what evaporation is.
   The water particles have gained more energy from the heating, and begin to move faster. The
   bonds between the water particles become weaker and some break off and become a gas
   particle instead.

Solids, Liquids and Gases
Complete the following table by writing 5 examples of solids, liquids and
gases. One example of each has been done to get you started.

        Solids                    Liquids                        Gases
Chocolate                 Water                       Nitrogen




Test the properties of solids, liquids and gases, following the teacher’s
instructions, and fill in the table below.

                         Solids             Liquids                Gases

     Shape

    Volume

Compressibility



Why does this happen?
All matter is made up of particles. In solids, liquids and
gases, the particles behave differently.

Solids
In a solid, the particles are locked into place. Even
though they are locked in place, they are still vibrating.
If you add heat, they vibrate more because they have
more energy.

Liquids
If you heat the solid, the particles will vibrate so much
they can’t stay in their place any more. They start
moving around. The solid has then melted into a liquid.
If you add more heat, they want to move around even
more because they have even more energy.

Gases
 The particles in a gas are free to move around and are not held by any
other particles. Gases have no definite shape.

Introduction
When we cook pasta, we frequently dissolve table salt in water. Is there a limit to how
much salt we can get into the water?
When ionic-bonded compounds (like table salt, NaCl) are dissolved in polar solvents

When this happens (called dissociation), ions are released into the solution. Is there a
limit to the number of ions that can exist in solution?

searchText:
Taboo – solids, liquids, gases

Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any of the
additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto different
      coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have all the cards back at
      the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile, and then
      describes the word at the top of the card without using the words below. The rest of
      their team must guess which word is described. Participants are not allowed to say
      ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the opposing team
      may challenge and the individual must move on to the next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as possible to
      the players in their team (a longer time may be required to allow more descriptions
      to take place) before play passes to the next team. There are no penalties for
      wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.
      Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other ways to
describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to reinforcing
the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could research
meanings of new terms.



Extension activity


   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.

   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated with the
      keyword they have written at the top of the card.

To recycle or to not recycle
Greywater is wastewater generated from washing dishes, laundry and bathing in homes. It makes up
50–80 per cent of residential wastewater. Greywater does not contain chemical and biological
contaminants. Greywater gets its name from its cloudy appearance and from its status as being
neither fresh (whitewater from groundwater or taps) nor heavily polluted (blackwater).
   If collected via a separate plumbing system, greywater can be recycled directly within the home
and garden. Recycled greywater of this kind is never clean enough to drink, but a number of stages
of filtration and microbial digestion can be used to provide water for washing or flushing toilets;
relatively clean greywater may be applied directly from the sink to the garden, because it receives
treatment from the soil and plant roots. Vegetables should not be watered with greywater.
   On 26 July 2006, 61.62 per cent of Toowoomba’s residents opposed the treating of sewage for
drinking water. Under the plan, wastewater would have been collected and put through a series of
purifying treatments, including ultrafiltration, reverse osmosis and oxidation. The treated water would
be pumped into a dam, where it would rest for three to five years — enough time to convince the

Possible Script:
Solar Eclipses

When the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, the Sun
temporarily disappears from the sky. The Sun, the Moon and
Earth are aligned and this is a solar eclipse. The Moon can be seen
blocking the Sun. When the Moon is close enough to Earth, its
disc is sufficiently large enough to hide the Sun. From Earth, a
total eclipse is observed. If the Moon is a little further away from
Earth, an annular eclipse is observed where the Sun's outer edges
remain visible to form a ‘ring of fire”.

Lunar Eclipses

When the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, the Moon is not
lit by the Sun. An equivalent phenomenon causes lunar eclipses.
In this case, Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon. The
Moon is no longer lit up by the Sun. Instead, it turns dark red due
to the deviation of the Sun's rays caused by Earth. This is known
as a lunar eclipse.

EXTRA WORKSHEET 2:                           Martians from Mars
VERBAL/LINGUISTIC                   SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


In 1858, the Italian astronomer Angelo Secchi (1818–1878) reported seeing
channels on the surface of Mars. These observations were confirmed in 1877
by another Italian astronomer, Giovanni Schiaparelli (1835–1910). Although
neither astronomer gave an explanation as to what they were, American
astronomer Percival Lowell (1855–1916) wrote three books (in 1895, 1906
and 1908) that suggested that the channels were canals dug by intelligent
beings (Martians) to move water from the polar caps to irrigate their farms.

Many astronomers, however, couldn’t see the vast network of canals that
Lowell suggested and the channels that could be seen were far too wide to be
dug by anyone. Although the 1910 Encyclopaedia Britannica expressed
serious doubts about them, public imagination was ignited: intelligent Martians
lived (or had lived) on Mars!

Lowell’s canals were not disproved until 1965 when the Mariner 4 space
orbiter sent back the first close-up images of the surface of Mars. Some
channels have been found to be natural canyons while others were an optical
illusion created by lines of craters.

VERBAL/LINGUISTIC LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL SCIENCE AS A HUMAN ENDEAVOUR


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


The Moon is the closest celestial body to Earth and so it’s not surprising that it
was the first to be explored. Apart from Earth, the Moon remains the only body
in space that humans have walked upon.


Early exploration
USA and the USSR (Russia) sent roughly 40 missions to the Moon between
1959 and 1969.

The Apollo missions
Between 1969 and 1972, six Apollo missions successfully landed two men
each on the Moon’s surface and brought them safely back to Earth. The
Apollo program, however, started with disaster: a fire raced through the
command module of Apollo 1 during a test of launch procedures, killing all
three astronauts on board. Apollo 13 also suffered disaster: an explosion and
multiple system failures caused its Moon landing to be abandoned and it was
under continued threat of further disaster on its way back to Earth.

 The first human to walk on the Moon was Neil Armstrong, followed shortly by
his crewmate Edwin (Buzz) Aldrin. They spent roughly a day on the lunar
surface, venturing outside of their lunar module for a total of 2½ hours. In
1972, Eugene Cernan was the last person to walk on the Moon. Since then,
the furthest a human has gone into space is into orbit around Earth, a few
hundred kilometres above its surface.

searchText:
Crater Formation

Background

Impact craters are formed when pieces of asteroids or comets strike the surface of a
planetary body. Craters are found on all the terrestrial planets, on the Earth’s Moon, and
on most satellites of planets. Various geological clues and studies of the lunar rocks
returned by the Apollo missions indicate that about 3.9 billion years ago asteroid-size
chunks of matter were abundant in the solar system. This was a time of intense
bombardment of the young planets, affecting Earth by breaking up and modifying parts of
the crust. Mountain building, plate tectonics, weathering and erosion have largely removed
the traces of Earth’s early cratering period. But the near absence of weathering on the
Moon has allowed the evidence of this ancient time to be preserved.

Impact craters are formed by the transfer of energy from a moving mass (meteorite) to a
stationary body (planet). Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. It is defined as one half
the mass of an object, times the velocity of the object squared (K.E. = ½mv2).

Objects in space move very fast, so this can be a huge amount of energy! In an impact the
kinetic energy of a meteorite is changed into heat that melts rocks and energy that
pulverizes and excavates rock. Simplified demonstrations of this transfer of energy can be
made by creating impacts in powdered materials. If identical objects are impacted into
powdered materials from different heights or using different propulsion systems to increase
velocities, then students can determine the effect velocity has on the cratering process.
The high velocity impact and explosion of an iron meteorite about 30 meters in diameter
could make a crater over one kilometre wide. This is how the Meteor Crater in Arizona was
formed.

Aim: To investigate what happens to the size of craters as the velocity of the impact is
     increased.

4. Measure the depth and width of the crater formed in millimetres.
5. Record measurements in the table provided
6. Level the sand again and repeat steps 3 – 5 another two times.

searchText:
Earth and space taboo
Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.


   1. Students work in teams (an even number with at least two people in each
      team).

   2. Each team needs a set of cards. It is worth copying each set onto
      different coloured paper and/or laminating them to ensure that you have
      all the cards back at the end of the activity in order to reuse them.

   3. The cards need to be cut out, and then shuffled and placed face down.

   4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
      and then describes the word at the top of the card without using the
      words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is described.
      Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes with’ and no
      gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

   5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
      opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
      next word.

   6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words as
      possible to the players in their team (a longer time may be required to
      allow more descriptions to take place) before play passes to the next
      team. There are no penalties for wrong guesses.

   7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
      point. Prizes/merits could be handed out to the winning team in each
      group.


This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research meanings of new terms.



Extension activity
   1. Each student puts a new vocabulary word at the top of a blank card.


   2. Each student then has to write a further five words which are associated
      with the keyword they have written at the top of the card.

searchText: Measure the Sun’s Size How can you measure the Sun’s real size? Description Make a pinhole viewer, and use it to measure the Sun’s size. You will need a bright sunny day. Age Level: 10 and up Materials • sheet of cardboard (like from a cereal box) • piece of white paper • small piece of aluminum foil, about 3 cm x 3 cm • pin or thumbtack • scissors • tape • ruler • string or yarn (about 60 cm long) • hardcover book (optional) Time Safety Preparation: 5 minutes Never look directly at the Sun! Activity: 20 minutes Cleanup: 5 minutes 1 Cut a square about 1.5 cm x 1.5 cm from the center of the cardboard. Tape the piece of aluminum foil over the square. Carefully use a pin or thumbtack to prick a hole in the center of the aluminum foil. You have now created a pinhole viewer. While you’re outside, hold the piece of white paper behind the pinhole viewer, so that sunlight shines through the hole and projects a circular image on the paper. Try to make the distance between the pinhole and the paper as large as possible. Tip Taping the white paper to a book will help keep the paper upright. 2 While holding the pinhole viewer steady, measure the size of the Sun’s image on the piece of paper in centimeters. Record this measurement below. While still holding the pinhole viewer steady, stretch a piece of string between the pinhole and the piece of paper. Measure that length of string in centimeters. Record this measurement below. Tip It would be useful to have a friend help you with the measuring. Step 6 The equation on the right is used to calculate the Sun’s diameter. Using sun image size (d) and the string length (l) you recorded above, along with the distance from the Sun to Earth (L), calculate the diameter of the Sun. Below is the actual diameter of the Sun. distance from Sun to Earth (L) = 149,600,000 km actual Sun diameter (D) = 1,392,000 km 3 The Sun’s light enters the pinhole and creates an image on the white piece of paper. Because of the geometry of the setup, we can use ratios to solve for the Sun’s real size. The ratio of the Sun’s size (D) to the distance between Earth and the Sun (L) is D/L. This ratio is equal to the ratio of the Sun’s image size (d) to the distance between the pinhole and the image (l) or d/l. Image from a tablet You can also try this measuring activity using the screen of a tablet or smartphone as the “Sun” in a dark room. Cast an image through the same pinhole viewer on a wall or a sheet of paper. If you measure L, l, and d as seen in the image below, you can calcu- late D (the height of your screen) just as you did for the size of the Sun. How close is your measured value to the real size of your tablet or smartphone screen? 4 Learn More For more info and other activities, visit: LawrenceHallofScience.org/do_science_now/diy_sun_science Credits This project was supported by NASA under award number NNX10AE05G. Any opinions, ﬁndings, conclusions or recommenda- tions expressed in this program are those of the author and do not reﬂect the views of NASA. The DIY Sun Science app allows families and educators to investi- gate and learn about the Sun at home, at school, or anywhere you go! The app features thirteen hands-on investigations, as well as images and videos. © 2014 The Regents of the University of California. All rights reserved. Lunacy
By Ken Kaye, Staff Writer
Sun-Sentinel
(Ft. Lauderdale, FL)




                                                 8|Page
 Aug. 11, 2003, pp. D1

The worst things in the world happen during a full Moon, right? Wrong.

For those given to lore, it might seem likely that a full Moon shone on the sinking of the
Titanic in 1912, the bombing of Pearl Harbor in 1941 or the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist
attacks.

The full Moon, after all, is frequently associated with dark calamities, if not werewolves
and haunted houses.

But that wasn't the case.

Surely, then, the Moon turned full on the day the stock market crashed in 1929, or that
Amelia Earhart vanished in 1937 or President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in 1963,
right?

Nope.

The fact is a full Moon … has been in the sky during very few major world events in the
past century, which would seem to debunk the myth that lunar forces inspire aberrant
behavior or influence the course of history on Earth.

"There are always lots of reports of strange things during a full Moon. But I think if you
look at overall statistics, there's no [link]," says Geoff Chester of the U.S. Naval
Observatory in Washington, D.C., which has kept a careful record of full Moons dating to
1700.

A review of full Moon dates, compiled by the Naval Observatory, shows that most of the
major events of our time took place during some other lunar phase.

For instance, when the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, Japan, on Aug. 6, 1945,
the Moon was in its last-quarter phase. When civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. was
assassinated in April 1968, the Moon was new. President Richard Nixon's resignation in
August 1974 came six days after the full Moon.

Even for humankind's major forays into space, when you might think a full Moon would
be appropriate, it was a no-show.

When Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space in April 1961, the
Moon was in its last-quarter phase. When Neil Armstrong took the first step on the lunar
surface in July 1969, it was during the gibbous waxing Moon.

Some major developments did happen close to a full Moon:

One day after a full Moon, on Feb. 20, 1962, John Glenn became the first American to
orbit the Earth.

                                                                                    9|Page
 Two days after a full Moon, on Jan. 28, 1986, the space shuttle Challenger exploded,
killing seven astronauts, including schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe.

But of the major historic milestones in the past 100 years, only D-Day, June 6, 1944,
when Allied Forces stormed the beaches of northern France to begin the conquest of
Germany in Europe, took place during a full Moon.

And that was deliberate: Military commanders wanted lots of Moonlight so airborne
troops could land near enemy lines and Navy ships could fire on German targets with
precision before dawn…

Strange Things Happen

From a global standpoint, full Moons have seen their share of mayhem:

    On Jan. 16, 1995, a Japan earthquake killed more than 400 people.
    On Nov. 11, 2000, 170 skiers and snowboarders were trapped and killed when their
      cable car caught fire while being pulled through an Alpine tunnel.
    On Jan. 28, 2002, more than 600 were killed in Nigeria, trying to flee explosions at
      an army weapons depot, only to drown.
Did the Moon actually provoke any of these episodes?

No way, astronomers and historians say.

"It's pure coincidence," says Travis Wright, an employee at Buehler Planetarium in Davie.
"I doubt that it has anything to do with the voice of the universe telling people what to
do."

On the other hand, astrologers, or those who think celestial bodies affect the course of
human events, say a full Moon makes people more amorous.

"The Moon affects tides, and since our bodies are mostly water, there probably is a
physical reaction," says Linea Van Horn, an accredited astrologer who works for
Astrology.com, the largest astrological site on the Internet, based in San Francisco.
"When it's big and beautiful in the sky, it does awaken something in us humans."

According to folklore, the full Moon usually has negative connotations, says Christine
Jackson, a professor of humanities at Nova Southeastern University in Davie.

For instance, she says it is believed the full Moon triggers more suicides than usual and
sends more people to mental institutions.

In fiction and film, the Werewolf needed the light of the full Moon to come to life, and
Dracula had to avoid Moonlight to suck blood from his victims.



                                                                                   10 | P a g e
 In the recent movie, Pirates of the Caribbean, moonlight revealed the pirates were half-
dead, nothing but skeletons.

"So the light of a full Moon can sometimes show death," she says

Only a Minute

Astronomically speaking, a full Moon occurs for about one minute, when the Moon and
the Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth. The reason this instant is so short is that all
three bodies are in constant motion.

However, planetarium officials consider the full Moon to occur over a full day and even
more loosely, over three days, says Jack Horkheimer, director of Miami Planetarium.

"The night before a full Moon and night after full Moon look that same to the untrained
eye," he says.

The Moon has four major phases in a month, or more precisely, 29.5 days: New Moon,
first quarter, full Moon, and last quarter.

Those phases are further broken down into waxing crescent, waxing gibbous, waning
crescent and waning gibbous, based on how much of the lighted surface is visible…

Horkheimer says the myth that the Moon creates strange events arises from ancient
times, when there were few cities and the countryside was extremely dark on Moonless
nights.

The full Moon provided enough light for people to attend festivals and other gatherings
at night. This was when they were most susceptible to thieves, pickpockets and robbers,
he says.

That led to the fear that the full Moon created havoc in people's lives, he says.

Today, police can't say for sure whether crime increases during a full Moon, other than to
say the "freaks" tend to come out. But then, they note such people come out the rest of
[the] time as well.

"In general, in South Florida, it's irrelevant whether the Moon's in or out," says Hollywood
Police Lt. Tony Rode. "We have our fair share of crime either way."

As for that term "lunatics," derived from "Luna," the Roman Moon goddess: Horkheimer
says the light of a full Moon might keep people up at night, and a lack of sleep might
make them cranky, if not crazy.

But does the full Moon inspire werewolves to howl or monsters to come out?

Only in people's imaginations, Horkheimer says.

                                                                                    11 | P a g e
 "People want to believe in the mysterious, in magic and in things beyond their control,"
he said. "So if something happens they can say it must have been the full Moon."

Moon Facts

    The Moon is believed to be 4.6 billion years old, the same age as the Earth.
    It has no atmosphere or water.
    It is comprised of a rocky material that is heavily scarred with craters from
     meteorite impacts.
    The same side is permanently turned toward Earth.
    The gravitational forces between the Earth and the Moon generate two ocean high
     tides per day.
    The word "lunatic" comes from the notion that the Moon's forces could make a
     person go crazy.
    The Moon is moving away from the Earth at a rate of 3.8 centimeters each year.
     When it formed, the Moon was about 14,000 miles from Earth; now it's about
     240,000 miles away.

Moon Nicknames

    January: Wolf Moon
    February: Ice or Snow Moon
    March: Storm or Worm Moon
    April: Growing or Pink Moon
    May: Hare or Flower Moon
    June: Mead or

searchText:
The Solar System

The Features of our Solar System
The solar system is made up of the Sun, the nine planets that orbit the Sun and various natural satellites (moons),
asteroids, comets and meteors.




The Terrestrial Planets

Terrestrial planets are those planets (and possibly dwarf planets) that are similar to Earth — with bodies largely
composed of rock: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Venus is the planet which is the closest size to Earth but
because of its thick poisonous atmosphere creating extremely hot surface temperatures, Mars is the closest in
environment to Earth.

The Gas Giants

The Gas Giants are planets with a composition largely made up of gaseous material and are significantly more
massive than terrestrials: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Ice giants are a sub-class of gas giants, distinguished
from gas giants by their lack of hydrogen and helium, and a significant composition of rock and ice: Uranus and
Neptune.

 of rock and ice. It has an eccentric squashed orbit that is highly tilted with respect
 to the other planets and takes it closer to the Sun than Neptune during a portion
 of its orbit. Pluto and its largest satellite, Charon, could be considered a binary

The large distances between the components of the solar system
Most of the solar system is empty space; distances are so huge it takes a long time to travel between
planets. Travelling at the speed of a fast passenger jet, 1000km, it would take 16 days to reach the Moon
~384,000km away. Astronauts reached the Moon in four days however, as they were travelling much
faster. They needed to reach at least 40,000km to escape Earth’s gravity (called the escape velocity).




Travelling to Mars will take a lot longer, however. Mars is 203 time further away from Earth than the
Moon is. Jupiter is 1635 times further away.

Compared to the large distance between the Earth and the Moon, the distances to the other planets
and the Sun is much greater again. The first four planets are relatively close compared to the outer gas
planets. Because of the vast distances in the solar system we use Astronomical Units. An astronomical
unit is the average distance from the Earth to the Sun.

The Night Sky

Visual objects in the New Zealand night sky include the Southern Cross, and Matariki
(the Pleiades)
People have grouped stars into imagined patterns called constellations since ancient history. The most famous
constellations are those that form the 12 signs of the zodiac (Leo, Aries, and Cancer etc.) but our most well-
known and visible constellation seen only in the Sothern hemisphere is the Southern Cross.




Because of Earth’s rotation the stars are not in the same place throughout the night

As the earth orbits the Sun, we see a different portion of the sky. There are some stars we see at all times of the
year from New Zealand, like the stars that form the constellation the Southern Cross, and others that we never
see, like the North Star.




Constellations are seen as a 2-dimensional view (like seeing them on a flat sheet) of 3-dimensional space – where
stars in a single constellation are at different distances from earth. Different constellations are seen at different
times of the year and from different places on Earth. Stars that make up a constellation may be brighter because
they are closer to Earth and/or they are bigger/brighter stars.
119 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Main constellations in the Southern Night Sky




Matariki

Matariki is the Māori name for a cluster of stars – a seven-star constellation that appears in late May or early
June each year. Each winter the stars of Matariki and Puanga signal the end of one year in Aotearoa and the
beginning of the next.

The rise of Matariki is a time to celebrate and prepare for the Māori New Year. It was a time when crops were
harvested, and seafood and birds were collected – a time of celebration and food, but also a time for preparing
and storing for times of shortage ahead. Matariki was a time to practise manaakitanga – to share kai and present
offerings to others.

        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Investigate how you can make a nail into a magnet using electricity.


        EQUIPMENT



Per Class
    1 jar with some sugar , one leaf and 5 paper clips (iron filings are very useful if
       available)
      1 magnet
      alfoil
      masking tape
      a compass (optional)

Per Group
     2 D batteries
     2 x 15 cm lengths of plastic coated copper wire
     10 paper clips
     1 large nail
     masking tape
     15cm of alfoil
     pop sticks

Preparation
      In a jar mix one teaspoon of sugar, five very small paper clips or pins and a leaf
       cut into tiny pieces

Safety
    Mains electricity must not be used to make magnets.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   An electromagnet is a temporary magnet formed when electric current flows
    through a wire or other conductor.
   Most electromagnets consist of a wire wound around an iron core.
   When an electric current moves in one direction through a wire, a magnetic field
    is created around the wire.
   When the wire is wrapped around an object to form a coil, the magnetic field
    around each wire is aligned right next to the field of the adjacent wires.
   All the coils work together to form a much stronger, single magnetic field.
   Electromagnets are a part of our everyday lives.
   They are useful because they act like magnets when the current is on and lose
    their magnetism when the current is off.
   Some electromagnets we use everyday are in school bells, telephones,
    automatic doors, video and tape recorders.

searchText:
What are forces?
A force can be thought of as a push or a pull. Every time you push or pull on
something, you are exerting a force. For instance, when you ride a bike, your legs are
exerting a force by pushing down on the pedals.

Effects of forces

Scientists say that when a force acts on something, a change occurs. Speeding up,
slowing down, changing direction and changing the shape of something are examples
of changes which can be produced by forces.

 Contact Forces occur when one object or person exerts a force through contact with
another object.

Friction

 Friction is an example of a contact force. Friction occurs between any two or more
surfaces that are in contact. The direction of the frictional force is normally opposite to
the movement of the object. Friction is the force that opposes
the movement of one body over another.

The effects of frictional forces can be an advantage or a
disadvantage. Without friction, we would not be able to walk or
hold objects. However, friction also causes moving parts to wear
or can generate significant amounts of heat.

Some ways to reduce the effects of friction are to add a lubricant, make the surface as
smooth as possible or reduce the force pushing the objects together.

Non-contact Forces are forces that act over a distance.

Gravity

Gravity is a pulling force that exists between things that have mass. The strength of
the force of gravity between two objects is determined by their mass. Earth has a
              very large mass so it exerts a large gravitational force on objects close
              to it. The gravitational force of attraction increases as the mass of the
              objects increases or the distance between them decreases.

Weight can be defined as the amount by which an object is pulled downwards by
gravity. It is expressed in newtons (N) and can be measured with a spring balance.
Weight is different to mass. Mass is defined as the amount of matter that makes up
an object and is measured in kilograms (kg).

Electric

Electric forces result from the pulling or pushing effects of electrical charges.
Electrical charges are the result of protons and electrons within atoms. Protons carry
a positive charge and electrons carry a negative charge. When the number of
electrons and protons in an atom are equal, the atom has no charge. If an atom has
unequal numbers of protons and electrons, then it will have an overall charge. More
 electrons than protons gives an atom a negative charge and more protons than
electrons gives it a negative charge.

Objects have a positive or negative charge because the atoms on their surface have
either an overall positive or negative charge. How charged objects affect each other is
governed by the charge law. According to the charge law, objects that have opposite
charges exert pulling forces on each other. These objects attract one another.
Objects that have the same type of charge exert pushing forces on each other. These
objects repel each other.




Magnetic

Magnets can affect one another or attract certain metals without being close to them.
All magnets contain one or more of the metals iron, nickel or cobalt, and magnets will
only affect materials containing these metals. Each end of a magnet is called a pole.
One pole is called north and the other is called south. When the pole of one magnet is
brought close to the pole of another magnet, the two poles either repel or attract one
another. Magnetic poles follow similar rules to those for electric charges. Opposite
poles attract and like poles repel.

   13.       Would you expect the gravitational force exerted by the moon to be

   15.       Why are electrical and magnetic forces considered non-contact forces?

Hooke’s Law
 Aim: to observe Hooke’s Law in different materials.


Equipment
                                                              Safety Information
• Retort stand
                                                              Masses – risk of injury

• Boss                                                        Ensure the equipment is well
                                                              secured on the desk.

• Mass hanger and 100g masses

• Spring

• Elastic band



Method
Step 1: Set up the retort stand, boss, clamp and spring as
        shown in the diagram.

Step 2: Fully secure the base of the retort stand to the desk
        and check it is firmly secure before continuing.

Step 3: Use the metre ruler to measure and record the original
        length of the spring (at 0g mass).

Step 4: Attach the mass hanger (with no masses on) to the
        spring. (The hanger should have a mass of 100g −
        check with your teacher if you are unsure).

Step 5: Measure the new length of the spring and record.

Step 6: Place a 100g mass onto the mass hanger. Measure
        and record the new length of the spring.

Step 7: Continue to repeat step 6 until you have added 1000g
        (the hanger + 9 masses).

Step 8: Carefully unload the spring and remove from the
        apparatus.

Step 9: Attach the elastic band to the clamp in place of the
        spring and repeat the investigation.

Hooke’s Law states that an object will be stretched or squashed to an extension (e) which is directly
proportional to the force (F) applied. Hooke’s Law only applies within the elastic limit of the object.

                                                   F=k×e

The spring constant (k) varies for different materials. If a spring is stiff (not easily stretched), it will have
a greater value of k.




Questions
 1. Calculate the extension of the spring and the elastic band and complete the table. To do this you
    need to subtract the original length of the spring (at 0g mass added) from the length of the spring.
    e.g. if the spring measured 6cm before any masses were added, and then measured 13cm with
    100g added. The extension at 100g is 13 – 6 = 7cm.

 2. Plot a graph to show extension against force for the spring and the elastic band. The extension
    should be plotted on the x-axis, in metres, and the force on the y-axis, in Newtons.
    To convert cm to m you will need to divide by 100. 100cm = 1m.
    100g = 1N.

 3. Look at your graph. Does the spring obey Hooke’s Law? Explain how you know.

 4. Look at your graph. Does the elastic band obey Hooke’s Law? Explain how you know.

 5. Which part of the graph represents the spring constant?

searchText: teachers guide Forces 1: Introduction to force Components NAME DESCRIPTION AUDIENCE Introduction to force This guide suggests teaching strategies to engage students’ teachers interest in learning about forces and their effects on teachers guide objects. Use the force A ‘Lego-mation’ movie shows different forces in action. students video Thinking about forces Questions about scenarios shown in the video promote class students discussion about forces. presentation Newton explained This background sheet for teachers summarises Newton’s teachers laws of motion and describes some common misconceptions background sheet held by students. Purpose Outcomes This resource is intended to Engage students’ interest Students understand that: in learning about forces and their effects on objects. • forces may change the position or motion of an object; • forces have strength (magnitude) and direction; and • forces may act through contact with objects or at a distance. Activity summary ACTIVITY POSSIBLE STRATEGY Teacher introduces the topic of forces and what they can do to whole class objects, through questions such as: • What forces can you name? (gravity, magnetism, friction …) • What can forces do to objects? (change their position, speed or shape …) • Do forces always have these effects on objects? (No – some forces don’t seem to have any effect on some objects) Teacher explains that students will investigate what forces can do to objects and why. Teacher shows ‘Lego-mation’ video, Use the force. teacher and whole class Students are asked to think about forces that are acting in each scenario included in the video. Teacher-led discussion and summary of forces depicted in the whiteboard summary video and their effects on objects. The presentation, Thinking about forces, contains questions to prompt discussion. Teacher asks students to call out what they want to know more Teacher uses these responses to select about. Responses may include: appropriate exploratory activities. • How do forces affect the motion of objects? • How do forces balance each other? ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 1 Licensed for NEALS Teacher notes This resource helps develop students’ understanding of Newton’s laws of motion. A summary of these laws is included in the background sheet, Newton explained. The ‘Lego-mation’ video, Use the force, is designed to engage students’ interest in forces and motion, and to elicit their prior knowledge and misconceptions about forces. It is recommended that students view the video all the way through, before examining it in detail to identify forces and their effects in some or all of the scenarios. The presentation, Thinking about forces, contains a series of still shots taken from the video to encourage class discussion. Teachers should decide which, and how many, scenarios to discuss. The following information is provided to assist with the discussion. Scenario 1 Magnetic force 1 Description Luke’s magnet pushes Vader’s magnet away. Vader’s magnet slides and stops. Question Why did Vader’s magnet move away from Luke’s? Answer It moved away because Luke’s magnet repelled it. Magnetic force between like poles (N and N, or S and S) causes magnets to repel one another. slide 2 Notes Magnetism is a force that can act at a distance or through contact. Friction only acts between objects in contact. Question Why did Vader’s magnet stop moving? Answer Friction between the magnet and table stopped his magnet from sliding further. Notes Vader’s magnet stopped sliding when the friction force balanced the magnetic force. Scenario 2 Magnetic force 2 Description The stormtrooper pushes Luke’s magnet towards Vader’s. Vader’s magnet slides and sticks to Luke’s. Luke and Vader fall off. Question What made the magnets slide towards each other? Answer Magnetic force between opposite poles attracts the magnets to each other. Notes When magnets are closer together, attraction is stronger. When slide 3 magnetic force is greater than friction the magnets slide towards each other. Scenario 3 Magnetic force 3 Description The stormtrooper hands Vader a paper clip, which is attached to the ground by a rope. Suddenly Vader is yanked upwards, suspended below a magnet hanging from a crane. Question What is holding Vader and the paper clip up? Answer Magnetic force holds Vader and the paperclip up. Question What other forces are acting on Vader? slide 4 Answer Gravity and tension in the rope are acting on Vader, preventing him from reaching the magnet. Notes Vader and the paper clip remain suspended below the magnet as long as the upward magnetic force balances the downward forces of gravity and tension. Scenario 4 Electrostatic force Description The stormtrooper and Luke hold a charged rod close to a pile of paper. Small pieces of paper jump up and stick to the rod. Question What forces are acting on the pieces of paper? Answer Electrostatic force makes the paper move toward the rod. Gravity is acting on the pieces, pulling them back down. slide 5 Notes When the rod is rubbed it gains (or loses) electrons and becomes electrostatically charged. The charged rod attracts the pieces of paper. The electrostatic force is stronger than gravity, so the pieces of paper move toward the rod. Eventually, charges on paper and rod leak away and the electrostatic force decreases until it is weaker than gravity. At this point the pieces of paper fall to the floor. ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 2 Scenario 5 Elastic force Description Vader releases the paper clip and jumps onto a weight suspended by elastic. The elastic stretches; then contracts, flinging him off. Questions What made the elastic stretch? What made it spring back? Answer Gravity (Vader’s weight) made the elastic stretch. The more it stretches, the greater the tension in the elastic. Elastic force made the material return to its original length. slide 6 Scenario 6 Tension 1 Description Luke and Vader are engaged in a tug of war. The rope isn’t moving. Questions What forces are acting in the tug of war? Why isn’t the rope moving? Answer The forces are: tension in the rope; friction between Luke’s and Vader’s feet and the ground; gravity; and the ground’s supporting force. Notes The rope isn’t moving because Luke and Vader are pulling in slide 7 opposite directions with an equal amount of force. Forces are balanced. Scenario 7 Tension 2 Description The stormtrooper joins Luke at his end of the rope and together they pull Vader along. Question What forces are acting when the rope starts moving? Answer The forces are: tension in the rope; friction between Luke’s, Vader’s and the stormtrooper’s feet, and the ground; gravity; and the ground’s supporting force. slide 8 Notes Horizontal forces are no longer balanced. Luke and the stormtrooper exert more force than Vader, so they pull him along. Scenario 8 Friction 1 Description Luke and Vader run and slide along the ground. Question What made Luke and Vader stop sliding? Answer Friction between their bodies and the ground stopped them sliding. Notes Friction opposes motion. Because it is strong, they soon stop sliding. The vertical forces (gravity and the ground’s supporting force) have no effect on their motion. slide 9 Scenario 9 Friction 2 Description Luke and Vader repeat their sliding competition, this time on ice. Question What forces are acting on Luke and Vader when they’re sliding along the ice? Answer When they’re sliding at constant speed the only forces acting on them are gravity (down) and the ice’s supporting force (up). Horizontal forces, air resistance and friction, are so small they can be ignored. slide 10 Notes: Vertical forces balance each other. If not, Luke and Vader would sink into the ice. There are no horizontal forces to make them go faster or slower, so they keep sliding at the same speed. Scenario 10 Air resistance Description The stormtrooper drops two pieces of paper at the same time: one flat; the other scrunched into a ball. Questions What forces are acting on the pieces of paper as they fall? Why does the flat piece of paper fall slower? Answer Forces acting on both pieces of paper as they fall are gravity (downwards) and air resistance (upwards). slide 11 Air resistance depends on surface area. The flat sheet has a bigger surface area, which means there’s more air resistance, so it falls slower. Notes If the experiment was repeated in a vacuum, both pieces of paper would fall at the same rate because of absence of air resistance. ast0478 | Forces 1: Introduction to force (teachers guide) developed for the Department of Education WA © The University of Western Australia 2013 for conditions of use see spice.wa.edu.au/usage version 1.0 revised May 2013 page 3 Technical requirements SPICE resources and copyright The teachers guide requires Adobe Reader (version 5 All SPICE resources are available from the Centre for or later), which is a free download from www.adobe. About This Unit
                This unit aims to introduce students to forces by including hands-on investigations in each lesson. There is a focus on evaluating the investigations
                throughout the unit. Initially, students are guided step-by-step through writing an evaluation, then scaffolding is gradually reduced in subsequent lessons.
                Students are supported to rearrange equations and there are several opportunities to practice calculations through the unit.

                The Forces Homework Grid provides suggestions for homework that will complement the unit.

                Lesson 8 is a revision lesson which will help students to recap key words and concepts by playing engaging mini-games. There is also an Escape the Room
                lesson which can be used as an additional revision lesson. The Forces Revision Pack contains a knowledge organiser, differentiated revision mats and
                some differentiated practice exam questions.

KS3 Forces      There are two assessment packs to allow you to choose the level that best suits your students. The Higher Assessment Pack contains a more challenging
Unit Overview   version of the assessment, while the Foundation Assessment Pack contains scaffolding for students who may require more support. Both assessment
                packs include evaluation sheets for students to identify their strongest and weakest areas, plus a series of feedforward sheets that students can complete
                in the following lesson to build on their areas for development.

EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:                           Leonardo da Vinci
SCIENCE AS A HUMAN ENDEAVOUR                              VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________


                                                           Leonardo da Vinci was born in Vinci,
                                                           Italy, in 1452. He was a brilliant
                                                           painter—the Mona Lisa and The
                                                           Last Supper are two of his works. It
                                                           was not until centuries after his
                                                           death in 1519 that people realised
                                                           how many technological designs he
                                                           had created.

                                                           Leonardo da Vinci examined the
                                                           structure of the heart by dissecting
                                                           the bodies of oxen and about 30
                                                           human subjects. He discovered that
                                                           the heart has four chambers, when
                                                           at the time it was only believed to
have two. Many of his observations and designs were recorded in back-to-
front mirror writing in his notebooks because he tried to disguise his ideas
from others.

Leonardo embarked on a quest for knowledge in a wide range of areas,
including geology, optics, acoustics, music, botany, hydraulics, anatomy and
naval armaments. He was said to be handsome, generous and charming, but
also unreliable and vain. He stood out in a crowd as he liked to dress in bright,
striking clothing while other men wore long, dark-coloured robes.




Copyright © Pearson Australia 2011 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd) ISBN 978 1 4425 2351 7   Page 1
 His designs for inventions included a self propelling car (shown below), a
crane for emptying ditches, a snorkel for breathing under water, a therapeutic
armchair, folding furniture, a type of armoured tank, a bicycle, spinning and
weaving machines, various weapons, and even a robot with limbs that could
be moved by a series of cables and pulleys. He designed a range of
wonderful but unsuccessful flying machines. Some resembled large butterflies
with four wings and included pedals, stirrups, harnesses, steering cables and
standing platforms. One of his designs could take off vertically and was
powered by a rotating blade—it was perhaps the first helicopter ever
imagined. The designs he imagined were ahead of his time and are evidence
of a great genius.




This self propelling car was just one of Leonardo’s designs. He planned for a series of
gears and leaf springs to power its motion.

Levers

A lever is one of the oldest and simplest machines used by
humans. A lever consists of just two parts - a beam (the long
part) and a fulcrum or pivot (hinge). The beam rotates
(turns) along the fulcrum. Levers are useful because they
allow humans to lift heavy weights by applying a smaller
force.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 3: How were the pyramids constructed? Science as a human endeavour Verbal/Linguistic Name: Class: Date: The great pyramid of Giza, near Cairo, Egypt, was constructed some 4500 years ago. It is believed to have been built by more than 20 000 workers, over a period of 20 years. The pyramid consists of approximately 2 million stone blocks with an average mass over 2 tonnes. It was developed to hold a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu, who ruled Egypt from 2589 to 2566 bc. It is a wonder of engineering how ancient pyramid builders cut, shifted and raised the heavy blocks of stone from which this and other pyramids were built. Some people have even suggested that aliens built the pyramids. Most scientists believe that a system of ramps was used to transport these stone blocks. They have not agreed on how these ramps were used, and a number of theories exist to try to provide an explanation. Theory 1 – Single ramp The pyramid of Giza stands almost 150 metres high. If a single ramp was used, it would need to have an incline no greater than 8 per cent, otherwise it would be too steep to use. For a single ramp to reach the top of the pyramid it would need to be more than 1 km long, and would require as much stone to construct as the pyramid itself. This theory seems unlikely. Theory 2 – External spiral ramp Instead of using a single ramp, it is more likely that a ramp may have spiralled around the pyramid. However, this theory means that the outer edges of the pyramid would not have been visible because they would have been covered by the ramp and scaffolding. The pyramid builders would have needed to check the angles of construction to ensure the pyramid came to a point at the top. As a result, this theory is also questioned. Theory 3 – Internal ramps While watching a documentary about the construction of the pyramids in 1999, Henri Houdin, a retired French civil engineer commented that: ‘If I had to build one now, I would build it from the inside out’. His son Jean-Paul, an architect, travelled to Egypt and created detailed 3-D computer models to investigate whether the pyramids could have been constructed using a system of internal ramps. The diagram on the following page outlines the steps in Jean-Paul Houdin’s internal ramp theory. Jean-Paul hopes to gain permission to explore the site to try to find evidence of internal ramps and tunnels in the pyramid over the years to come. As yet, we still don’t know if any of these theories are correct and there is much debate about the issue. As new theories are proposed and tested, we move a little closer to unlocking a long-held secret. 1 State: a how long the pyramid of Giza took to build. b how many builders assisted in the project. c how many stones were used. d the average mass of these stones. 2 If a single ramp was used, explain why it could not be constructed with an incline greater than 8 per cent. 3 Outline the major problem with the single ramp theory. 4 Using a ramp that spiralled around the pyramid also presents a key problem. Outline this problem. 5 Houdin’s theory sprung from a comment his father made while watching a television documentary. Discuss what this tells us about scientific discovery. 6 Use the diagram on the previous page to answer the following questions about Jean-Paul Houdin’s theory. a What was the purpose of the straight ramp used for the first 16 or so years of the pyramid’s construction? b Explain what happened to the limestone blocks that made up this ramp.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 7 Forces extra worksheet 3: Forces produced by ice and steam Science understanding Verbal/linguistic Cracking ice When water freezes, it expands by 9%.This expansion exerts a force on whatever is around the water. In this case, it was glass, which has shattered. Solid gold metal sinks when dropped into a pot of liquid gold. This happens because as a liquid cools, the tiny particles that make it up move more slowly and usually pack together more closely. Being packed more tightly together, solid gold has greater density than liquid gold. At temperatures below 4°C, when liquid water cools to form ice, something unusual happens. Instead of its particles being packed more closely, they become linked in a more open structure as ice crystals. As a result, the particles take up more space as ice than they do as water. The force of this expansion can crack rocks, burst water pipes and damage the foundations of buildings. Full steam ahead! As water particles are heated, they gain energy and break free of their liquid state. In becoming a gas, the particles move freely to fill the available space. If this space is limited, pressure builds up as more steam is produced. Such pressure can exert a large force if it is suddenly released. Steam under pressure can make can make a saucepan lid jiggle up and down on a pot on the stove. On a larger scale, these forces can be used to power a steam engine, as shown below, or to turn the turbines of a power station. Water inside the boiler of the engine is heated to produce steam. Pressure builds inside the boiler and is released by a valve into the engine. The pressure of the steam pushes the piston in one direction. A valve slides across so that the next burst of steam pushes on the other side of the piston. This movement of the valve enables the flow of steam to push the piston back and forth. The piston is connected to the crankshaft, which turns the wheels of the locomotive. 1 State the percentage by which water expands when it is frozen. 2 Propose why the glass bottle shown in the illustration has cracked. 3 Explain why solid gold metal sinks in liquid gold, but ice does not sink in water. 4 When a person is exposed to very cold conditions, their extremities, such as the fingers and toes, and their face can develop frostbite. Propose how the freezing of water to form ice crystals in the skin can damage the body’s tissues. 5 State whether particles of a liquid gain or lose energy as they are heated. 6 In terms of the particle model, explain why gases spread out to fill the container in which they are held. 7 Recall three situations in which the pressure of steam can be used to apply a force. 8 Propose the purpose of the safety valve in the steam engine shown in the illustration. 9 Predict whether a steam engine would work if the steam was not kept under pressure. Justify your response.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 1: Leonardo da Vinci Science as a human endeavour Verbal/linguistic Name: Class: Date: Leonardo da Vinci was born in Vinci, Italy, in 1452. He was a brilliant painter—the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper are two of his works. It was not until centuries after his death in 1519 that people realised how many technological designs he had created. Leonardo da Vinci examined the structure of the heart by dissecting the bodies of oxen and about 30 human subjects. He discovered that the heart has four chambers, when at the time it was only believed to have two. Many of his observations and designs were recorded in back-to-front mirror writing in his notebooks because he tried to disguise his ideas from others. Leonardo embarked on a quest for knowledge in a wide range of areas, including geology, optics, acoustics, music, botany, hydraulics, anatomy and naval armaments. He was said to be handsome, generous and charming, but also unreliable and vain. He stood out in a crowd as he liked to dress in bright, striking clothing while other men wore long, dark-coloured robes. His designs for inventions included a self propelling car (shown below), a crane for emptying ditches, a snorkel for breathing under water, a therapeutic armchair, folding furniture, a type of armoured tank, a bicycle, spinning and weaving machines, various weapons, and even a robot with limbs that could be moved by a series of cables and pulleys. He designed a range of wonderful but unsuccessful flying machines. Some resembled large butterflies with four wings and included pedals, stirrups, harnesses, steering cables and standing platforms. One of his designs could take off vertically and was powered by a rotating blade—it was perhaps the first helicopter ever imagined. The designs he imagined were ahead of his time and are evidence of a great genius. This self propelling car was just one of Leonardo’s designs. He planned for a series of gears and leaf springs to power its motion. 1 Recall when and where was Leonardo born. 2 State what he was most famous for immediately after his death. 3 a Explain what was unusual about the way Leonardo recorded his ideas in his notebooks. b Propose a reason why he may have done this. 4 a Name three of Leonardo’s designs. b Explain why people often comment that Leonardo da Vinci was ahead of his time. 5 a Propose why the desire to fly has fascinated people for so long. b Recall the flying machine that is used today that is similar to a sketch made by da Vinci. 6 Imagine that you are Leonardo da Vinci, alive and well in Australia today. Construct a sketch of an invention that you think may be in use by the end of your lifetime.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 8 Machines extra worksheet 2: Why do you weigh more on shag carpet? Science Understanding Verbal/linguistic Name: Class: Date: Want to gain a few kilograms? Just weigh yourself on shag carpet! People have long realised that if they put their bathroom scales onto carpet, particularly with thick pile, they too pile on the weight. The scales read about 10% more than if the scales were placed on a hard floor. To discover why this happens, we need to look more closely at what is happening inside the scales. Four levers extend inwards from the corners and cross over in its centre. Multiple levers are used to better distribute a person’s weight. When a person stands on the scales, these levers transfer the person’s weight to a spring-loaded metal plate. If we imagine all four levers operating as a single lever, the following illustration shows how they operate inside the scales. Because the distance from the fulcrum to the load is much shorter than the distance from the fulcrum to the effort, the spring experiences a much smaller force through the levers than if these were not used. Using the levers allows the spring to be much lighter in weight. A rack and pinion system converts the motion of the metal plate into the reading on the circular dial. Now we see how a set of scales work, so why do they read differently when placed on shag carpet? On a hard surface, the base of the scales bows downwards by a small amount and the fulcrum tilts in slightly. As a result, the scales record a slightly shorter distance between the load and the fulcrum than they would if the fulcrum was not tilted. On thick carpet, however, this base is supported and stays flat. The corresponding distance between the load and the fulcrum is now slightly increased (see the illustration below). This is increase is translated on the scales as an increase in mass, and the scales register a higher reading. Bathroom scales are actually calibrated on a hard floor, so this is where they give a true reading. So, if you’re ever trying to lose weight, don’t go near shag carpet! 1 State whether the lever in a set of bathroom scales is a first-, second- or third-class lever. 2 Explain why four levers are used instead of a single lever. 3 Describe how using these levers allows a much lighter spring to be used rather than the spring that would be required without the levers. 4 In terms of the distance from the fulcrum to the load and the distance from the fulcrum to the effort, explain why the effort force produced is much smaller than the load force. 5 Describe the role of the rack and pinion gear system in the scales. 6 State whether the distance from the load to the fulcrum is greater when scales are placed on hard floor or shag carpet. 7 Describe the difference this makes to the reading on the scales.
