title: I am Joe's heart
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿I am Joe's Heart I'm certainly no Beauty. I weigh 400grams, am red-brown colour and have an unimpressive shape. I am the dedicated slave of you. I hang by ligaments in the centre of his chest. I am about 15 cm long and, at my widest point, 10 cm across-more pear-shaped than valentine. Whatever you may have heard about me from poets, I am really not a very romantic character. I am just a hard working four-chambered pump-actually two pumps, one to move blood to the lungs, the other to push it out and into the body. Every day, I would say, I pump blood through 96,000 kilometres of blood vessels. That's enough pumping to fill an 18,000 litre tank car. When Joe thinks of me at all, he thinks of me as fragile and delicate. Delicate! When so far in his life I have pumped more than 300,000 tons of blood? I work twice as hard as the leg muscles of a dash runner, or the arm muscle of a heavyweight boxing champ. Let them try to go at my pace and they would turn to jelly in minutes. No muscles in the body are as strong as I am-except those of a woman's uterus as she expels a baby. But uterine muscles don't keep at in day and night for 70 years, as I am expected to do. That, of course, is a slight exaggeration. I do rest-between beats. It takes about three tenths of a second for my big left ventricle to contract and push blood out into the body. Then I have a rest period of half a second. Joe almost never thinks of me-which is good. I don't want him to become one of those heart neurotics and worry us both into real trouble. When he does worry about me it is almost always about the wrongs things. One night, as he was drifting off to sleep, Joe was listening to my quiet thumping-that's the opening and closing of my valves-and he thought he heard me "skip" a beat. He was quite worried. Was I giving out on him? He needn't have been concerned. From time to time, my ignition system gets momentarily out of whack-just like the ignition system on Joe's car. I generate my own electricity , and send out impulses to trigger contraction. But occasionally I will misfire, piling one beat on top of another. It sounds as if I have "skipped"-but I haven't. Joe would be surprised how often this happens when he isn't listening. After a nightmare he sometimes wakes up and worries because I am racing. That's because when he runs for his life in his dreams, I run too. Joe's worries actually aggravates things-makes me go still faster. If he would calm down, so would I. But if he can't, there is a way to slow me down. The vagus nerves act as a brake. They pass up through the neck-behind the ears, at the hinge of the jaws. Gentle massage here will slow my beat. Joe blames almost everything on me-fatigue, dizzy spells and such. But I have little to do with his fatigue, and his occasional dizzy spells usually trace to his ears. From time to time he will be doing his desk work, and will get a sharp pain in the chest. He fears that he is about to have a heart attack. He needn't worry. That pain comes from his digestive tract-payment for the heavy meal eaten a couple of hours earlier. When I am in trouble, I usually send out a pain signal only after undue exertion of emotion. That's the way I tell him I am not getting enough nourishment to carry the work he is loading on me. Joe had a heart attack five years ago and didn't even know it. He was too busy to notice that tiny twinge of pain in his chest. The artery that clogged was a small one on my rear wall. It took me two weeks to sweep away the dead tissue and repave the area with a scar not much larger than a pea. Joe comes from a family where heart disease has occurred often, so statistics say that I am going to give him trouble, too. Of course, he can't do anything about his heredity. But he can do a lot to minimize the risk. Let's start with overweight. Joe is getting extra padding around the middle and jokes about his middle-age spread. It's no laughing matter. Every kilogram of his excess fat contains something like 640 km of capillaries which I have to push blood through. And that is in addition to the work of carrying around each extra pound. And that brings me to Joe's blood pressure. It's 140/90-the upper limit of normal for his age. The 140 measures the pressure I work against while contracting, and the 90 is the pressure while I am resting between beats. the lower figure is the more important. The higher that figure rises, the less rest I get. And without adequate rest a heart simply works itself to death. Joe could give me a break in other ways. He is a competitive, driving, worrying sort of fellow-you know, the successful-businessman type. He doesn't realize that his constant fretting continually stimulates his adrenal glands to produce more adrenaline and noradrenalin. If Joe relaxes, I relax. Exercise is another thing. Joe is one of those weekend athletes who take it in big doses. He still like that rushing-up-to-the-net bit in tennis, as if he were a college boy. When he does this, my work load goes up as high as five times normal. What Joe should be doing is taking regular, mild exercise. A walk of a mile or two a day would help. Climbing a couple of flights of stairs to his office wouldn't hurt either. His office is on the tenth floor, but he could walk up the first two flights and then catch the elevator. Little things like that would do a lot. Fatty deposits are already beginning to block some of my arteries. This regular exercise causes new blood pathways to develop. Then if one artery closes down there are others to nourish me. I'm not the demanding type. I'll do the best I can for Joe under any circumstances. Just the same, there are those breaks he could give me: slim down a bit, take regular exercises, relax a little more, cut down on fats and smoking. If he would only do those things, I could keep on working for Joe for a long time. Questions Using the above article, your text and general knowledge answer the following questions. 1. Why do animals need a heart? 2. It has often been said your heart is the size of your fist. Use the information in the above and a ruler to find if this is accurate. Write a comment to explain what you found. 3. Why is your pulse rate not constant? 4. Why do you think fit athletes have a lower resting heart rate? 5. Some say we love with our hearts. Explain why you think this is an unreasonable suggestion. 6. What is a heart attack? 7. Why do you think a person's blood pressure increases as they gain weigh? 8. Why does worrying negatively affect your heart? (use the term adrenalin in your answer) 9. What causes a heart to beat? 10. Draw the flow of blood through the heart on the diagram below and label as many of the parts of the heart you can.

reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Incredible Edible Cell Purpose: You will use several different food items representing the various organelles or cell structures found in plant and animal cells to construct an edible cell model. This activity will help you learn more about the different parts of a cell and their functions. Background: All cells have a cell membrane , which forms a barrier to separate the cell from its environment . The cell membrane surrounds a gel-like fluid called cytoplasm , which is the medium that holds all the organelles of the cell. The large nucleus of a cell is similar to your brain because it functions as the cell’s control centre . The nucleus contains genetic material that is used as instructions for directing cell functions. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) surrounds the nucleus and helps to form and move proteins throughout the cell. Attached to the ER are ribosomes , which produce proteins and can also be found floating elsewhere in the cytoplasm. The “p owerhouses” of the cell are the mitochondria , which convert food energy to usable energy. Water, food, and other materials are stored in vacuoles . Chloroplasts are present only in pant cells and are the site for photosynthesis. Materials: Milk Arrowroot biscuit, Milk Coffee biscuit, icing, a pop stick, 2x jaffas , 4 jelly beans, 2 x green tic tac or mini m&m , 6 small strips of liquorice, some 100’s & 1000’s. Procedures: Do NOT eat any of the materials unless given permission by your instructor!! Use gloves when handling food items! Draw a table into your lab notebook, completing the table by filling in the main function of each organelle – nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, cytoplasm, chloroplast, endoplasmic reticulum, ribosomes. Label the edge of a piece of paper with your name and each cell type (animal or plant) , and a legend indicating which lolly will represent each organelle 1857375 130810 Animal Plant Name Legend Animal Plant Name Legend If you are making an animal cell, use a milk arrowroot base. If you are making a plant cell, use a milk coffee base Spread frosting evenly over the base to represent the cytoplasm. Assemble your model by sticking the appropriate “organelles” into the “cytoplasm,” showing correct spatial relationships between different types of organelles. Extension Questions: Given the function of mitochondria, what ti ssue might contain cells with a high concentration of mitochondria? Why? Why could a cell be called “the functional unit of life?” Why is it important to have a cell membrane when there is a cell wall? How is t he nucleus the “command centre” of the cell?

searchText:
Investigating bones

 Teaching notes

Suggested starter activity

Establish that bones need to be strong to support the weight of our body by
discussing the size and shape of the femurs.

Demonstrate the need for their shape by showing that a rolled paper tower will
support a pile of books.

Show that bones need to be flexible by hanging a weight on a straw and a
thick, brittle length of spaghetti. Stress that brittle bones break easily and ask
if anyone knows about brittle bone disease.

Main activity

NB: A risk assessment should be carried out before this practical is used with
students. See CLEAPPS (www.cleapss.org.uk) for further information. When
heating the bone goggles should be worn at all times as they may shatter. As
an alternative bones could be heated in an oven prior to the lesson. If using
chicken bones which may be contaminated with salmonella ask students to
wash their hands thoroughly after handling them.

Students should work in groups of 2 or 3.

Each group will need:


      worksheet
      2 bone samples
      Bunsen burner
      heatproof mat
      splint
      goggles
      metal tongs
      beaker




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2015        24274                              Page 1 of 4
                                                            Investigating bones



Ask students to note down their initial observations of the bone. Then discuss
the second section of worksheet. Stress need for careful handling of bone in
flame as too tight a squeeze will shatter the hot bone! Goggles must be worn
at all time and hot bone must be left on the mat.




Further activities



Research and write notes on brittle bone disease.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2015      24274                             Page 2 of 4
                                                              Investigating bones




    Bone is a composite material. It needs to be strong but flexible. Its
    strength comes from the mineral, calcium phosphate, and its flexibility
    from an organic material, collagen.




Your task: to investigate the two factors in bone and their effect on
the composite material by removing each material from bone.

Task 1 – initial observation of bone

● Look at your piece of bone and describe it in words.
● Draw your sample labelling any features that you notice.
● Feel the bone and describe its texture and flexibility.

Task 2 – removing the collagen

You can roast the collagen out of the bone.

● Hold the fresh piece of bone in tongs and place in the hottest part of the
  Bunsen flame.
● Move the bone about in the flame until the bone becomes blackened.
● Carefully place the very hot bone onto a heatproof mat and leave it to cool.
● Write up your investigation so far; include a labelled diagram to show how
  you heated the bone.
● When it has cooled down handle the bone and compare it with your initial
  observations.

Task 3 – removing the calcium phosphate

You can use a chemical reaction to remove this from bone.

● Put your piece of bone into a beaker so that it lies comfortably across the
  bottom.
● Carefully pour some vinegar or lemon juice to cover the bone.
● Label your beaker and place on the windowsill for two or three days.
● Write up your investigation so far; include a fully labelled diagram of the
  bone in the acid.
© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2015       24274                             Page 3 of 4
                                                             Investigating bones


After 2 or 3 days:

● Have a beaker of water ready on your table.
● Collect your bone in its beaker and very carefully use tongs to remove it
  from the acid and rinse it thoroughly in the beaker of water.
● Place your rinsed bone onto a paper towel.
● Handle your rinsed bone and compare it to your initial observations.

searchText:
Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?

Aim
To find out how the strength of a tube of paper (bone) changes as its length
increases. I will do this by hanging weights on the ‘bone’ until it breaks.

Independent and dependent variables
A variable is something in your experiment that changes. It may change
because you change it (this is the independent variable) or it could change
as a result of doing the experiment and you are going to measure this change
(the dependent variable).

Tasks
A.    For this investigation, write down the independent and the dependent
      variable.
          independent variable – the variable you are going to control.
          dependent variable – the variable that you will measure when you do
           the experiment.

B.    Draw a table to input the following data (choose the appropriate units for
      each entry);
          length of bone (there are 5 lengths to investigate)
          diameter of bone
          mass needed to break bone.

C.    You do not want any other variables to change. These are control
      variables and must be kept the same. Read through the method below
      and write down the control variables.

D.    Make five paper bones using the following instructions. The bones should
      be of different lengths – 20cm, 30cm, 40cm, 50cm and 60cm.
      1.   Take the longest paper (60cm) and roll it up tightly around a pencil.
      2.   Use a 5cm length of sellotape to hold the curled paper in place in the
           middle. Remove the pencil.
      3.   Measure the diameter of the bone accurately.
      4.   Mark the mid-point of the ‘bone’.
      5.   Repeat this for each of the bones.
      6.   Remember they should all be made using paper of the same width
           and rolled to the same diameter.
      7.   We will assume the thickness of each piece of paper is the same.

E.    Test the strength of the bones using the following
      method.
      1.   Set up the stands as shown in the diagram.
      2.   Rest the longest (60cm) bone on the clamps.

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013        20719                           Page 1 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?
    3.   Hang a 100g weight on the midpoint of the bone.
    4.   Keep adding weights until the ‘bone’ breaks (bends).
    5.   Record the data in your table.
    6.   Repeat steps 5-8 with the other 4 lengths of bone.
    7.   Draw a graph of your results and make a conclusion.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013    20719                        Page 2 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?

Teaching notes

Context
Students investigate how the strength of a tube of paper (bone) changes as its
length increases. They do this by hanging weights on the mid-point of the
‘bone’ until it breaks (bends). This investigation could feature whilst teaching a
topic on bones, joints or movement, but it is meant to build on their practical
skills. It requires students to do the following;

    -     identify an independent and dependent variable
    -     pick out control variables and understand why this is important
    -     draw a table for their results
    -     carry out an investigation in a methodical way and record accurate
          data
    -     draw a graph of the data with a line of best fit
    -      make a conclusion.

ISAs at GCSE level require students to understand and use variables.
The teacher can discuss the different types of variables with the students –
independent, dependent and control variables.

In this investigation the variables are;

         independent – length of bone
         dependent – mass required to break the bone
         control – diameter of bone, width of paper, length of sellotape,
          weights put onto midpoint of bone, paper thickness, overhang of bone
          on clamp.

Emphasis should be placed on the need to make the test valid. If more than
one independent variable were to change, the experiment would not be valid.

Equipment per group
         2 x retort stands, clamps and bosses.
         100g weights with holder and hook (wide enough to hang over the
          bone)
         5 x 5cm lengths of sellotape
         ruler
         5 sheets of paper (one each of the following dimensions):  20cm x
          21cm
          30cm x 21cm
          40cm x 21cm
          50cm x 21cm
          60cm x 21cm.


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013        20719                           Page 3 of 4
     Investigation – how does the length of a bone affect its strength?
The paper used in the experiment should be cut to size before the lesson and
preferably marked with an arrow to indicate the way it should be rolled up.

The investigation can get a bit noisy with falling weights so encourage your
students to put their hands under the weights to catch them.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013      20719                           Page 4 of 4

 Information sheet

We know that our kidneys are responsible for removing waste from our bodies but they also play a vital role in maintaining the
precise composition of fluids in our bodies. This is known as osmoregulation and is an example of homeostasis. Through
filtration, re-absorption and secretion they ensure the proportion of water, ions and other solutes in the body fluid remains
balanced.


      Every minute 1 200 ml of blood is processed by the kidneys. The capillaries of the glomerulus filter blood. Large cells and
      molecules such as red blood cells and proteins remain in the capillaries whilst blood plasma which contains dissolved
      substances, is filtered out. In all, about 180 litres of filtrate is formed each day. This is an enormous amount of fluid on its
      way to be stored in the bladder and it is important that most of the water from it is re-absorbed, returning to the
      bloodstream or the person would quickly become dehydrated.

      The glomerulus is not where the re-absorption of water and solutes is controlled. Experiments show there is no link between
      the amount of filtrate produced by the glomerulus and the amount of urine produced.

      The re-absorption of water and solutes is regulated further along the kidney tubule. The hormone ADH controls the
      permeability of the walls of the collecting ducts. When the walls are made more permeable in response to ADH, more water
      is reabsorbed from the urine by osmosis. A small volume of urine is produced and it is more concentrated.

      If a person has had a drink or has not been sweating much there is relatively more water in their blood stream. Less ADH is
      released. The walls of the collecting ducts become less permeable and no water is removed from the urine. A greater
      volume of dilute urine is produced.

      The kidneys also control the level of solutes (dissolved substances) in our blood.
      Although glucose is present in the filtrate from the glomerulus, it is not usually
      present in urine. Glucose is re-absorbed into the blood stream. It is moved into
      the capillaries by active transport.

      Sodium chloride is also moved out of the kidney tubules by active transport.
      Unlike osmosis and diffusion, active transport requires energy to 'carry' the salt
      molecules across the cell membrane. So, although they are relatively small
      organs, the kidneys require a significant amount of energy to function.
 Kidney questions


  1. Why do you think the word for 'bladder' originates from a word which means 'to blow'?

  2. Many small structures found inside the body have names which were first used in the 1600's. What invention
     might have contributed towards the discovery of these structures? Explain your answer by using an example.

  3. Negative feedback is quite a tricky concept to describe. Imagine trying
     to explain it to your parents or carers. Can you make it simple by
     describing an 'every day' example of negative feedback?

  4. List two important functions of the kidneys.

  5. The job of the glomerulus is quite simple. Can you explain what it does?

  6. Where is most of the work of the kidney carried out?

  7. Kidneys make up only 0.4% of our body mass yet they use 10% of the
     energy produced by the body. Why is this?

  8. Why do we need kidneys?
 Teaching notes

Activity instructions:

   1. Working in groups, students draw graphs from the data sheet in tables A, B and C.
   2. Ask them to describe in simple terms what the graphs are showing.
   3. Then read the text as a group or whole class.
   4. Students then match the graphs and tables to relevant parts of the text, providing evidence for the statements made.
   5. Students can then answer the questions.


Suggested answers - kidney questions

   1. Bladders were used as the first footballs and had to be inflated.
   2. The microscope was being used around this time. Many structures are too small to be seen with the naked eye, e.g.
      capillaries. They would have been visible for the first time under a microscope and their discoverers would have given them
      names e.g. the glomerulus would have looked like a ball of thread.
   3. You are talking too loudly in class; teacher tells you to talk more quietly; you drop the volume a bit; the teacher continues to
      tell you to talk more quietly until your voice is an appropriate volume; the teacher stops giving you the instruction to talk
      more quietly; the drop in your volume is being fed back to and monitored by the teacher who continues to issue instructions
      (hormones like ADH) until the appropriate level is restored.
   4. Removal of waste e.g. urea; regulating salt and water levels; balancing proportions of water and solutes; osmoregulation;
      homeostasis
   5. The glomerulus filters blood allowing a large proportion of blood plasma to pass out of the capillaries and into the kidney
      tubules. It prevents red blood cells and most proteins from leaving the blood stream.
   6. Further along the kidney tubule, in the loop of Henle and collecting duct.
   7. A large amount of blood plasma is filtered by the kidneys every hour. The filtered liquid contains dissolved substances such
      as ions and glucose. Most of these solutes are needed by the body and have to be re-absorbed. The solutes are moved by
      active transport which requires energy.
   8. Kidneys are essential for removing waste products from the blood stream and for maintaining the correct water/solute
 balance in the body

Find a Friend: Leaf Structure and Function Activity

Teacher Instructions

This activity is good for consolidating or checking learning in a plenary or for revision.
Cards can be printed out A4 or A5 and laminated for repeated use.

How to use:
There are 3 types of card:

* — orange - diagram (with a part labelled as X);
« — blue - name of a part;
* green - description or function of a part.

Give each student in the class one of the cards. This can be random or differentiated by giving easier cards
to weaker students and more tricky cards to higher-ability students. Unused cards can be put onto a table
for students to go to if they can't find their ‘friends’. Where there are more students than cards, give one
card to a pair of students.

Students should then move around the room and find their two ‘friends’ with the matching diagram,
name and function. This encourages discussion and students that are unsure can get help from
their peers.

Once the students have found their friends, the cards can be stuck onto a board, wall or window to form a
display that students can refer to if necessary.

searchText: Levels of Structural Organization in the Human Body The human body has 6 main levels of structural organization. We will begin this lesson with the simplest level within the structural hierarchy. Chemical level– is the simplest level within the structural hierarchy. The chemical level includes the tiniest building blocks of matter, atoms, which combine to form molecules, like water. In turn, molecules combine to form organelles, the internal organs of a cell. Cellular level– the cellular level is made up of the smallest unit of living matter, the cell. Individual cells may have some common functions but vary widely in size and shape. Each type of cells carries out a set of unique tasks within the human body. Tissue level– Tissues are groups of similar cells that have a common function. A tissue must contain two different types of cells. The four basic tissue types in humans include epithelium, connective, muscle, and nervous tissue. Each tissue has a characteristic role within the human body which we will discuss later. Organ level– an organ is a structure composed of at least two different tissue types that perform a specific function within the body. Examples include the brain, stomach, and liver. Complex functions begin to emerge at this level. Levels of structural organization that make up the human body. Organ system level– One or more organs work in unison to accomplish a common purpose. For instance, the heart and blood vessels work together and circulate blood throughout the body to provide oxygen and nutrients to cells. Besides the cardiovascular system, the other organ systems of the body are the integumentary, skeletal, nervous, muscular, endocrine, respiratory, lymphatic, digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems. Organismal level– The organismal level is the highest level of organization. It is the sum total of all structural levels working together. In short, it is the human being (or organism) as a whole. Review  Name the six different levels of structural organization in the human body and explain their relationships.  List the 11 organ systems of the human body and explain their major functions. Check your understanding. Answer the questions below using complete sentences. 1. In the hierarchy, at which level of structural organization would an immunologist’s field of study be considered? Why? 2. What is the correct structural order of the following terms: atom, organ, cell, organism, tissue? 3. Which organ system includes the heart and blood vessels? Which organ system includes the kidneys? 4. List the order of the levels of organization in biological life forms from simplest to most complex and give an example of something from each level of the scale. This system was developed in France in 1791 and was updated in 1960. The metric system is based on multiples of 10. Each type of measurement (length, mass, volume, energy, and so on) has a base unit. Larger and smaller units are named by adding a prefix to the base unit. For example, the basic unit of length is the metre. The prefix is kilo- means multiplied by 1000, so one kilometer is 1000 metre. The prefix milli- means divided by 1000, so one millimeter is one thousandth of a metre. 1 The table shows the most commonly used metric prefixes. Prefix Symbol Relationship to the Base Unit 9 giga- G 10 = 1 000 000 000 mega- M 106 = 1 000 000 kilo- k 103 = 1000 hecto- h 102 = 100 deca- da 101 = 10 100 = 1 deci- d 10-1 = 0.1 centi- c 10-2 = 0.01 milli- m 10-3 = 0.001 micro- F 10-6 = 0.000 001 nano- n 19-9 = 0.000 000 001 Conversion factors: 1 cm = 10 mm 1 mm = 1000 Fm 1 cm = 10 000 Fm = 10 -2 m = 10 -3 m = 10 -6 m Complete the following conversions: a) 2.7 cm = ___________ mm b) 1.5 mm = ___________ Fm c) 26.1 mm = _______________Fm d) 19.2 cm = ___________ mm e) 0.30 mm = ______________Fm f) 4.2 Fm = ______________ mm g) 30 mm = ______________ cm h) 10 Fm = _______________ cm i) 0.0574 cm = ___________ Fm j) 645 Fm = _______________ mm 2 The circle of light seen through the microscope is called the field of view. It is the area of a slide that you can observe. The distance across the field of view is called the field diameter. The actual measurements for the field diameters of objectives lenses on the microscopes are known, they are listed below on the table: objective lens Field diameter Field diameter (mm) (Fm) 4x 4.5 10 x 1.8 1800 40 x 0.45 2. To calculate the actual size of the object a. Place objects at the edge of the field of view. b. Estimate how many of the objects fit across the diameter of the field of view. c. Record the objective lens that has been used and the diameter of this objective lens (from the table above). Calculate the actual size by using the following formula: Actual Size of Specimen = field diameter # of specimens fitting across the field diameter Example 1: A student was examining strands of his hair under a microscope at medium power, (∴field diameter = 1800 µm ). He estimated that when measured width-wise, 20 strands of his hair would fit across the diameter of the field of view. What is the actual width of each hair strand? Actual Size of Specimen = field diameter # of specimens fitting across the field diameter = 1800 µm 20 = 90 µm ∴ each hair is 90 µm in width Example 2: A cheek cell as observed through the 4x objective lens, (∴field diameter = 4.5 mm ). The number of cheek cell that were estimated to fit across the diameter of field of view were 3.5 Estimate the actual width of the cheek cell. State your answer in mm. (Answer: width of the cheek cell = 1.3 mm) 3 3. To calculate the magnification of a drawing Magnification: the comparison of the actual size of the object with the size of its image is referred to as magnification. To calculate the magnification of a drawing a. Record the actual size of the specimen from the above calculations. b. With a ruler measure the length of the drawing of the specimen in the same direction as you estimated the size of the object. This is the drawing size. c. Calculate the magnification of the drawing using the following formula: Magnification of drawing = width of drawing (measured with a ruler) Actual size of specimen Example 1 (See: Calculation 2, Example 1 above) A student was examining strands of his hair under a microscope at medium power, (∴field diameter = 1800 µm ). He estimated that when measured width-wise, 20 strands of his hair would fit across the diameter of the field of view. a. What is the actual width of each hair strand ? Answer: each hair is 90 µm in width. b. Next, the student made a scaled drawing of his hair. He then measured the width of his drawing. It measured 4 mm. What was the magnification of the drawing ? Magnification of drawing = width of drawing (measured with a ruler) Actual size of specimen = 4mm 90 µm = 4000 µm 90 µm = 45 ∴the diagram represents a 45X magnification of the actual specimen 4 Assignment Answer the following questions, showing all the steps. 1. A student is looking at a piece of string using the high power objective lens. She estimates that 5 pieces of string fit width-wise across the field of view. Calculate the width of each piece of string. (Answer: width of each strand = 90 µm) 2. Another student is observing onion cells using the high power objective lens. She estimates that three cells fit across the field diameter width-wise. a. Calculate the actual size of one cell. (Answer: 2.a. Size of one cell = 150 µm) b. The student draws the cell diagram, she determines the width on one onion cell to be 22 mm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing. (Answer: 2.b. Magnification of the drawing = 145x) 3. A student learned that the actual size of a specimen she was examining was 150 µm. She estimated that 10.5 specimens would fit across the field diameter. What objective lens was most likely used. (Answer: objective lens most likely used was 10x) 4. The actual length of a specimen was determined to 795 µm. How long would a diagram of the specimen be if the diagram represented a 180x magnification of the specimen? express your answer in centimeters. (Answer: specimen drawing143100 µm, = 14.3 cm) 5. Ten perfectly square grains of sand were found to fit across the field diameter when the 10x objective lens was in place. a. What is the actual size of a grain of sand ? (Answer: 5.a. Actual size of one grain of sand = 180 µm) b. If the grain of sand was magnified 100 x, how wide was the grain of sand in the drawing ? (Answer: 5.b. specimen drawing = 1.8 cm) 5

 Name: ________________________                           Date: ______________________


HANDOUT 5.1-2: FUNCTIONS OF MICROSCOPE PARTS
Ocular: This is the eyepiece lens that usually magnifies by a power of 10. (Note: To determine
the power of the microscope, one multiplies the power of the ocular by the power of the
objective lens being used.)

High-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the longer of the objectives. Its
lens has a magnifying power usually of 43.

Low-power objective: It is located just above the stage. It is the shorter objective. Its lens has
a magnifying power usually of 10.

Stage: This is a horizontal platform just below the objectives that supports the microscope slide
for observation.

Revolving nosepiece: The objective lenses are attached to this part. It can be manually rotated
to select the objective lens that you wish to use.

Stage clips: They clamp over the edges of the microscope slide to secure it to the stage.

Diaphragm (or condenser): Located just below the stage, it can be hand adjusted to regulate
the amount of light entering the microscope. An image viewed through the microscope should
not be dark but should have plenty of light.

Mirror: This is adjusted to reflect light from the microscope lamp up into the microscope.
Although the mirror is sometimes used to regulate the amount of light entering the microscope,
this is not good technique.

Coarse adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is always used first, and it is used
only with the low-power objective.

Fine adjustment: This is used to focus the microscope. It is used with the high-power objective
to “fine tune” the focus.

Arm: This is the back of the microscope and it is used along with the base to transport the
microscope.

Base: This is the bottom of the microscope and it is used along with the arm to transport the
microscope.

Note: Both eyes should be open when viewing through the microscope. This prevents eye
fatigue, which occurs when the non-viewing eye is kept closed. Keeping both eyes open does
take some practice, but it is highly recommended.

searchText:
Modelling the circulatory system

Starter

The PowerPoint or interactive could be used as a quick labelling activity to introduce
the modelling activity.


Modelling the circulatory system

Depending on the group the students could be asked to design their own simulation
using the following resources.

Resources
    –    2 large hoops
    –    100 red and blue cards
    –    2 boxes/bucket
    –    labels for heart, lungs and cells


Task

Assign students to a role: Lungs (1 person), cells (1 person), heart (2 people to hold
hoops), blood (rest of class or a smaller group).

Arrange students around the room (refer to animation on slide 4).
Students move around to represent blood flow – picking up red cards at the lungs;
going through the hoop (heart); dropping off the red cards at the cells and picking up
blue cards; returning back through the heart (hoop) to lungs and dropping of blue
cards.
The circulation will stop when all the blue cards are at the lungs and the red cards are
at the cells.


Discussion

There are many difficulties with this model. Get the students to recognise some of
them and suggest how the model could be improved. The following questions could
be asked to stimulate discussion.

Did the model show how oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood? – oxygen
in red blood cells, carbon dioxide dissolved in plasma.

In the model circulation stopped, why does this not happen in reality? – discuss that
concentration gradients are maintained in lungs due to gas exchange and blood flow
and in cells due to respiration.

Was the movement of the blood realistic in the model? – discuss network of blood
vessels.

Ask students to draw the model and evaluate it.

Activity sheet – Cells


What are cells?
All living things are made up of tiny parcels of matter called cells. Cells are the smallest
units of living things. This is why they are sometimes called the building blocks of life.
  Living things may be made up of just one cell or many billions of cells. Anything that is
made up of one or more cells is considered a form of life or lifeform.
    The bodies of all types of animals, including humans, are made up of cells. Different
types of cells have different functions or jobs. Human bodies are made up of hundreds of
different types of cells, including types of blood cells, nerve cells and skin cells.
   All types of plants are made up of cells, too. Plant cells and animal cells have some
similar parts and some different parts.

    controls what the cell does
    cytoplasm (say ‘site-o-plaz-em’) – the main fluid substance inside a cell, which helps protect the cell’s contents
    cell membrane (say ‘sell mem-brain’) – the thin skin around an animal or plant cell that holds the cell together

searchText:
Activity sheet – Cells


Animal cells
Most types of animal cells have a centre called a nucleus near their middle, which is
surrounded by a jelly-like substance called cytoplasm. Around this is the cell membrane.
   Cells also contain things called proteins and organelles. Proteins are a special kind of
nutrient that are an essential part of all living things. Organelles are tiny, living machines that
are found inside cells. The organelles perform various jobs to keep the cell alive. Types of
organelles include:
    ● mitochondria, which provide energy for the cell to use
    ● ribosomes, which are like protein factories
    ● vacuoles, which are water-filled organelles that can have many functions
    ● Golgi bodies, which process proteins.

searchText:
Activity sheet – Cells


Plant cells
Like animal cells, most plant cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane. Plant cells
also have a hard cell wall made of cellulose. Also like animal cells, plant cells contain tiny,
living machines called organelles. Golgi bodies and ribosomes are two organelles found in
plant cells. They have special jobs to do in the cell to help the plant grow and to keep it
healthy. Plant cells also contain large water-filled containers called vacuoles.
   Green plants contain important organelles called chloroplasts. These parts have a
chemical called chlorophyll in them. It is green. Green plants get their green colour from
the chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are involved in the way that green plants use sunlight to
produce food, through photosynthesis.

searchText:
Activity sheet – Cells


Cell division
Cells do not last forever. They grow old and eventually die, so they need to be replaced.
For example, skin cells in humans get worn out and are replaced continually. The flaky bits
of dry skin that you scrub away are made of dead skin cells. Underneath this skin, healthy
new skin cells are ready to replace the lost cells.
   Cells also make living things grow bigger or stronger, by producing more of themselves.
For example, a plant grows taller and gets more leaves as new cells are made.
    To make more of themselves, cells separate into two parts that are the same. This is
called cell division. Its scientific name is mitosis.

      1 Use the letters in the circle to complete these forms of the word division.

   old cells and (kill / create) new cells for growth. This process is called mitosis. Through
   mitosis, a (cell / plant) splits into (three / two), creating an (identical / adult) copy of

searchText:
Photosynthesis word challenge
Teaching notes
The aim of this challenge is to make links between a word, image or sound
prompt and the topic of photosynthesis.
The activity helps students explore and extend their understanding of
photosynthesis. It is also useful to highlight misconceptions.
The activity is described here with some examples.
Prior learning: Leaf structure, testing for starch, process and word equation
for photosynthesis.


Running the activity
Students work in groups of two or three.
To keep things moving, have a time limit on responses. Use Teachit Timer (free
to all) to structure the session.
At its simplest:
Students are shown a word prompt and each group has to make a connection
between it and the topic of photosynthesis.
To add more challenge:
      Generate a random number, between one and twelve.
      Select a structure card from a set of three, 'Words', 'Connections’ or
       'Steps'.
The structure cards give the following instructions:
      Words - make a link to photosynthesis using the specified number of
       words.
      Connections - make the specified number of links between the word
       prompt and photosynthesis.
      Steps - using the specified number of short sentences or phrases (joined
       by words such as 'because') get from the word prompt to photosynthesis.


For example:

Word prompt                       Animal
Random number                       2
Structure card                    Steps

In this round, students must link the word 'animal' to the topic of
photosynthesis in two steps.
E.g 'a rabbit' (one step) 'because it eats plants which carry out photosynthesis'
(second step)

Each group receives a set of word-prompt cards, a set of structure cards and

Groups work independently of the class.
They can bring their best links to the class for discussion.

Have a presentation ready to use with the class (see the PowerPoint for

searchText:
Plant pops
Teaching notes

This activity is designed to give students a sense of the challenges facing ecologists when
assessing the population of different plants.

This activity, with elements of a competitive game, is a useful alternative when a field trip
or access to the school field is not possible.

The aim is to assess the accuracy of using quadrats as a technique for estimating the
population of a plant species. The activity helps students understand the significance of
positioning quadrats randomly and that populations can only be estimated as it is not
possible in practice, to count all the individuals in an area.

However, this activity is not designed to be an accurate representation of how quadrats
are used in the field. It is a fun activity to do on a wet day which will get students thinking.

The activity is based on the game ‘Battleships’.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              20087                                   Page 1 of 6
                                                                            Plant pops
Preparation

Equipment per pair of students:

     X2 sheets of blank grids
     stopwatch
     pencil

Each student should have a sheet of blank grids. The first blank grid on the sheet is to
record the distribution of the plants in their survey area. The second blank grid is their
record of the ‘throws’ they have made onto their partner’s sample area.

The grids represent plots of land. You could assign a specific habitat to the plots e.g.
saltmarsh, woodland, chalk downland, water meadow, heathland, sand dune.

A home learning task could be given as preparation for this activity. Students could find
images of a plant species linked to one or more of the habitats listed above. They could
write a description of the plant and it’s habitat in their own words, using more than one
source of information. They should write a list of references at the end.

Some suggestions of plants:

        Sea lavender Limonium vulgare – saltmarsh
        wood sorrel Oxalis acetosella – woodland
        wild thyme Thymus praecox – chalk downland
        creeping buttercup Ranunculus repens – water meadow
        tormentil Potentilla erecta – heathland
        eyebright Euphrasia sp – sand dune.

A follow-on home learning task could involve students finding out how ecologists working
in the field, ensure that they have placed their quadrats randomly; or they could research
other methods of surveying plants.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013            20087                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                 Plant pops
The activity

 Explain to students that their grids represent areas of land and that they are going to
investigate the most effective way of estimating the population of a certain species of
plant, using a quadrat. For convenience, the ‘quadrat’ is the same size as one square on
the grid.

 From the beginning they will know the actual population size of the plant species. Explain
that there are constraints on ecologists working in the field and that they do not have the
resources to count all the individual plants in the area. How many random throws of the
quadrat will give the best estimate?

Play

  I.   Decide for the class what percentage of the grid is to be occupied by the plant
       species. Each square is 4% of the whole, so choose multiples of 4, e.g. 32% = 8
       squares.

 II.   Without showing others, students shade in the required number of squares on their
       first grid. The plants may be regularly spaced, clustered or concentrated in one
       small region.

III.   Player 1 gives coordinates for a square, player 2 puts a cross through the square on
       their coloured grid and says if a ‘hit’ has been made. Player 1 marks the square on
       their empty grid to show if it was a hit or a miss.

       Each turn represents one throw of the quadrat.

       Play continues as Player 2 now gives the coordinates for a square.

       In this initial game, play continues until all the plants have been found on one of the
       grids. Students need to time how long this takes.

IV.    Class discussion

       How long did it take them to find all the plants on one grid? How many ‘throws’ of
       the quadrat do they feel would have given a reliable estimate of the population?

       What do they feel is a reliable figure? +/– 5% or 10%? What might it depend on?

       Plants may not be evenly spread over the area of the grid. Will the reliability of their
       estimate compromised by the positioning of the plants?

V.     Now they are ready to investigate further. Students can decide to limit the number

Preparing Unstained Red Onion Cells for a
Microscope Slide

Method
1.   Cut off a small piece of red onion
2.   Use forceps or your fingernail to peel away a very thin layer of skin from the inside
3.   Spread and smooth the onion skin flat on the middle of the microscope slide
4.   Add 2 - 3 drops of distilled water
5.   Carefully place a cover slip over the skin
6.   Gently dab the edges with a paper towel to absorb any excess solution
7.   Place the microscope slide onto the stage and secure with the stage clips
8.   Ensure the magnification is at the lowest setting to begin with (usually 4x or 10x)

9.   Use the adjustment knobs to focus on and observe the cell at a higher magnification

Method
1.   Cut off a small piece of onion
2.   Use forceps or your fingernail to peel away a very thin layer of skin from the inside

Plenary activities

1. Microscopy – taboo (pages 12-13)

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the keyword
at the top of your card. This must be accomplished without using the word itself or any
of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card. Before the lesson, copy
and cut up the taboo cards; each group of students will need a set.

 1. Students work in groups of at least four. Give each group a set of cards. Each
    group then splits into two teams.

 2. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 3. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile and
    describes the word at the top of the card without using the ‘taboo’ words. A
    member of the opposing team could sit by the clue-giver so that they can
    challenge if a taboo word is used. The rest of the clue–givers team must guess
    the word being described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or
    ‘rhymes with’ and no gestures, sounds or drawings are permitted.

 4. Should the clue-giver be correctly challenged or if their team correctly guesses
    the word then they must move on to the next card.

 5. Each clue-giver is allowed one or two minutes to describe as many words as
    possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next team. There
    are no penalties for a wrong guess.

 6. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding other
ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary in addition to
reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term.

Suggested further activities could include:

       meanings of the keywords.

      Give each student a blank card to put a keyword onto. They then write a further

       or group activity.

searchText:
Investigating Seed Dispersal by Wind
Aim: To investigate how effective the drop and roll seed dispersal is.

Equipment:
• Some fruit with seeds, e.g. sycamore fruit

• Metre ruler

• Masking tape

• Electric fan



Method:
Step 1: Decide on a fixed height to drop the fruit from (ensure you are standing on a flat and
stable surface)

Step 2: Make a small cross on the floor below your dropping point, with the masking tape

Step 3: Drop your fruit above the cross, at your fixed
height, one at a time

Step 4: Use your metre ruler to measure how far from
the cross each fruit has travelled

Step 5: Carefully record all your results in a table

Step 6: Repeat the investigation, but this time place
the electric fan about half way up the height of your
dropping point (on a desk will work well), and pointing
to where your fruit will fall. Make sure it is switched
on and at the same speed each time

Step 7: Carefully record all your results in a table



Questions:
 1. Which conditions caused the seeds to be dispersed furthest?

 2. How do you think some fruit and seeds are adapted for wind dispersal?

 3. Why was it important to keep the fan switched on at the same speed?

 4. Other than collecting repeated results, how could you check if your data is reliable?
                                                                         Investigating Seed Dispersal by Wind


Answers:
 1. Which conditions caused the seeds to be dispersed furthest?
    It is expected that the seeds will have dispersed further in the windy conditions.

 2. How do you think some fruit and seeds are adapted for wind dispersal?
    Some fruits and seeds are lightweight; they have a wing-like structure to help them to be carried
    in the wind; and a large surface area.

 3. Why was it important to keep the fan switched on at the same speed?
    To ensure the investigation is valid (a fair test).

 4. Other than collecting repeated results, how could you check if your data is reliable?
    Compare results with another pair / group. Use secondary sources such as the internet or books.
    Ask another scientist to carry out your investigation and compare the results.

searchText:
Skeletal system – comprehension
Task

Read the text in the box and then answer the questions.
 The skeletal system is a body system made up of bones along with cartilage,
 ligaments and tendons. There are 206 bones in the adult human body, which
 make up a skeleton. Bones are living tissue that can grow and repair itself.
 The skeleton has four main functions: support, protection, movement and the
 production of red blood cells.

 Without the support of the skeleton, the body would be completely floppy
 and limp. Having a skeleton gives the body support and holds the organs in
 place.

 The skeleton protects the organs because the bones are strong and hard.
 The rib cage protects the lungs and heart. The vertebrae of the spine protect
 the nerves of the spinal column.

 Muscles attach to the bones by tendons and this allows the bones to move
 when the muscles contract. Where two bones meet there is a joint.

Find a Friend: Specialised Cells Activity

Teacher Instructions

This activity is good for consolidating or checking learning in a plenary or for revision.
Cards can be printed out A4 or A5 and laminated for repeated use.

How to use:
There are 3 types of card:

orange - diagram (with a part labelled as X);
blue - name of a part;
green - description or function of a part.

Give each student in the class one of the cards. This can be random or differentiated by giving easier
cards to weaker students and more tricky cards to higher ability students. Unused cards can be put onto
a table for students to go to if they can't find their ‘friends’. Where there are more students than cards,
give one card to a pair of students.

Students should then move around the room and find their two ‘friends’ with the matching diagram,
name and function. This encourages discussion and students that are unsure can get help from their
peers.

Once the students have found their friends, the cards can be stuck onto a board, wall or window to form
a display that students can refer to if necessary.

searchText:
Focus 4.4: Reproduction

Stages of pregnancy—page 1

Skill: interpreting
Reproduction begins when sperm are ejaculated into the vagina. Once inside the vagina, the sperm move
towards the fallopian tube in search of an egg. If an egg is encountered, the sperm will surround it, but only
one will fuse with the egg and fertilise it. Fewer than one hundred sperm make it as far as the ovum or egg.
Once the egg is fertilised, the surface of the egg changes to stop any more sperm getting in. The fertilised
egg forms a zygote in the fallopian tube and begins its five-day journey to the uterus. Along the way, the
zygote divides several times to form new cells.
By the time it reaches the uterus, it has become a clump of up to 80 cells, called the morula. In
the uterus the cells continue to divide, forming a fluid-filled ball called a blastocyst. As the cells in the
blastocyst multiply, they start to move around and become different from each other. For the first eight
weeks, the developing individual is known as
an embryo.
After eight weeks the embryo becomes a foetus. The foetus is protected by a pool of amniotic fluid,
surrounded by the amniotic membrane. Oxygen and nutrients come from the placenta via the umbilical

cord.

       They are both ventricles
       They both receive blood from atria
       They both send blood out of the heart.

4) The chambers on the left of the diagram are named ‘right, the chambers on the right of
   the diagram are named ‘left’.

    *This is because if the heart was in your body, then the sides would be reversed – they
    would be on the correct sides.

Note: pupils usually understand the logic behind this better if they pretend to transplant the
heart diagram into themselves.


5) Differences:

    The left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right ventricle. The left ventricle sends
    blood out of the heart through the aorta rather than the pulmonary artery. The left
    ventricle is pumping out (oxygenated) blood to the body, whereas the right ventricle is
    pumping out (deoxygenated) blood to the lungs.

8) Valves.

    *This is important to make the heart as efficient as possible e.g. if blood could flow
    backwards, less blood may be in the ventricles to be pumped out and extra work
    would be needed to get the blood back into the atria. Blood might back up in the atria.

9) *It leaves the pulmonary artery (deoxygenated), goes to the capillaries in the lungs
   (and becomes oxygenated). It returns to heart through the pulmonary vein and goes
   into the left atrium. It goes through a valve and into the left ventricle. It is pumped out
   of heart through the aorta.


10) The heart has two sides with two chambers on each. The top chambers are called
    atria. They receive blood. Blood then flows through valves into the ventricles (bottom
    chambers). Valves stop the blood flowing backwards. The right side receives
    deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava. This blood exits through
    the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
    The left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary vein
    and exits through the aorta to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker wall to pump

 CELL STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION
The History of Cell Biology

Read the passage below. Answer the questions that follow.

    The discovery of cells was made possible by the development of the
    microscope in the 17th century. In 1665, the English scientist Robert Hooke
    used a microscope to examine a thin slice of cork. Hooke described it as
    consisting of “a great many little boxes.” These “little boxes” reminded him
    of the cubicles or “cells” in which monks lived, so he called them cells.

       What Hooke had observed were actually the remains of dead plant cells.
    The first person to observe living cells was a Dutch trader, Anton van
    Leeuwenhoek. Although van Leeuwenhoek’s microscope was rather simple,
    in 1673 it was powerful enough to enable him to view the world of
    microscopic organisms which had never before been seen.

       About 150 years passed before scientists began to organize the observations
    begun by Hooke and van Leeuwenhoek into a unified theory known as the cell
    theory. This theory has three parts:

       (1)    All living things are composed of one or more cells.
       (2)    Cells are the basic units of structure and function in an organism.
       (3)    Cells come only from the reproduction of existing cells.

    (usually X4 or X10) until you hear it click.

    stage clips.

 4. Using the coarse adjustment knob, slowly lower
    the objective lens until it is close to the slide,
    but not touching it. Make this adjustment while
    viewing the microscope slide from the side and
    not through the eyepiece lens.

                                                         Photo courtesy of euthman (@flickr.com) - granted under creative commons licence

    whilst observing through the eyepiece lens for
    the image to come into focus.

    more clearly.



Remember:
• DO NOT let the lens touch the slide – it could

Your Heart
The heart is a muscle in your chest made up of four chambers:

•   the right atrium;

•   the left atrium;

•   the right ventricle;

•   the left ventricle.

Your heart is protected by your ribs and pumps blood around your
body. This is what happens:

Your blood ‘picks up’ the oxygen from your lungs and then it travels
to your heart. The heart pumps or pushes the blood around your
body by using the muscles in its walls. These muscles contract
to push the blood around the body. Arteries carry the blood to
every part of your body so your muscles and organs can use the
food and oxygen to make them work. Veins carry blood back to
your heart when all the oxygen has been used so the blood can be
pumped back to your lungs again to ‘pick up’ more oxygen.

searchText:
Name: ______________________                                             Date: _________________



        Physical and Chemical Properties of
                    Substances
All substances can be identified by the characteristics they possess.

Some of these characteristics can be observed without altering the chemical composition of the
substance. These are called the physical properties of the substance. Physical properties may
include:

       colour, odour, boiling point, melting point, freezing point, electrical conductivity, thermal
       conductivity, magnetism, opacity, malleability, density and hardness.

Some of these characteristics can only be observed when a substance is chemically transferred
into another through a chemical reaction. These are called the chemical properties of the
substance. Chemical properties may include:

       flammability, heat of combustion, toxicity, reactivity with water, reactivity with oxygen,
       reactivity with acids, radioactivity, pH level and chemical stability.

If a substance experiences a change in any of its physical properties, this is referred to as a
physical change. Examples of physical changes include painting a wall to change its colour,
melting gold to change its shape or running electricity through an electrical cord. During a
physical change, the chemical composition of the substance does not change and no new
substances are created. Physical changes are often reversible.

If a substance experiences a change through its chemical properties, this is referred to as a
chemical reaction. Examples of chemical reactions include burning wood, frying an egg or the
process of photosynthesis. During a chemical change, the chemical composition of the original
substances changes and new substances are created. Chemical changes are often irreversible.

                     AP CHEMISTRY
                     SUMMER WORK


      NAMING & WRITING THE FORMULAS OF
           CHEMICAL COMPOUNDS
 Summer Work: Naming & Writing Formulas                                    AP Chemistry

Naming Simple Compounds

Molecule or molecular compound is an assembly of two or more non-metal atoms
tightly bonded together.

A diatomic molecule is a molecule made from two atoms of the same element. The
following seven elements form diatomic molecules in their natural state:

       H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2, I2

An allotrope is one of two or more distinct forms of an element, such as: graphite and
diamond (for carbon) and dioxygen (O2 - usually referred to simply as oxygen) and ozone (O3).

Molecular compounds (also known as covalent compounds) are composed of
nonmetal elements that bond together into larger particles using covalent bonds (bonds
created by the sharing of their valence electrons.

       Molecular formulas show the exact number of atoms of each element in the
       molecule.

       Empirical formulas are the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a molecular
       compound or an ionic compound...

Ionic compounds are composed of ions and usually contain both metals and non-metals.
The ions in an ionic compound form when the metal atoms give one or more electrons to the
nonmetal atoms. Consequently, the metal ion is positively charged (called an cation) and the
nonmetal ions are negatively charged (called the anions). Ionic compounds must be electrically
neutral, so the sum of the charges of the anions and cations must equal zero. Because the
formulas of ionic compounds must be empirical formulas, make sure the subscripts are reduced
to their simplest ratio.

Atom

      They’re at their simplest form.
      Contain a nucleus, protons, neutrons and electrons.
      8 is a magic number and makes them stable.
      Protons are positive and electrons are negative.

Ion

      An atom can give or receive an electron to become an ion.
      It can be either a positive or a negative charged atom.
      It has an atomic weight.
      It is an element on the periodic table.
      Can also be a combination of elements.
      Needs to be balanced.

Molecule

      2 or more chemically bonded atoms.
      Small, found everywhere.

Element

      Listed on the periodic table.
      Can be solid, liquid and gas.
      Contain protons, neutrons and electrons.
      Have atomic mass which is the sum of protons and neutrons.
      Contain all the same kinds of atoms.
      Can’t be chemically broken down.

Compound

      Group of molecules.
      Can form chemicals such as carbon dioxide, water, nitrous
       oxide.

Mixture

      When 2 or more substances are not chemically combined but
       are found together.
      Go through different processes.
      Different from a compound.
      For example air, soil, cake mixture.

searchText:
Atoms and Ions (p13-14)
Atoms are electrically neutral (have no charge) because they contain an
equal number of ____________ ____________ and ____________ ____________ .
If an electron is removed or added, the atom becomes _____________ and
is now called an _____ .

When an electron is removed from an atom, the atom becomes a
____________ ____________ _____ . A positive ion is known as a _________ .
When an electron is added to an atom, the atom becomes a ____________
____________ _____ . A negative ion is known as an _________ .

The charge of an ion is written after the symbol of the element and in
superscript for example Na+ and O-2.

Cations
A cation is formed when an atom loses electrons. An atom will form a
positive ion if its outermost electron shell is almost empty. It will lose all
the electrons in the outermost shell so that only filled shells remain.

Draw a lithium atom and a lithium cation in the space below.




Almost all cations come from ________ atoms because they have _____
electrons in the outermost shell.

Anions
An anion is formed when an atom gains electrons. This will happen when
the outermost electron shell is almost full. The atom will gain electrons
until the outermost shell is full.

Draw a chlorine atom and a chloride ion in the space below.




All anions come from ____ - __________ elements because they have almost
_______ outermost electron shells.
 Naming Ions
The name of a cation (positive ion) is the same as the name of the atom.
For example a sodium atom loses one electron to become a sodium ion.

Sometimes atoms can form more than one type of cation. Iron can lose
two or three electrons to become Fe2+ or Fe3+. To distinguish between the
two ions, scientists add a roman numeral to the ion name to indicate the
number of electrons lost, for example Fe(II) and Fe(III).

Anions (negative ions) are named differently. The name of an anion is the
same as the name for the atom but ends in –ide. For example, a chlorine
atom becomes a chloride ion.

Questions
1. What are the three parts of an atom and what is the charge on each?




2. Which part of an atom can be lost or gained to form an ion? Why do
   you think this part of the atom can be lost or gained?




3. In your own words, define the term ion.




4. What is the difference between a cation and an anion?




5. If a neutral atom lost two electrons, what would be the charge of the
   ion?


6. If an atom has three more electrons than protons, what charge would it
   have?
 7. Use the tables in the text book to complete the information in the table
   below.

Potassium                                 Sodium
Beryllium                                 Fluorine

Copper (II)                               Iron (III)


8. Use your periodic table to predict the ions that are formed from the
   following atoms and give the name of each ion.

 Element       Ion     Name of Ion       Element       Ion      Name of Ion
 Calcium                                 Selenium
 Arsenic                                  Caesium
  Boron                                   Barium
Rubidium                                  Astatine



                               Polyatomic Ions
All the ions looked at so far have been made of one atom with a charge.
These ions are called monatomic ions. Some ions are made from
molecules (two or more atoms chemically combined) which have a charge.
These are called polyatomic ions.

Some examples of common polyatomic ions are given below.

                     Ammonium              NH4+
                     Nitrate               NO3-
                     Hydroxide             OH-
                     Sulphate              SO42-
                     Carbonate             CO32-
                     Phosphate             PO43-

Chemical and Physical Changes
 Aim: To distinguish between chemical and physical change.

This investigation is split into four activities. Your teacher will instruct you of the order of the activities
and let you know when to swap.
                                            Safety Information
Activity 1 – Burning magnesium              Bunsen burner – risk of burns/scalds.
Equipment:                                  Handle with extra care. Rinse any burns under
                                            cold running water for 10 minutes and inform
• Bunsen burner
                                            the teacher immediately.
• heatproof mat
                                            Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• tongs                                     Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher immediately.
• magnesium (2cm strip)                     Magnesium – risk of eye damage.
                                            Do not look directly at the light created by the magnesium.
Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 3: Holding the magnesium with the tongs, carefully hold the magnesium in the flame until it ignites.


Activity 2 – Cooking a pancake
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner                • mini frying pan                 • small cooking spatula

• heatproof mat                • pancake shaker (made up         • cooking oil
                                 to a batter with water)
• gauze

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the frying pan onto the gauze.

Step 3: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 4: Add a small amount of cooking oil to the pan and heat gently.

Step 5: Reduce the heat from the Bunsen burner and add a small amount of pancake batter to the frying pan.

Step 6: As the edges of the pancake batter begin to solidify, gently loosen with the spatula until you can
loosen the whole pancake from the base of the pan.

Step 7: Flip the pancake and finish cooking on the other side.

     Check with your teacher before consuming anything in a lab – it may not be safe to do so.

                                                                              Chemical and Physical Changes

Activity 3 – Boiling water
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• thermometer

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add 150ml of water to the beaker and place the thermometer into the water.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the water gently until you see bubbles begin to form and the water starts to boil.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.


Activity 4 – Melting chocolate
Equipment:
• Bunsen burner

• heatproof mat

• gauze

• beaker

• square of chocolate

Method:
Step 1: Set up the Bunsen burner on the heatproof mat and ensure the air hole is closed.

Step 2: Position the tripod and gauze over the Bunsen burner and place the beaker onto the gauze.

Step 3: Add the piece of chocolate to the beaker.

Step 4: Light the Bunsen burner and adjust the air hole to produce a blue flame.

Step 5: Heat the chocolate gently until you see that it is beginning to melt and become liquid.

Step 6: Switch off the Bunsen burner and leave the equipment to cool.

Chemical comprehension
Task

Read the text below and then answer the questions in full sentences.
                                                                              lines

 Atoms may form molecules. A molecule consists of two or more atoms           1-2
 joined together.

 If atoms are of the same element, they form molecules of the element.        3-5
 If atoms of two or more elements are joined together by chemical
 bonds, they form molecules of a compound.

 During a chemical reaction a different substance is made. These             6 - 10
 substances are products of the reaction. The starting chemicals are
 called reactants. The products can have very different properties from
 the reactants.

 A compound has a fixed composition e.g. iron sulphide (FeS) contains      11 - 12
 one atom of iron and one atom of sulphur joined together.

 Chemical reactions can take place between elements and compounds.         13 – 15
 There are three things to look out for that show a chemical reaction is
 occurring.

     There may be a temperature change. Most chemical reactions           16 - 18
      transfer thermal energy to the surroundings, so we can measure an
      increase in temperature.

     A gas is produced – bubbles show that gas is being produced. If a    19 - 21
      reaction is carried out in a beaker placed on a mass balance, then
      the mass of the beaker will go down as the gas produced escapes
      into the air.

     There may be colour change.                                                22

  1. What is a molecule?
  2. What does molecule of a compound mean?

      start and end of a reaction?
  5. What does having a fixed composition mean?

  7. Why might the mass go down during some reactions?

searchText:
Chemical and Physical Change

Chemical and Physical change
Physical changes do not produce a new substance. Changes in
state (melting, freezing, vaporization, condensation, sublimation)
are physical changes. Examples of physical changes also include
bending a piece of wire, melting icebergs, and breaking a bottle



A chemical change occurs when a new substance is formed and
is not easily reversible. Observations to show a chemical change
could be a colour change, a new smell, the chemicals get hotter
or colder or a gas is produced.




Evidence for Chemical and Physical change

Examples of Physical Changes                       Evidence of Chemical Changes

    crumpling a sheet of paper                        Burning wood – temperature change
    melting an ice cube                               Mixing acid with universal indicator – colour change
    breaking a bottle                                 Seeing bubbles when vinegar and baking soda are
No change in temperature, colour,                         mixed – a gas is formed
                                                   Burning sulphur – creates a new smell
gas or smell




Observing reactions
To observe means to record or make note of something we have experienced. We also think of observations as
watching something, but in Science, observations may be made with any of our senses (by seeing, feeling,
hearing, tasting, or smelling) or even using tools to make observations that are then changed into something
our senses detect.

Observation tools include thermometers, microscopes, telescopes, radars, computer sensors and spaces probes.
Sometimes these tools can observe and collect data that humans cannot directly sense. By using these tools
scientists can often make many more observations and much more precisely than our senses are able to.




74 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 Chemical and Physical change in everyday situations




Reactants and products in a chemical change
A chemical change is a process that produces a chemical change to one or more substances. A chemical change
will produce a new substance. Other observations may include a temperature change, a colour change or
production of gas. Chemicals that are used, and you start with, in a chemical change are known as reactants.
Those that are formed are known as products.




Chemical equations
We show chemical changes as equations. All reactants must go to the left of the arrow and all products go to
the right of the arrow. An arrow must be used and not an equal sign. The arrow shows a chemical reaction,
where the reactants change into products.

change




a. Identify each step as either physical or chemical change

b. List THREE observations that might indicate a chemical change

searchText:
DESIGNING A COLD PACK



Background

Cold packs are applied to sporting and other injuries to decrease
the blood supply to an area. This will reduce bruising and swelling
that may result from an injury. Many ready made, instant cold
packs consist of a sealed plastic bag of crystals with a small bag
of water inside. When the water bag bursts the crystals dissolve
and this causes the temperature to drop to about 1 0 C for about
20 minutes.

Part A

The purpose of this investigation is to decide which chemical
works best as the “crytsals” at reducing temperature when mixed
with water

Equipment

Thermometer
4 test tubes and test tube rack
10 ml graduated cylinder
spatula
distilled water
ammonium nitrate [NH4NO3] (5 g)
sodium ethanoate [NaCH3COO] (5 g)
sodium chloride [NaCl] (5 g)
calcium chloride [CaCl2] (5 g)


Test to find out which powder would be best suited to making a cold pack.
Explain how you tested this and what results you got.


Part B (for the experts)

Extra Equipment

Clean and reuse the 4 test tubes from Part A
A scale or balance measuring in grams

Using only the powder you decided on in Part A, decide what is the
optimum mass to use with 30 mls of water. How many moles is this and
 what concentration will it give? Once again explain how you tested this
and what results you got.
