searchText:
Chapter 5                                    Chemical
reactions
              More balancing
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1:

chemical equations
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                     LOGICAL/MATHEMATICAL


Name:___________________________Class:_____________Date: _____________

Balanced chemical equations show the atoms and molecules that take part in
a chemical reaction. These equations take into account the Law of
Conservation of Mass by ensuring that there is the same number of each
atom in the products as there is in the reactants.

Equations are balanced by adding coefficients (numbers) to the chemical
formulas in the equation. The coefficient multiplies every atom in the
molecule. For example, putting a coefficient of three in front of the chemical
formula for water (3H2O) gives a total of 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 oxygen
atoms.


Method 1: Using integer coefficients
Many chemical equations can be balanced by simply balancing the number of
each type of atom in the reactants and products one by one. Take for
example the combustion of methane, which has the unbalanced chemical
equation:

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Step 1: Balance the carbon atoms (C). There is one carbon in the reactants
and one in the products, so no change is necessary.

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 2: Balance the hydrogen atoms (H). There are four hydrogen atoms in
the reactants and two in the products so the water molecule is multiplied by
two.

   CH4         +              O2                             CO2                +           2H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 3: Balance the oxygen atoms (O). There are two oxygen atoms in the
reactants and four oxygen atoms in the products (two from the carbon dioxide
and two more from the two water molecules). Therefore, the oxygen molecule
in the reactants is multiplied by two.

   CH4         +             2O2                             CO2                +           2H2O

 methane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 4: Check that the equation is balanced by looking at the number of each
atom on either side of the equation.

   Reactants: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O

   Products: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 2
 Method 2: Using half-integer coefficients
One of the challenges when balancing chemical equations is that not all
equations can be balanced using the same method. Therefore, scientists
develop different strategies for dealing with different equations.

One useful strategy is to first balance the equation using half-integer
coefficients such as 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and so on. However, it doesn’t make sense
to have half a molecule so the whole equation is then multiplied by a factor
of two.

This technique comes in handy when you find that there is an odd number of
an atom of one side of the equation and an even number on the other side of
the equation. Take for example, the combustion of ethane, which has the
unbalanced chemical equation:

   C2H6        +              O2                             CO2                +               H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 1: Balance the carbons (C) by multiplying the carbon dioxide by two.

   C2H6        +              O2                            2CO2                +               H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 2: Balance the hydrogens (H) by multiplying the water by three.

   C2H6        +              O2                            2CO2                +           3H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


Step 3: Balance the oxygens (O). There are 2 oxygens in the reactants and
7 oxygens in the products. There is no way we can balance the oxygens by
multiplying any single molecule by an integer. Therefore we multiply the
oxygen molecule by 3.5 to give 7 oxygen atoms in the reactants and 7 in the
products.

   C2H6        +            3.5O2                           2CO2                +           3H2O

  ethane       +           oxygen                    carbon dioxide             +           water


            Copyright © Pearson Austral

 Naming ionic compounds
The name of an ionic compound is simply the name of the cation combined with the
name of the anion. For example, the name for the compound made from magnesium
cations (Mg2+) and oxide anions (O2-) is magnesium oxide.

However, some metallic atoms can produce several cations with different charges.
For example, copper atoms can form copper cations with charges of +1 or +2. To
distinguish between these ions, the charge of the ion is included in the ion name
using Roman numerals: the two types of copper ions are named copper (I) ion (Cu+)
and copper (II) ion (Cu2+). The Roman numerals are also included in the name of the
compound. When copper (I) ions form an ionic compound with chloride ions (Cl-), the
compound is named copper (I) chloride. Similarly, when copper (II) ions form an ionic
compound with chloride ions (Cl-) it is named copper (II) chloride.



Chemical formulas
The chemical formula for an ionic compound combines the chemical symbols for
each ion in the compound, but you don’t include the charges on the ions. Sodium
chloride, made from sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl-), has the chemical
formula NaCl.

However, you must ensure that the total charge of the cations and anions in the
crystal lattice adds to zero. For example, the chemical formula for magnesium
chloride is MgCl2. This is because the magnesium ion (Mg2+) has a charge of +2 and
the chloride ion (Cl-) has a charge of -1, so each magnesium ion needs two chloride
ions to balance the total charge.

Similarly, the formula for sodium nitride is Na3N. The sodium ion (Na+) has a charge
of +1 and the nitride ion (N3-) has a charge of -3, so there must be three sodium ions
to balance the charge of each nitride ion in the crystal lattice.

§ Read the following text about scientists and cross out the incorrect verb alternatives. The verbs are
underlined. The first one has been done for you. Remember that historical recounts should be
written in past tense.

People often made-up-/ make up models to explain / to explained things. Scientists perform /
performs experiments which show / shows them how something acts, or what something looks /
looked like. This information is used to develop / to develops a model. The model of the atom has
underwent / has undergone many changes.

The idea of atoms is suggested / was suggested by Democritus in ancient Greece (460 - 370 BC).
He logically deducted / deduced that matter could not continue to be cut into smaller pieces forever,
and that eventually there had to be / have to be a smallest particle, which he calls / called the atom
(about 400 BC).

In England, John Dalton (1766 - 1844) heard / heared about the experiments of other chemists.
From their results he concluded / concludes that the atoms of the same element was / were identical
and cannot be / could not _be broken. In a chemical reaction, the atoms were separated, joined or
rearranged. Dalton’s model of the atom were / was like a ball (1803).

When English scientist Joseph Thomson (1856 - 1940), and other scientists, experiment _/
experimented with electricity, they finded / found that cathode rays are / were made up of tiny
particles which travelled / travel in straight lines and carried / carryed a negative electric charge.
These cathode rays came / comed from the negative terminal (ie the cathode) and travelled to the
positive terminal (ie the anode), when very high voltages have / were applied. Thomson concludes
Zconcluded that the rays make up / were made up of electrons, which were very small (they was/
were 2000 times lighter than a hydrogen atom) and had / have a negative charge. But if negative
electrons came / come from neutral and relatively large atoms, the atom had to / has to look like a
plum pudding: the dough of the pudding was a uniform substance with a positive charge and
contained / contain tiny sultanas with a negative charge (1904).

(248 In the following text about atoms and radioactivity, there are 12 spelling mistakes. Underline the
incorrectly spelt words and write them correctly in the margin.

Radioactivity had been discovered and alpha particles were identified as tiny positive protons. A
student of Joseph Thomson, the New Zealand born Ernest Rutherford (1871 - 1937), shot a beam of
alpha particals at a very thin sheet of gold foil. He expected the protons to fly straight threw the
foil, practically uneffected by the positive and negative particles in the gold atoms. Rutherford was
suprised to find that some protons were deflected, some even bounced back to the sauce. Based on
his measurements, Rutherford concluded that the atom’s protons had to be concentrated in a small
nucleus leaving the electrons to suround it. The mass of the atom was determined by the nucleus,
which was much heavier than the electrons, and its size was determined by the electrons, which
moved around the nucleus. Rutherford’s model of an atom looked like a spherical cloud of negative
electrons with a positive nucleus in the centre. If the atom was as big as a football feild, the nucleus
would be as big as a tennis ball (1911).

The German Max Planck (1858 - 1947) formulated the quantum theory: Energy is given out or taken
in by atoms only in lots (called quanta). Niels Bohr from Denmark (1885 - 1962) concluded that
electrons jumped from one energy level to another, each jump being worth one gantum of energy.
As a result the atomic model became like a soler system: a small nucleus, containing the heavy
positive protons, was surrounded by several orbits on which the tiny negative electrons circled the
nucleus (1913).

Erwin Schrodinger (1887 - 1961) and Wolfgang Pauli (1900 - 1958), both from Austria, proposed
another model for the atom: The electron shells contained subshells of various shapes, each with a
maximum of two electrons. But it was impossible to state where a particular electron was at any
time; one could only say where an electron was most likley to be. Thus the atom appered like a
nucleus inside many electron clouds (1926).

When the English scientist James Chadwick (1891 - 1974) discovered the existance of neutrons,
which were as heavy as protons but carried no charge, the atomic model changed to include neutrons
inside the nucleus together with the protons (1932).

searchText: ﻿History Of the Periodic Table Dmitri Mendeleev Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian scientist born in Siberia in 1834, is known as the father of the periodic table of the elements. The periodic table of the elements is an important tool used by students and chemists around the world to help them understand and simplify the often complex world of chemical reactions. Mendeleev was Professor of Chemistry at the University of St. Petersburg (now Leningrad) in Russia. Mendeleev's work as a whole amounted to more than 400 books and articles as well as a large number of manuscripts which are preserved at the University of Leningrad. Mendeleev dedicated his life to research and education. Mendeleev made it his special responsibility to educate people wherever he went. When he traveled, Mendeleev would ride in the third class section of the train just to share findings with peasants over a cup of tea. In 1869 Mendeleev arranged all the known elements (63 at that time) in order of increasing mass of the atoms. He found that the properties of elements repeated themselves at regular intervals. He arranged them in the form of a table so that athe elements with similar properties would fall into a vertical comumn. Because the properties of elements repeated themselves at regular intervals or periods the table is called the Periodic table of elements. Mendeleev left gaps in the table to make the elements fit into proper columns and announced that the gaps represented elements not yet discovered. Mendeleev predicted the properties of the undiscovered elements by judging the properties of the elements above and below the gap in the table. Mendeleev died on January 20, 1907 at the age of 73. A copy of the Periodic table was carried high over his funeral procession as a fitting emblem of Mendeleev's career. For more information on History of Periodic Table or on the discovery and naming of each element simply click on the hyperlink! The Periodic Table The Periodic table of the elements was devised by Dimitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev arranged the known elements in order of increasing atomic number and noticed that the properties of the elements repeat themselves at regular intervals. If you are not familliar with the Periodic Table take some time to examine the elements in the table below.If you click on an element the name and number will appear in the boxes below. Try to memorise the names and symbols of the first twenty elements. Teacher Area Student Area Periodic Table of the Elements Top of Form H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar K Ca Sc Ti V Cr Mn Fe Co Ni Cu Zn Ga Ge As Se Br Kr Rb Sr Y Zr Nb Mo Tc Ru Rh Pd Ag Cd In Sn Sb Te I Xe Cs Ba La Hf Ta W Re Os Ir Pt Au Hg Tl Pb Bi Po At Rn Fr Ra Ac Bottom of Form Top of Form Name Number Mass Bottom of Form Legend Metals A solid substance that is a good conductor of eat and electicity. Can be formed into many shapes. Metalloid "Middle elements" - conduct heat and electricity better than nonmetals, but not as well as metals. Easier to shape than nonmetals, but not as easy as metals. Solid at room temperature. Nonmetals A poor conductor of heat and electricity. Not easily formed into shapes. Note The Lanthanum and Actinium series have been omitted Information about Elements. Elements are represented in the Periodic Table by their chemical symbols. The chemical symbol may be one letter as in Carbon, or two letters as in Na (Sodium). If their are two letters in the symbol the second is always written in lowercase. Besides the chemical symbol the Periodic Table usually gives the Atomic Number (above the symbol) and the Mass Number (below the symbol). Often the Mass Number is replaced by the Relative Atomic Mass Structure of the Periodic Table The Periodic Table is structured so that elements underneath each other have similar chemical properties The vertical columns which make up the Periodic Table are called Groups. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties. Some groups have special names for example the elements from Group I are called the Alkali Metals The Horizontal rows of elements are called Periods. The Atomic Number increases by one as you move across a period Copyright 2003 - Tony Burke- All Rights Reserved

Name:______________________________________ Class: ________________ Date: _____________


                       How to Balance Chemical Equations
The Law of Conservation of Mass states that matter is never created or destroyed.
When writing chemical equations, the Law of Conservation of Mass has to be satisfied.
The number and kind of atoms contained in the reactants must equal the number and
kind of atoms in the products. If the atoms are not equal, we have defied the Law of
Conservation of Mass. Therefore, we must balance the equation.

Balancing chemical equations is easy if you follow some rules.

       You can only add a coefficient in front of a chemical formula
       You cannot change any subscripts, nor add any subscripts
       You may not place a coefficient in the ‘middle’ of a chemical formula
       You must end up with the same number and kinds of atoms on both sides of the
       equation when you are finished. Count atoms on both sides upon completion to
       check yourself.

Practice with this example.          Reactants are on the left side of the arrow -
CO + H2          CH3OH               products are on the right.

Count the number of atoms on the left side of the arrow, and compare it with the
number of atoms on the right side.

If you draw a vertical line under the arrow, you can easily see the two sides of your
equation. List the atoms as shown.

CO + H2            CH3OH

C -1               C–1
O–1                O–1
H–2                H–4

If you list the atoms in the same order on both sides, you can easily see which atoms
are equal and which are not. Here, you see that we do not have the same number of
hydrogen atoms on both sides. We must follow the rules above to balance this
equation. Add a coefficient of 2 in front of the H2, but do not change any subscripts.

CO + 2H2            CH3OH             For every molecule of CO, we must use 2 molecules
                                      of H2 to produce 1 molecule of CH3OH.

The 2H2 means there are 2 molecules of H2 – therefore there are 4 atoms of hydrogen.
Recheck the number of atoms for accuracy. The number of atoms on both sides of the
equation is now equal. We have satisfied the Law of Conservation of Mass.
 Name:______________________________________ Class: ________________ Date: _____________


Here’s another example:

Al + O2           Al2O3                  Count the number of atoms and list them under
                                         the equation. Compare each side.
Al – 1            Al – 2
O–2               O–3

You might try adding a coefficient of 2 in front of the Al to balance the aluminum atoms.

2Al + O2            Al2O3
                                          It’s OK if the first coefficient you try does not
Al – 2              Al – 2                balance the equation.
O–2                 O-3


But: How should we fix the number of oxygen atoms? By looking at the subscripts for
oxygen, you see that we cannot get them to match without adding coefficients. If we
add a coefficient of 2 in front of the O2 on the left, we will then have 4 oxygen atoms.
We cannot achieve 4 oxygen atoms on the right using a coefficient. Let’s try the lowest
common multiple of 2 and 3. That number is 6. We will attempt to have 6 oxygen
atoms on both sides of the equation.

To do this, add a coefficient of 3 in front of the oxygen on the left, and a coefficient of 2
in front of the Al2O3 on the right. Remember, you cannot add a coefficient in between a
molecular formula.

2Al + 3O2                  2Al2O3          Now we have balanced the number of oxygen
                                           atoms in our equation, but have caused the
Al – 2                     Al – 4
                                           aluminum atoms to be unbalanced.
O–6                        O–6

         The coefficient is multiplied by each subscript to get the total number of atoms.

Replace the ‘2’ in front of the Al with a ‘4’ to balance the number of aluminum atoms.

4Al + 3O2                    2Al2O3         Now we have a balanced equation.



Difficulties encountered when balancing equations like the one above may be solved if
you are patient, follow the balancing rules, count numbers of atoms correctly, and give
the ‘trial and error’ method a try.
 Name:______________________________________ Class: ________________ Date: _____________

Practice balancing these equations. Start by drawing the dividing line and counting
atoms. Be sure to follow the Law of Conservation of Mass. Check your answers.

   1. Zn + HCl              ZnCl2 + H2




   2. C12H22O11            C + H2O




   3. Fe + O2            Fe3O4




   4. SnO2 + C              CO + Sn

   6. CaC2 + H2O             C2H2 + Ca(OH)2

searchText: ﻿Important Definitions Nucleus: The core of an atom. Proton: Has a positive charge and is found in the nucleus of an atom. Neutron: Has no charge and is found in the nucleus of an atom. Electron: Has a negative charge and is found in a cloud around the nucleus. Atomic Number: The number of protons in an atom. Mass Number: The number of protons and neutrons in an atom.

searchText: Ionic Compounds Ionic compounds are formed from a positive ion and a negative ion combining together. The ions combine together so that the positive charges and the negative charges balance each other out to form a neutral compound . Table salt is a common ionic compound. searchText: ﻿Ions and Compound Formation Atoms consist of a central nucleus made up of positively charged protons and neutrons which have no charge. The nucleus is orbited at high speed by much smaller negatively charged electrons. Protons and neutrons have the same mass, while electrons have about 1/2000th the mass of protons and neutrons. An atom has an equal number of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges balance each other to produce a neutral atom (one with no overall charge). The simplest atom is hydrogen, whose nucleus contains only a single proton, orbited by a lone electron. All other atoms contain the three types of particles. Scientists use two special numbers to describe atoms. The atomic number of an atom is the number of protons it contains and the mass number is the number of particles in an atom’s nucleus (the number of protons + neutrons). The atomic numbers of hydrogen, helium, lithium and beryllium are 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. Scientists use the following notation to describe an atom’s structure: If we know the atomic and mass numbers of an atom, we can figure out how many protons, electrons and neutrons it contains. For example, potassium has an atomic number of 19 and a mass number of 39. This means there are twenty protons in the nucleus. Because the number of electrons is the same as the number of protons, there must be 19 electrons whizzing around the outside of the atom. The mass number of 29 tells us there are 29 particles in the nucleus, but since we know 19 of these are protons, the other ten must be neutrons. Electron Shells Electrons orbit the nucleus in special regions, or shells. Only 2 electrons may fit in the innermost shell of any atom, then up to 8 in each of the next 2 shells for elements up to atomic number 20. The inner most shells are ‘filled’ first. This may be compare to filling spaces on a bookshelf, where we fill the bottom shelf first, then only move up if each lower shelf is filled. Take sodium, for example, with 11 electrons. 2 electrons orbit in the inner shell, 8 in the next, leaving one to orbit in the third shell. Atoms can become charged if they gain or lose electrons. Charged atoms are called ions. For example, sodium has only one electron in its outermost shell. This means that sodium will readily give up this electron. When it loses this electron, sodium becomes positively charged. Conversely, the chlorine atom forms a negative ion when it gains an electron. When sodium and chloride are able to exchange an electron, an ionic bond forms between them and the compound, sodium chloride, is formed. The molecular formula for this is: NaCl. Magnesium readily gives up its 2 outermost electrons, forming Mg2+. So when magnesium combines with chloride the molecular formula is MgCl2, because 2 chloride ions are needed for each magnesium ion in order to balance the charge. Questions 1. searchText: ﻿CHEMICAL CHANGE ISOTOPES Isotopes: atoms of one element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The number of protons is fixed for any given element, however the number of neutrons can often vary. The Mass Number of an element is always a whole number but because there can be more than one type of the same element, the RAM of an element (this is the number underneath the symbols on the periodic table) is often not a whole number because it is an average of two or three isotopes of the same element. Example Chlorine has two isotopes and can have either 18 neutrons or 20 neutrons (the number of protons ‘Z’ is always 17). 3517­Cl or 3717Cl (Chlorine Isotopes) In nature any random sample will contain 3/4 (75%) of 3517Cl and 1/4 (25%) of 3717Cl. To calculate its Relative Atomic Mass (RAM) we do the following. 75% x 35 + 25% x 37 RAM = 35.5 On the periodic table you can see that the RAM is 35.5 Try this: Natural Silicon in silicon ore contains 92% 2814Si, 5% 2914Si and 3% 3014Si. Calculate its the RAM of silicon in nature.

searchText: Law of conservation of mass Purpose To attempt to verify & observe the Law of Conservation of Mass - In any chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants is always equal to the mass of the products. You will need Balance (accurate to 0.01 g), 100mL beaker, 50mL vinegar, 10g baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate), 100mL conical flask, balloon, weighing paper, graduated measuring cylinder, funnel. What to do Record the mass of the empty 100mL beaker. Pour about 15 mL of vinegar into the beaker. Record the mass of the beaker & vinegar. Weigh out ~5 g of baking soda onto a piece of weighing paper. Record the exact mass of baking soda used. Place the beaker/vinegar and the weighing paper/baking soda on the pan of the laboratory balance. Measure and record the mass of these reactants/containers. Carefully pour the baking soda into the beaker of vinegar and allow the reaction (fizzing and bubbling) to complete. Measure and record the mass of the remaining products. Record the mass of the empty conical flask. Pour about 15 mL of vinegar into the 100 mL flask using the funnel to make certain the neck of the flask does not get wet. Obtain the mass of the flask & vinegar. Prepare the sample of baking soda as before and now determine and record the mass of the reactants, the flask and the balloon (which will be the cover for this container) Add the baking soda to the flask and quickly cover the mouth of the flask with the balloon. Measure and record the mass of the products/container/balloon. Results: trial one Item Mass (grams) Beaker + Vinegar Baking soda Total (beaker and reactants) Final mass (after reaction) Difference Results: trial two Item Mass (grams) Conical flask + Vinegar Balloon Baking soda Total (flask, balloon and reactants) Final mass (after reaction) Difference Questions What evidence was there that a chemical reaction occurred? Account for the difference in mass for trial one. Account for the difference in mass for trial two. Did the experiment demonstrate the law of conservation of mass? Explain. Suggest two improvements that could be made to the method that would increase the accuracy of this demonstration .

searchText: 152 Classic chemistry experiments 61. Mass conservation Topic Mass conservation. Timing 20 min. Description Students react potassium iodide with lead nitrate. They weigh reactants and products to show there is no mass change. Apparatus and equipment (per group) 3 ▼ Two < 100 cm beakers 3 ▼ 10 cm Measuring cylinder ▼ Access to an accurate balance (0.01g). Chemicals (per group) –3 ▼ Potassium iodide solution 0.01 mol dm –3 ▼ Lead nitrate solution 0.009 mol dm (Harmful). Teaching tips Students get confused with errors in an experiment. This is a good opportunity to reinforce the idea of errors and that small differences do not necessarily indicate weight loss or gain. The teacher can state that if weight is gained or lost, the results would be repeatable, and therefore the same for all groups in the class. Emphasise the process of not trying to weigh exact amounts of reactants, you simply require an accurate mass. Background theory Accuracy in measurements, errors, and repeatability. Safety Wear eye protection. Ensure students wash their hands thoroughly after the experiment. Answers 1. Yes, this is confirmed by the colour change. 2. Potassium iodide + lead nitrate → potassium nitrate + lead iodide 3. Although at some degree of accuracy the experiment appears to show a mass change this is within the limits of experimental error and these results tend to indicate no mass change. Classic chemistry experiments 153 Mass conservation Introduction The aim of this experiment is to show that mass is not gained or lost in a chemical reaction. Potassium iodide solution Lead nitrate solution Top pan balance Tare 11.04 g on/off What to record Record the total mass of the reactants and the products. What to do 3 1. Measure approximately 5 cm of potassium iodide in the measuring cylinder and pour into one beaker. 2. Rinse the measuring cylinder. 3 3. Measure approximately 5 cm of lead nitrate in the measuring cylinder and pour into another beaker. 4. Zero the balance then place both beakers on the balance at the same time. Accurately measure their total mass. 5. Take them off the balance. 6. Carefully pour the contents of one beaker into the other making sure there is none spilt. 7. Zero the balance again, place both beakers back on the pan and measure the mass. Safety Wear eye protection. Solutions of lead compounds may be toxic – wash your hands thoroughly at the end of the lesson. Questions 1. Has a chemical reaction occurred? 2. Complete the word equation: potassium iodide + lead nitrate → __________ + ___________ 3. Comment on your result.

searchText: ﻿The alkali metals, found in group 1 of the periodic table (formerly known as group IA), are very reactive metals that do not occur freely in nature. These metals have only one electron in their outer shell. Therefore, they are ready to lose that one electron in ionic bonding with other elements. As with all metals, the alkali metals are malleable, ductile, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. The alkali metals are softer than most other metals. Cesium and francium are the most reactive elements in this group. Alkali metals can explode if they are exposed to water. The Alkali Metals are: Lithium Sodium Potassium Rubidium Cesium Francium The 38 elements in groups 3 through 12 of the periodic table are called "transition metals". As with all metals, the transition elements are both ductile and malleable, and conduct electricity and heat. The interesting thing about transition metals is that their valence electrons, or the electrons they use to combine with other elements, are present in more than one shell. This is the reason why they often exhibit several common oxidation states. There are three noteworthy elements in the transition metals family. These elements are iron, cobalt, and nickel, and they are the only elements known to produce a magnetic field. The Transition Metals are: Scandium Titanium Vanadium Chromium Manganese Iron Cobalt Nickel Copper Zinc Yttrium Zirconium Niobium Molybdenum Technetium Ruthenium Rhodium Palladium Silver Cadmium Hafnium Tantalum Tungsten Rhenium Osmium Iridium Platinum Gold Mercury Rutherfordium Dubnium Seaborgium Bohrium Hassium Meitnerium Ununnilium Unununium Ununbium The 7 elements classified as "other metals" are located in groups 13, 14, and 15. While these elements are ductile and malleable, they are not the same as the transition elements. These elements, unlike the transition elements, do not exhibit variable oxidation states, and their valence electrons are only present in their outer shell. All of these elements are solid, have a relatively high density, and are opaque. They have oxidation numbers of +3, ±4, and -3. The "Other Metals" are: Aluminum Gallium Indium Tin Thallium Lead Bismuth Non-metals are the elements in groups 14-16 of the periodic table. Non-metals are not able to conduct electricity or heat very well. As opposed to metals, non-metallic elements are very brittle, and cannot be rolled into wires or pounded into sheets. The non-metals exist in two of the three states of matter at room temperature: gases (such as oxygen) and solids (such as carbon). The non-metals have no metallic luster, and do not reflect light. They have oxidation numbers of ±4, -3, and -2. The Non-Metal elements are: Hydrogen Carbon Nitrogen Oxygen Phosphorus Sulfur Selenium The halogens are five non-metallic elements found in group 17 of the periodic table. The term "halogen" means "salt-former" and compounds containing halogens are called "salts". All halogens have 7 electrons in their outer shells, giving them an oxidation number of -1. The halogens exist, at room temperature, in all three states of matter: Solid- Iodine, Astatine Liquid- Bromine Gas- Fluorine, Chlorine The Halogens are: Fluorine Chlorine Bromine Iodine Astatine The six noble gases are found in group 18 of the periodic table. These elements were considered to be inert gases until the 1960's, because their oxidation number of 0 prevents the noble gases from forming compounds readily. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in their outer shell (2 for Helium, 8 for all others), making them stable. Helium Neon Argon Krypton Xenon Radon

Teaching notes

This activity works just like the traditional game of battleships. It is played
in pairs and they need a copy of the periodic table.

Each student needs a grid to mark their own battleships on and one to
mark their turns on. They then add battleships to their grids (they should
all be simple rectangles and can be placed horizontally or vertically on the
grid).

They could add the symbols for the elements to each square that their
battleships cover.

They should take it in turns to choose a square by reading out the
coordinates and name of the element occupying that square in the
periodic table. If they get a hit they get another go. When one of their
battleships has been hit the student should tell their opponent what type
of vessel they have hit.

The first person to sink their opponents’ battleships wins, (or set a time
limit and the winner is the person with the most ‘hits’).

CHAPTER 7: Elements, compounds and mixtures

The periodic table — atomic
structure
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................

As the early scientists discovered more and more elements, it became more important that they agreed
on names for the elements. Each element was given a name and a symbol. During their experiments, the
scientists also found that some of the elements had things in common. Because of this they decided to
organise the elements into groups.
   The person who finally worked out a system for sorting the elements into groups was a Russian
scientist called Dmitri Mendeleev. His system is called the periodic table and a modern version is used
by scientists today. A small portion of the periodic table is shown below.
                                                                                   The atomic number of an element is the number of
                                                                                 protons present in each atom. For example, all
                                                                                 hydrogen atoms have only one proton inside the
                                                                                 nucleus, so the atomic number of hydrogen is 1.




                                                                                       A simplified diagram of a hydrogen atom



   Atoms are electrically neutral; that is, the number of protons in an atom is the same as the number of
electrons. The atomic mass of an atom is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in
the atom.

review the structure of an atom in your textbook.

Thermal decomposition
Sometimes when chemicals are mixed they react to form a new substance and
sometimes a chemical will just need heat to break apart.
The word thermal means heat and another way of saying breaking down is
‘decompose’ – so thermal decomposition means to break down with heat.
One example of this happening is chalk. The chemical name for chalk is calcium
carbonate and when heated it breaks down into a chemical called calcium oxide and a
gas called carbon dioxide.

                                                     Carbon cycle jigsaw
Teaching notes

This jigsaw helps students engage with the carbon cycle. Students
often struggle to link processes together in science and the carbon
cycle can be difficult in this regard, particularly for lower ability
students.

As an initial task, students are asked (either individually or in pairs)
to cut out and put together the pieces of the carbon cycle. This
gives them some familiarity with the key parts and processes
involved.

Students can then use the jigsaw they have created to do individual
research on the carbon cycle. There is a worksheet that follows on
from the jigsaw activity (resource 19849, ‘Carbon cycle questions’).

The diagram can either be printed on paper each time it is used, for
each student/pair to stick into their books, or it can be printed on
card for multiple uses.

Page 2 shows the completed image, which could be used for class
discussion.

A jigsaw for the nitrogen cycle is also available (resource 19846,
‘Nitrogen cycle jigsaw’), along with a set of questions (resource
19847, ‘Nitrogen cycle questions’) and a consolidation activity
focused on improving exam answers and based on peer-assessment
strategies (resource 19848, ‘Nutrient cycles peer assessment’).

There are also two fully interactive resources, one for each of the
nutrient cycles, available from the Teachit Science Biology whizzy
things page:

http://www.teachitscience.co.uk/whizzybiology.

title: Carbon Cycle Notes
subject: Science
searchText:
The Carbon Cycle
All living things are made of carbon.
Carbon is also a part of the ocean, air, and even rocks.
The Earth is a dynamic place, carbon does not stay still.
In the atmosphere, carbon is attached to some oxygen in a gas called
carbon dioxide.
Plants use carbon dioxide and sunlight to make their own food and
grow.
The carbon becomes part of the plant.
Plants that die and are buried may turn into fossil fuels made of
carbon like coal and oil over millions of years.
When humans burn fossil fuels, most of the carbon quickly enters
the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and traps heat in the
atmosphere.
Without it and other greenhouse gases, Earth would be a frozen
world.
Humans have burned so much fuel that there is about 30% more
carbon dioxide in the air today than there was about 150 years ago,
and Earth is becoming a warmer place.
Ice cores show us that there is now more carbon dioxide in the
atmosphere than there has been in the last 420,000 years.

Chapter 6                                     Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 4: Changing climate of
Antarctica
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                      VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


In 2009 it was reported by the U.S. Geological Survey that the ice sheets in
the southern part of the Antarctic Peninsula (Figure 1) were disappearing and
that the change in the amount of ice was significant. Since 1998
approximately 4000 square kilometres of ice has been lost from one area.
This area of ice lost is about one and a half times the size of the Australian
Capital Territory (ACT). This loss of ice is regarded as very strong evidence of
the effects of global warming on the planet.




Figure 1
This map identifies the main areas of Antarctica.


However, in the same year it was reported by the Australian Antarctic Division
that the ice is expanding in eastern Antarctica (see Figure 1) and parts of
eastern Antarctica are becoming cooler. Ice core drilling in the ice off
Australia's Davis Station in East Antarctica revealed that in 2008 the ice had a
maximum thickness of 1.89 metres. The ice had not been this deep for 10




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 years. Since the 1950s, when continuous record began, the average
thickness of the ice at Davis has been 1.67 metres.

Data collected do not provide any evidence of large scale melting of ice over
most of Antarctica. The loss of ice in the west over the last 30 years has been
more than offset by increases in the Ross Sea Region which is just one part
of eastern Antarctica.

Over the past 30 years the area of sea ice around Antarctica has expanded.
The changes in Antarctic sea ice are thought to be an outcome of
modifications in the path followed by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (see
Figure 2). Warm moist air is directed towards Antarctic causing the ice to melt
in the west and increased snow fall in the east.




Figure 2
When the Antarctic Circumpolar Current moves closer to Antarctica it carries warm moist air
towards the continent.




Effect on plants and animals
Flowering plants


             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 2
 Antarctica is home to only two species of flowering plant and both these grow
on the Peninsula. The range (area over which they are found) and abundance
(number of plants in an area) have both increased in the last few decades.

Krill

Krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that are a very important food source for
animals in the Antarctic. Krill numbers in Antarctica have declined by as much
as 80% since the 1970s. Krill feed on algae that live just under the surface of
sea ice. Where the amount of sea ice is decreasing, so too does suitable
habitat for krill.

Krill feed the fish of Antarctica and are the main food source for baleen
whales. In the years 1925 to 1975 baleen whales were hunted and their
numbers decimated. Without krill it will be difficult for baleen whale numbers
to recover to pre-hunting levels.

Penguins

With the shrinking sea ice in western Antarctica, the Adélie penguins
(Pygoscelis adeliae) have declined in numbers over the last 20 to 25 years. In
other parts of Antarctica the colonies are stable or increasing in numbers.
Adélie penguins feed only on krill. The penguins nest on land and parent birds
go out to the sea ice to find food for their chicks. A reduction in the amount of
sea ice not only reduces the Adélie penguins’ food supply, it also increases
the distance the parent birds have to travel to find food.

Some penguins are benefiting from the changes taking place in Antarctica.
Gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis papua) (Figure 1a) are nesting on the Antarctic
Peninsula. Studies of the bones and other remains found in penguin colonies
indicate that Gentoo penguins did not nest in this area before 1950. These
penguins feed on fish and squid as well as krill.

Chinstrap penguins (Pygoscelis antarctica) (Figure 1b) are also benefiting
from the changes. Where Adélie penguins are abandoning their nesting sites
Chinstrap penguins are taking their place. There is no evidence of Chinstap
penguins on the Antarctic Peninsula until about 50 years ago when the
average temperatures started to rise. Chinstrap penguins eat a wider variety
of food than the Adélie penguins and they also prefer open water.



             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 3
 a                                                          b
Figure 3
Gentoo (a) and Chinstrap (b) penguins both benefit from the warmer conditions in Antarctica.

searchText: Global Systems An ecosystem , short for 'ecological system', includes all the living organisms ex isting together in a particular area. These plants and animals within an area interact with each other and with the non-living elements of the area, such as climate, water, soil and so on. An ecosystem can be very small, such as a puddle or an area under a large rock, or it can be vast, such as an ocean. A sustainable ecosystem is one that is diverse and supports all of the living things in that ecosystem. Biosphere is all of the ecosystems in the world added together. In this part of the term we will look at some of the different systems that work together in world and see how some of them are changing. Key words Word Meaning Ecosystem Sustainable ecosystem Biosphere Producers Plants that make food for an ecosystem by photosynthesis. Primary consumers (herbivores) Animals that eat plants . Secondary consumers (carnivores) Animals that eat primary consumer animals. Tertiary consumers (carnivores) Animals that each primary and secondary consumer animals.

Nature’s time machine
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................


Secrets in the ice
Scientists may not have discovered a time machine yet, but they do have
a way of looking back over 300 000 years by looking at ice cores.
Scientists drill into the ice of Antarctica and collect samples from deep
down. Ice cores provide information about the Earth and the atmosphere
over hundreds of thousands of years.
    For thousands of years, snow has fallen in Antarctica. The snow
turns to ice, which builds up over time. Dust, gases and other
substances from the air become trapped in the ice. The trapped
substances provide information about what was in the air at the time the
snow fell.
    By studying dust in the ice cores, scientists can work out when
certain volcanoes have erupted. They have linked radioactive
substances in the ice to nuclear disasters in various parts of the world.
The dust and radioactive substances were probably carried to Antarctica
by the wind.

searchText:
LESSON 8 E&C                        FLASH LIGHTS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
       Apply their understanding of simple circuits, batteries, copper wire and globes to
        construct a torch.
       Use conductors and switches to construct a torch.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
       blu-tac
       masking tape


Per Group
       2 D batteries (1.5 volts)
       two lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation
        removed at each end
       one small globe (have some spares)
       cardboard cylinders (recycled such as from paper towel or rolled up card)
       aluminium pie dishes (small)
       alfoil
       paper clips or split pins


Preparation
       Collect a variety of light sources e.g. pen light, torch, candle, sparkler, bedside
        lamp, kerosene lantern, mosquito lantern, spotlight, flare or emergency beacon
        (preferably one powered by battery, one by mains power and one chemical).

Safety
    Care must be taken if using sparklers and other light sources.
        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


Light Sources
     Chemicals: candles, flares, sparklers, kerosene lamps, mosquito lanterns.
     Battery: torches, pen light, toys that light up, caving head lamps, spotlights.
     Mains Power: bedside lamps, house lights.


History of Flash lights
      Searching in a dark closet before 1896, one had to use a candle or kerosene
       lantern. Accidents occurred and fires followed. A safer alternative was needed.
      In 1896, the first flashlight was invented.
      Portable electric lights were called "flash lights" since they would not give a long
       steady stream of light. The bulbs were inefficient and the batteries were weak,
       allowing the user to flash the light on for only a few seconds.
      Very early lights did not have an on/off switch, just a ring that would push against
       a band of metal. When batteries and bulbs became more efficient, the switch
       was improved.


Example of a Torch
           LESSON OUTLINE



  1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Show students a variety of light sources e.g. pen light, torch, candle, sparkler,
       bedside lamp, lantern or spotlight.


                                                     They all produce light.
 How are all of these items similar?

                                                     Various answers.
 How are they different?                             They use different sources to
                                                     produce light. Eg mains electricity,
                                                     batteries or chemicals.


 How could you make a light source?                  Batteries,   some    wires   and    a
                                                     globe.




2. Activities and Strategies
      Discuss the aim, equipment and method. Students can make the torch in a variety
       of ways. Encourage creativity.
      Students design and construct a simple torch using
            2 batteries
            1 globe (test these first)
            A cardboard cylinder (as the battery case and torch shaft)
            An aluminium pie dish (as the reflector)
            A combination of two split pins and a paper clip as a switch
            Copper wire


      10 minutes: discussion in groups of what they will do and drawing their design.
      40 minutes: build the torch.
      Suggestions for the torch once students have attempted their own.
           All wiring and the switch should be on the outside of the cardboard
              cylinder
           Break the circuit using two split pins bridged by a swivelling paper clip.
           Ensure the circuit is complete, no breaks other than the switch.
              Pack the back of the torch with a ball of aluminium foil.
             Cut a small hole in the pie dish to enable it to touch the battery.
             The wire where it joins the globe and the base of the globe must not touch
                the pie dish so these need to wrapped in masking taps or blue tack to
                keep them separated.
             The wire joins the globe between the pie dish and the cylinder.


        Groups to demonstrate their working torches.


3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate)


    What problems did you have and                      Various.
    how did you overcome them?


    What would you do differently next                  Wiring, number       of     batteries,
    time?                                               connections.




4. Reflection

        Write a conclusion to describe how your torch works and what changes you would
         make to improve your design.




          EXTENSION ACTIVITIES



    Build a torch with internal wiring, with a pressure switch (using sponges), or one that
     allows you to change the batteries.

Circuits you can try are on an attached sheet. Each component (buzzer, motor, etc.) on the board will work when DIRECT CURRENT (from a battery or D.C. power supply) is connected to them. They are not designed to work with alternating current (A.C.), which is the type of current we receive through the mains power supply. Each component has a certain amount of Resistance to electric current. It is helpful to be aware of the approximate resistance of each component, especially when you want to predict what will happen before you connect up a circuit. The resistances liven are the MEASURED RESISTANCES, when a 6 volt battery was connected to them. An explanation of resistance is given in the section on "Electricity - the main concepts" (a) Globes - There are two types, the only difference being their resistance. (i) one marked 6v 2w - resistance 27 ohms. (ii) the other marked 3.8 V 0.3 A - resistance 18 ohms. Globe (ii) glows more brightly than globe (i) when each is separately connected to a 6 volt supply. (Try it). The electric current flows into the base of the globe, through the filament and out of the metal side of the globe. The current can also flow in the reverse direction. The reason for the glass casing is to protect the filament from being knocked or touched when it gets white hot. and to keep oxygen away from the filament. If the filament was exposed to oxygen when it was hot it hot, it would instantly burn out. (b) continuity tester - This has many uses. When the two probes are connected together (that is, there is no resistance between them) the light emitting diode (L.E.D.) lights up. Therefore, if the L.E.D. lights up brightly when the probes are being used, the ~two points being touched by the probes are connected electrically. Other uses are listed in the ex]experiment section. The continuity tester works best when connected to a nine volt D.C. supply. (c) variable resistor - (Also known as a Potentiometer, or POT for short). The resistance between the centre socket and the ~o outer sockets can be changed from 10 ohms up to 10k ohms (10,000 ). The resistance between the two outer sockets is always 10k ohms. There is a protective 10 ohm resistor on the central socket of the pot on the demonstration board. If there was no resistor, the pot could BURN OUT Ok~ if a power supply is connected only across the pot. This is a danger with the students' pot, as there is no resistor attached to the central terminal. Students should always ensure that the pot is in series with another component such as a globe. (d) motor - The resistance of the motor is around 18 ohms when running with a 6 volt battery supply. The motor will change direction of spin if the leads in the two motor sockets are swapped. The optimum voltage supply to run the motor is only 3 volts, but it can run comfortably at 9 volts, provided it is not left running for a long period of time. It will spin at 6 900 revolutions per minute at these voltages, if not restricted. Provided in the kit is one means of restriction - an icypole stick, with a hole to fit onto the motor shaft. See later experiments with the motor for details. (e) buzzer - The resistance of the buzzer is around 600 ohms. There are two other sockets connected to the POSITIVE TERMINAL of the buzzer, each with an additional l50 ohm resistance. These resistors decrease the current going into the buzzer, and hence make in softer. If the students are using the demonstration board, you may PREFER to have them use only the "soft" volume socket. You can do the same with the students boards (as outlined in the later experiments). The buzzer needs at least S volts power supply with the positive of the supply connected to the positive of the buzzer. the following information provides suggestions for extended experimental options in the physics using the Electricity Demonstration Board. In other words. let them solve the problem. A.CHARACTERISTICS OF SOLAR PANELS. There are various aspects of the solar panels that can be investigated. (a) Plotting the light intensity on the panels against the current and voltage output. The output of the panels can be placed in series with a milliammeter and 100 ohm resistor, with a voltme[er in parallel ~ith the 100 ohm resistor. A light intensity meter used b>photographers can be used to measure the light intensity at the panel surface usin~ a 150 ~,~tt ii~ht globe as the source. (b) Using the set up as in (a), determine the percentage efficiency of the solar panels. For a particular distance of the panels from the ligh~ source (say x cm), the surface area of a sphere of radius x can be calculated (say area Y cmz). Assuming the light globe actually emits 150 joules per second as light, and that the light is evenly distributed over the imaginery surface of the sphere or radius x, it is easy to calculate the amount of light energy per second reaching the solar collectors. Using_' the P = IV for the output of the solar panels, you can determine the percentage efficiency of the panels. This efficiency can be determined for various distances from the globe. ~c) A variation on (b) could be to use colour filters to see if the panels are sensitive to particular colours. Ad.~ustment of distance may be necessary to keep the overall light intensity on the panels constant. There are a range of extensions to this topic, including visiting showroom of the latest solar technology, and writing up on their research. Students could also construct their o~ solar water heater, and determine the efficienc~~ of energ~ transfer. T]~_ ELEtmfRIC ~FoTOR The measureable parameters relevant to the motor are (a) its ms~ximum speed of rotation, (b) the best operating voltage, and the current dra~ by the motor at this voltage (the power consumed for various voltages can be determined); (c) the output power of the motor, and hence its relative efficiency' for a Oarticular load on the motor: (di the ms~ximum torque of the motor. Some of these parameters are more difficult to measure than the others, particularly (c) and (d). SUGGESTIONS (a) Use a stroboscope to determine the frequency of rotation for various inpu~ voltages immx. 9 volts, for short time only). Plot f vs input voltage. ib) From the graph of (a), determine the minimum voltage for ms~ximum f. (c) Put a piece of pencil with its lead removed on the end of the shaft so that it can act as a pulley. A long cotton thread with a light weight can be attached to the pulley. If the motor is then raised to a height of at least 2 metres, the students can then attempt to determine the power output (rate of change of potential energy of the weight) versus the input power to the motor. Because of the speed of the motor, students may wish to gear the speed of rotation do~, or file most of the pencil shaft down - the motor can make a light weight move ~.~]ERY rapidly. The challenge is to get the motor operating_ at its optimum efficiency! ld) By having a long ic.vpole stick firmly attached to the shaft lyou may want to file a The school will probably have other motors that students can compare. Students may not be aware of how many motors are in the average house. There maybe anything up to forty motors in one home, including in toys (trains and slot cars), appliances with moving parts - vacuum, dishwasher, washing machine, video, tape recorder and player, record player, exhaust fans, hair dryer, blow heaters, cooling fans, electronic type~Titers and printers, food processors. mix-masters, electric can openers, tumble driers, refrigerators and freezers (you hear the motor going on or off occasionally), electric tools in the workshop - drills, grinders, electric planes and touters, electric saws, etc. Try and estimate how many motors you have in your home. 7. ENERGY CHANGES - THE ~I4iN CONCEPTS There are a number of energy transformations that can be sho~m using the demonstration board. (a) If you have a circuit with a battery and a light globe {as with a torch), the energy changes that take place are - chemical energy (stored in the battery), electrical energy (transferred through the wires by means of electric current) and finally light and heat energy (given off by the light globe). searchText: ﻿Electric Current Electric current is a measure of the rate of flow of charge (electrons) The charge flows when the circuit is complete. Charge is measured in coulombs (C) The rate of flow is the number of coulombs flowing per unit of time. When 1 coulomb of charge flows in 1 second it is called an ampere (A) Current is measured using an ammeter. Ammeters are connected in series with the source of electricity An ammeter is connected from its positive terminal to the positive terminal of the source. The usual current flowing in our homes is about 8 A Voltage Voltage is a measure of the electrical pressure which causes the electrons to flow in the circuit. It is measured in volts (V) A volt meter is used to measure the voltage. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the appliance to be measured. A volt meter is connected from its positive terminal to the positive terminal of the source. Some typical voltages are : dry cell 1.5 V house voltage 240 V car battery 12 V smoke alarm 9 V Electricity is transmitted from the power stations at very high voltages ie. 66 000 V

Task

   1. Read carefully through the text.
   2. Put the images in the order that they appear in the text.
   3. Glue the images in the spaces provided on the worksheet and quote a small
       part of the text that you are linking the image to – this cannot be more than
       eight words! Next, say why you are matching the image to that piece of text.



        When you think about the word ‘current’ what is the first thing that
        comes to mind? Perhaps the current in a river or something present-
        day?

        The current of a river is the flow of water. As the current flows from high
        ground to low ground it can carry things with it, like leaves, twigs and
        even boats. Current can only flow from high ground to low ground.

        Current in an electrical circuit is very similar, it also flows and carries
        electrical charge. The electrical current that flows in one direction is
        called direct current. Just like a river, it cannot flow backwards and
        forwards, it can only flow from one side of the battery to the other.

        As long as the current flows through the wires and cell any components
        in the circuit, like lightbulbs or buzzers will work. However, it is very
        important that there are no breaks in the electrical circuit because if
        there were, the electrical charge would not be able to flow back to the
        cell.

        We can think of the cell as being responsible for ‘pushing’ the current
        around the circuit. A bigger push from the cell will mean that more
        current can flow.

        To measure the current we use a piece of equipment called an
        ammeter, and it is placed in the circuit so that it can measure the
        current that flows through it. An ammeter measures current in units
        called ‘amps’ or ‘amperes’. Amps are given the unit symbol, A, for
        example, 10 A is 10 amps. Remember that the ammeter must be part of
        the circuit and not on the outside of it.

searchText: ﻿Batteries and Cells A cell is a device which converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It is used in an electrical circuit to drive motors, lights etc. A battery is a combination of cells. The cells are connected in either series or parallel to provide higher voltage or longer life. When connecting cells in series, connect them positive to negative. Electrical circuits An electrical circuit allows electrons to flow from the source, through conductors and return to the source. When they flow through an appliance energy is transferred to the appliance and it works. ie a light glows or a motor runs. The electrons will not flow unless the circuit is complete. Circuits can be represented by circuit diagrams. Symbols represent the various parts of the circuit.

searchText: Electricity and Safety Electricity can be dangerous for a number of reasons. It can cause fires. Remember , if current runs through a wire with high resistance it produces heat. This is good in a toaster, but not so good in some other situations. If resistance it too high in a wire it can over heat and cause a fire. This sometimes happens because too much current is put through a wire or a short circuit has occurred. What is a short circuit? Sometimes electricity takes a short cut through the wrong wire or through some other object that conducts electricity, such as a metal knife. We call this a short circuit. A short circuit is usually made accidentally. It bypasses part of a circuit. This can happen when two bare wires in a circuit touch each other. The part of the circuit bypassed by the short circuit stops working , and a large amount of current could start to flow through the short cut . This can generate a lot of heat in the wires and cause a fire Electricity can give you and electric shock . This is where current flows through a person. The heart and nerves of the bod y are controlled by electrochem ical impulses, so a large current can disrupt these and cause injury. An electric shock can also cause burns on the skin and internal tissues. Being Safe. Make sure wires are insulated. That is they have a plastic coating on them. If a wire has frayed insulation, have it repaired. Do not use electricity near water. Do not overload any one power outlet. Fuses and Circuit Breakers . Every electrical device in your home that is connected to a power supply is protected by a fuse somewhere along the circuit connecting it to electrical supply. The biggest fuses in your house are located in the fuse or circuit breaker panel . This is mounted on the wall where electrical power lines come inside your house and split into the c ircuits that run through your home . Without fuses, power surges from electric generators or short circuits within your house could burn out appliances, circuit boards and wiring. Any of these could lead to fires or further damage to the electrical systems within the building. Fuses all contain a filament or strip made of metals. This filament melts and break s when a certain current or "load" has been exceeded. It mel ts and breaks the circuit. This stops the current and prevents a fire. A new fuse must be used to re-establish the circuit. Depending on the circuit, different fuses will burn out(melt) at a specific current. Most household ci rcuits carry 10, 15 or 20-amp. Fuse wires are one-time use. Once they burn out, they have to be replaced. Circuit Breakers are like light switches. They do the same job as fuses but do not “burn out” when the current gets too high. When they overheat they switch off and lock. This "lock" (actually its more of a spring) causes the switch to shut off. You can flip the breaker to reset it, but generally if it’s too hot, it won’t stay on until it has cooled to a safe operating temperature. Make sure plugs and appliances have an earth wire. W hen a short circuit in the appliance occurs the earth wire allows the electricity to be safely conducted to the earth. This is better than the electric current running through you to the Earth. If in doubt use a qualified electrician .

searchText:
Electricity – pairs game

Introduction

A simple game designed to increase students’ confidence in the symbols of circuitry. Most
students have played ‘pairs’ at some time or other, so the rules are generally known to all.


Instructions

Divide the class into groups of between two and four players. Photocopy one set of the
sheets (as well as a sheet of answers) for each group. It is best to photocopy them onto
card or stiff paper that is thick enough so the typing cannot be seen through it!

Cut the sheets into individual cards. Remove any pairings not relevant to your group.

The aim of the game is to make pairs. A pair consists of symbol or graph with its
appropriate name. The answer sheet is given to each group to help them check the
pairings are correct.


Rules of the game

The cards are shuffled and spread out randomly face down on the bench.

The first player turns over two cards. If they are a pair, the player removes them and has
another go. If they are not a pair they are turned face down again. When the first player
has finished their go, play moves to the next player.

The winner is the one with the most pairs at the end.


Variations

One player can be nominated in each group whose sole responsibility is to check the
answers.

Groups of students can be formed according to their ability and different groupings of
cards given to them. The less able may find that sheets one and two are enough to start
with.

Also, with a bit of manipulation the names can be photocopied onto one colour of card and
the symbol or graph onto another. Therefore, when a student picks up a pair of cards they
are picking up two different colours. The game is faster this way.

searchText: ﻿ Electricity is a form of energy where the energy supply comes from rapidly moving electrons. You may remember from year 8 that there are two main forms of electrical energy; • Static electricity • Current electricity Try this exercise to reacquaint you with static electricity 1. STATIC ELECTRICITY: SOURCES OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY A convenient source of electrical energy in the laboratory is the cell. The electrons the cell releases come from chemical reactions that occur within it. That is, cells are electron sources, and they can 'pump' electrons around an electrical circuit. A battery is made up of two or more cells linked together. 2. CIRCUITS a) Simple Circuits A circuit is a completed loop of conducting material joining the terminals of a cell or a battery. In the drawing of circuits, the following symbols are used: A circuit is drawn using straight ruled lines and in a rectangular shape even though in reality it may look quite different. Draw examples of circuits in the space below. i) a cell, a switch, a globe ,an ammeter, a resistor joined by conducting wires. ii) 2 cells, 2 globes, a bell and a resistor joined by conducting wires b) Electric Current An electric current is a flow of charged particles, pumped by a cell, around a circuit. In metals, the electric current is a flow of electrons. For a current to flow, the circuit must be complete. The size of current flowing around a circuit can be determined by examining the brightness of a globe in the circuit (the brighter the globe, the greater the current). A switch is a device for breaking a circuit. I can be drawn open or closed. Questions 1. In which of the following will an electric current flow? 2. Consider the following circuit: Which globes will glow when the following switches are on? i) Switch A ii) Switch A and Switch C iii) Switch B and Switch C iv) Switch A and Switch B 3. Now you draw a circuit in which there are 3 globes and 2 switches and 2 cells. When 1 switch is closed only 1 globe glows and when the other switch is closed the 2 other globes glow. ACTIVITY 1: Simple Circuits Materials: 1 electricity kit Examine all the components of the kit carefully and make sure you understand what each is. Method: 1. Build each of the following circuits and determine whether the globe is off, dim or bright. Draw each of the circuits and write your answer under each circuit diagram.. 2. Using 2 cells, 1 switch, 2 globes and conducting wires, build as many different circuits as you can, in which the light globes glows when the switch is on. Draw each of these circuits in the space below.. 3. Complete the tables by either connecting Put a  for lamp ON up each circuit, or by "tracing" the electron and a X for lamp OFF flow around the circuit. PROBLEM SHEET 1 – Simple Circuits 6. Complete the tables for the switches in the following circuits: 3. RESISTANCE Resistance in a circuit is any device that restricts or inhibits the current through it. 1. If a device e.g. a piece of wire, has a high resistance then the flow of electricity through it is greatly reduced. 2. If a device has a low resistance then the flow of electricity through it will be only slightly reduced. 3. The greater the resistance of a device, the smaller the current that will flow through the circuit. 4. When an electric current flows through resistance in a circuit, some of the electrical energy is transformed to heat energy i.e. heat is produced when electricity flows through resistance. 5. The greater the resistance, the greater the amount of heat produced. 6. Different conductors can have different resistance properties. For example, copper has a low resistance but nichrome and tungsten have high resistance. Light globes contain a piece of high resistance wire, which produces much heat (and thus light) when an electric current is passed through it. Thus, a light globe can be regarded as a device with high resistance. Example 1. Which of the following circuits has the greater resistance? 2. Which of the following circuits has the lower resistance? ACTIVITY 2: Resistance Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 1. How bright is the globe ? ______________________________________________________ 2. Replace the copper wire with a piece of nichrome wire (of the same length as the copper wire). How bright is the globe now ? ___________________________________________ 3. Compare the brightness of the globe with that obtained for the copper wire. _______________________________________________________________________________ 4. Which wire has the greater resistance, copper wire or nichrome wire? ______________________ 5. Now replace the nichrome wire with a small piece of 'steel wool' wire. Describe what happens to the globe now. ___________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened with the ‘steel wool wire’ . ____________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 7. Electrical energy is more easily transformed to heat energy using ______________ resistance wire. Application of Resistance 4. SHORT CIRCUITS A 'short circuit' is an alternative conducting pathway of lower resistance, which by-passes a particular resistance, globe or other appliance in a circuit. It is not necessarily the shortest path however. E.g. in the following circuit, the light globe will not light up because of the 'short circuit' between points A and B (i.e. it is 'easier' for the electrons to travel through wire AB rather than through the light globe.) ACTIVITY 3: Short Circuits Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 2. Sides A and B are made of two wires each, joined together by twisting the ends 3. Place another conducting wire between A and B. This is the short circuit. 4. Predict what you think will happen. ________________________________________________ Test your prediction. 5. What happens to the globe when the wire between A and B is connected ? ______________________________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened to the globe. ______________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 5. FUSES Fuse wire is a relatively high resistance conductor with a low melting point. A fuse wire will melt if too large a current is passed through it. When it melts the circuit is broken and current can no longer flow. A fuse is a protective or safety device, included in a circuit, which melts when a short-circuit or overload results in too high a current passing through the circuit. In circuit diagrams, a fuse has the symbol Example In which of the following circuits would you expect the fuse to blow if a wire was placed between A and B? ACTIVITY 4: Fuses Method: 1. Identify the following statements as true or false a) An electric current can flow more easily through a wire of high resistance than through a wire of low resistance. b) Wire with high resistance restricts the flow of electricity through it. c) If a wire has a low resistance, it will probably heat up considerably when a current is passed through it. d) A 'short circuit' is a circuit which is very small. e) A 'short circuit' can occur if in a particular circuit an alternative pathway of low resistance is produced. f) Fuse wire is made from wire which has low resistance and low melting point. g) Fuse wire is made from wire which has high resistance and high melting point. h) Nichrome wire has a higher resistance than copper wire. i) The wire used to make the filament in a light globe has high resistance and low melting point. 2. searchText:
Making an Electromagnet
 Aim: To build an electromagnet

Equipment:
• Insulated copper wire                               Safety Information
                                                      Take care when handling and cutting
• Wire strippers
                                                      wire to avoid cuts.
• Battery (9V)

• Iron nail (approx. 50mm)

• Crocodile clips - optional

• Paperclips

Method:
Step 1: Wrap the copper wire around the iron nail, leaving
about 10cm lengths at each end. Try not to wrap it overly
tightly around the nail - you should be able to remove the
nail from the coil after wrapping.

Step 2: Carefully strip the insulation from the ends of the
wire to expose the copper inside and to make a connection.
(Or connect with crocodile clips, if available).

Step 3: Connect the exposed ends, one to each terminal of
the battery.

Step 4: Test your electromagnet by observing whether it
attracts the paperclips.



  Exploring further
  You could investigate how the number of coils in your wire affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the number of batteries connected affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the metal core inside the coil affects the strength of the electromagnet.

Better Magnets Using Electricity
An Electromagnet can be made by winding a piece of insulated wire
around a piece of steel bar and connecting it to a power source
(battery or power pack). Your task is to test several different designs of
electromagnets to see which works best.

Test 1.
Does an electro-magnet work best using a small battery or a large battery?

Make your electro-magnet by winding the wire around the bolt and see how many
paperclips it can pick up using the ‘D’ battery (larger one) and then the ‘AA’
battery (smaller one).

Number of paperclips picked up by the small battery: _______________

Which one worked best? __________     How much better was it? _______________

Test 2.
Does an electromagnet work better with a few loops of wire or lots of turns of wire?

Make your electro-magnet (use the best battery from the previous test) and see
how many paperclips it can pick up with 1 metre of wire wrapped around it (only
use ½ the wire in loops) and then 2 meters of wire (wrap the whole wire around the
bar).

Number of paperclips picked up magnet with 1 meter of loops: ______________

Number of paperclips picked up magnet with 2 meter of loops: ______________

Which one worked best? _________     How much better was it? _______________


Test 3
Use the best number of loops and the best battery from the previous tests and
make an electro-magnet using a plastic pen instead of an iron bar or bolt.

Did this type of electromagnet work better than a normal one with an iron centre?



Electromagnet Questions

   1.     Using your results from above, what features would a really powerful
          electromagnet have?
 2.   Give 2 reasons why are electromagnets more useful than normal
     magnets?
