LESSON 5 E&C                        CONDUCTORS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Classify materials as conductors or insulators.
      Describe the role insulators and conductor in everyday appliances.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
      a selection of insulators and conductors:
            insulators (wooden pop sticks, plastic spoons, glass jars, paper, rubber,
              ceramic tiles, cotton, foam cups, kitchen sponge)
             conductors (alfoil, iron nails, steel wool, coins, copper, aluminium cans,
              drawing pins, paper clips)

Per Group
      2 D Batteries (1.5 volt)
      3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
       at each end
      2 globes
      cardboard (1 piece about 10x10cm)
      paper clips
      a few insulators and conductors as listed above
      masking tape


Preparation
     Collect a range of materials to test; students could bring one each from home.

Safety
    Mains electricity must not be used.

        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS
 Circuits
      A circuit is a path in which electricity flows.
      Electrons are tiny particles that are found in atoms.
      Electric current is the movement of electrons, which creates the flow of
       electricity.
      The power supply pushes electrons through a circuit. This power supply can
       come in many different forms (for example, a battery is a power supply).
      You can think of the power supply as a pump that creates pressure to force
       water to flow in a hose.
      In a series circuit the batteries and light bulbs are connected in a line. There is
       only one path for the electrons to flow along. Therefore, the current through each
       of the circuit elements is the same.
      This is why when one Christmas tree light blows, the rest do not light up.
      Electricity can be transferred to heat, light, sound and motion energy.


Conductors and Insulators
      A conductor allows electricity to flow through it. Examples include metals such as
       wire made of aluminium, steel or copper.
      An insulator does not allow electricity to flow through it. Examples include non
       metals such as plastic, wood and foam.


Additional Information
      A parallel circuit is one in which electric current travels along more than one path
       (as in the home), because there is more than one path for the electricity to
       follow. Some parts of the circuit can be on while others are off.
      Voltage can be thought of as electrical pressure, which pushes the electrons
       through the circuit. Electric pressure is measured in volts.
      The most basic electrical devices in the home e.g. a kettle, are made from
       simple pieces of wire which resists the flow of electricity. The wire will become
       warm, perhaps red hot when electricity flows through it.
      The household voltage in Australia is 240 Volts.
      Wiring in houses is designed to have very low resistance so they don’t become
       warm with electricity flowing through them.
           LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Direct students into groups.
      The students to design a simple circuit using two batteries, a globe and copper
       wire.
      The circuits should be built and taped onto a sheet of cardboard or their desk to
       hold the components in place.
      The group with their globe shining first is the winner.
      The teacher introduces the concept of materials that conduct electricity
       (conductor) and those that do not (insulators).

 conductors.

 What do we call materials that do                       Insulators.
 not let electricity pass through
 them?

                                                         Foam, plastic, wood.


                                                         Break the circuit and then place
 How could we test materials to see                      the materials one at a time and
 if they are conductors or insulators?                   see if the globe still glows.




2. Activities and Strategies
      Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity.
      Revise what is meant by a prediction and ask students to predict whether the
       globe will shine with each material (therefore a conductor) or not (therefore an
       insulator).
      Groups to break the circuit using two drawing pins a few centimetres apart.
      Groups test the different materials to see if they are conductors or insulators and
      record their observations.


3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate)

Cow’s Eye Dissection
Purpose: To identify and examine the various parts of a cow’s eye.

Materials: gloves     scissors   scalpel     forceps   cutting mat    newspaper
cow’s eye

Procedure:
Part A: External features of the eye
1. There is some fat around the eye. What colour it the fat?

2. What is the purpose of the fat around the eye?

3. What is the job of the muscles on the outside of the eye?

4. Cut the fat and muscles off the eyeball so that you can see the sclera.

5. What colour is the sclera? ________        iris? ________   pupil? ________

6. The cornea is the tough, clear covering over the iris and pupil. It is
   normally clear and colourless; however in your cow’s eye it may be cloudy.
   Why do you think it may have become cloudy?


7. The optic nerve carries information from the retina to the brain. Identify the
   optic nerve on the back of the eye. Describe what it looks like.


Part B: Internal features of the eye
1. Carefully use the scalpel to make a small cut near the centre of the eye.
   With the scissors, cut around the entire eye so that you have two equal
   hemispheres.

2. What colour is the sclera?

3. What did you notice about the texture of the sclera? Why is this important?


4. The jelly inside the eye is the vitreous humour. Gloop your vitreous
   humour onto the parts identification worksheet.

5. What is the job of the vitreous humour?


6. Pick up the back of the sclera, which contains the optic nerve. The retina is
   a thin layer on the inside of the sclera. Gently peel off the retina with the
   forceps and place it on the parts identification sheet.

7. What is the purpose of the retina?

8. You may have found it difficult to remove the retina because it was attached
   to the optic nerve. This area is called the __________ __________.
 9. They black, shiny layer under the retina is the choroid coat. It contains
   blood vessels that provide nutrients for the eye. Why is the choroid coat
   dark?


10. Use the forceps to carefully peel the choroid coat from the sclera and
   place it on the parts identification sheet.

11. You have now removed everything from the back half of the sclera.
   Place it on the parts identification sheet.

12. Pick up the front half of the sclera that contains the cornea, iris and lens.
   Remove the lens with the forceps.

13. When you remove the lens, you should notice a watery fluid between the
   lens and the cornea. This is the aqueous humour. What is its function?


14.   Look at the lens. Is it concave or convex?

15.   Gently squeeze the lens. Why is it important that the lens is flexible?

16.   Place the lens on the newspaper. What do you notice about the writing?

17.   Place the lens on the parts identification sheet.

18. Use your fingers to carefully remove the iris. When you look at the iris
   closely, you should be able to see thin lines. These are the muscles that
   cause the iris to contract or dilate. Draw the iris in the space below.




19.   What is the purpose of the iris?


20.   What is the hole in the iris called?

21.   Is the iris transparent, translucent or opaque?

22.   Place the iris on the parts identification sheet.

23.   Cut the cornea out of the sclera. What is the purpose of the cornea?

24. With your scalpel, cut through part of the cornea. You should feel and
   hear it crunch. The cornea is made of multiple layers to make it thick and
   strong. Why must the cornea be tough, especially in grazing animals such
   as the cow?


25.   Place the cornea on the parts identifications sheet.

searchText:
LESSON 4 E&C                     SWITCHED ON




           AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
          Explore the concept of flow of electricity in simple circuit and how this can be
           controlled using switches.
          State that adding more batteries make globes shine brighter.


           EQUIPMENT


Per Class
          masking tape
          a bag of lollies e.g. M&Ms

Per Group
          2 D batteries (1.5 volts) per group
          3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
           at each end
          1 small globe (have spares)
          pop sticks for supporting batteries
          blu-tac
          alfoil
          4 drawing pins
          4 large paper clips
          2 split pins
          1 sponge cut in half (optional for extension)

Preparation
          Extension: cut sponges in half and cut a small square from the middle of each
           using a Stanley trimmer. The squares should be a uniform size i.e. 3cm x 3cm.
Safety
           Mains electricity must not be used.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   Electrons flow from the negative end of the battery.
   As each electron move through a conductor, it pushes on the one ahead of it,
    such that all the electrons move together as a group.




   The tube is full of marbles, just as a conductor is full of electrons. If a single
    marble is inserted into this full tube on the left-hand side, another marble will
    immediately try to exit the tube on the right.
   Light globes consist of a glass bulb, which has a filament in between the two
    wires which go into and out of it. The filament is made from a very thin wire,
    which has a high resistance to electricity.
   This resistance causes the filament to heat up and glow when electricity
    passes through it.
   The electric current travels along the wire, enters the filament, heats up the
    filament, creates light and exits the globe through the other wire.
   The light that is seen from the light globe is the glow of the filament.
   Voltage e.g. 1.5 volts is a measure of how much energy each electron is given
    by the battery.
   A pressure switch is shown below that is suggested in the extension activity.
       LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
 Take students outside.
 Have all students stand in a circle arms distance apart. They are the carriers of
   electricity (electrons). They release their arms once in position.
 Nominate two students to be the battery, they form an arch with their arms held
   high for students to walk though.
 Nominate a student to stand next to the battery and hold a bowl of M&Ms or
   similar at the edge of the circle.
 Nominate two students to be the light, they form an arch with arms together out at
   waist height. Students need to bend down to pass through.
   The students are given an M&M as they pass the battery as energy. They then use
   some of this energy to get under the arch of the light and they must keep some of the
   M&M in their mouth to make it back to the battery to be given more energy. The
   students must walk around the circle and always stay an arms width apart.

title: EXP-How Sound Travels
subject: Science
searchText:
How Sound Travels


Objectives:

1. To demonstrate that sound moves through different states of matter.

2. To observe that sound moves better through a solid than it does through a
  liquid or a gas.

Materials needed:

Demo: bell, tuning fork, cork, balloon, two spoons, musical triangle, slide
   whistle, two wood blocks, windup clock, 12" ruler, large jar filled
   with water, paper bag, metal can and lid, plastic container with lid,
   metal bar, music box motor.

Each group needs: meter stick, windup clock, self-sealing plastic bag filled
    with water, a block of wood (the same thickness as the plastic bag of
    water), two plastic cups with one end of a string through the hole in
    the bottom of one cup and the other end of the string through the hole
    in the bottom of the other cup. Knot the ends of the string to stop it
    from pulling out of the holes (home-made telephone), a third plastic cup
    with a string attached to the bottom of the cup, a metal rod.

Strategy:

Have the children identify different sounds made behind a screen (or desk) by
using various materials: ringing a bell, hitting a tuning fork on a cork,
blowing up a balloon and releasing air by stretching the neck of the balloon as
the air escapes, tapping two spoons together, striking the musical triangle,
blowing a slide whistle, hitting two wooden blocks together and ringing an
alarm clock. Record the children's answers on the board. Show the materials
used and check against the predictions made.

Hold a ruler over the edge of a desk and vibrate it asking such questions as:
What is happening? What is your evidence? What is always happening to an
object when it is making a sound?

Strike a tuning fork on a cork and quickly lower it into a glass of water.
Ask the questions stated above. Does sound travel through other things?

Activities:

Demo: Does sound travel through paper? through plastic? through metal?
   1. Put a ringing alarm clock in a paper bag.
   2. Close the bag. Can you hear the clock ringing now?
   3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 using a plastic container and a metal can.

    Does sound travel through water?
    1. Fill a glass jar nearly full of water.
    2. Have one student cover one ear with her/his hand. Put the other
      ear against the glass jar.
    3. Ask another student to hit two spoons together under water.
      Do you hear a sound?

Sound travels through different kinds of matter. Sound travels through gases,
liquids and solids.

Group: What kind of matter does sound travel best in--air, water, wood or
    metal?
  A. 1. Hold a plastic bag of water against one of your ears. Cover
       your other ear with your hand. Have someone hold a ticking
       clock against the bag of water. Listen.
    2. Keep the clock in the same place. Remove the bag of water. Listen.
    3. Place a block of wood between your ear and the clock. Listen.
       Do you hear the clock best through the air, the water or the wood?
   B. 1. Place the clock 20 cm away from your ear and listen to the ticking.
    2. Have your partner hold the clock at the 20-cm mark on the meter
       stick. Place your ear at the end of the meter stick and listen.
    3. Have your partner hold a metal rod to your ear and place the clock
       against the rod 20 cm away from your ear. Listen. Does sound move
       differently through some solids than it does through others?

  C. 1. Take the plastic cups (telephone) and hold your cup to your ear
       while your friend talks slowly and clearly into the other cup. Keep
       the string tight. How does it work? What is vibrating? How do the
       vibrations of your friend's voice reach your ear?
    2. Can a third person talk and listen if another cup with a string is
       attached? Take the separate cup with the string and attach it to
       the first line. Keep all strings tight while one friend talks into
       one cup and the other two friends listen. Can you hear the message
       of the third party? How many lines could you attach? Does each
       addition weaken the vibrations?

Draw three squares on the board and in each square draw molecules spaced
accordingly to illustrate the three states of matter: gas (molecules far
apart), liquid (molecules closer together) and solid (molecules closest
together). Have students identify the different states of matter for each
square.

Finally, take the small music box motor, hold it in your hand and allow the
music to play. Ask the students if they hear the music. Now place the music
box motor on top of your desk or on a large surface area and listen to the
melody. Is there any difference? Can the students hear the music now? Why?

title: EXP-Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
subject: Science
searchText:
Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
It is not uncommon among concertgoers to leave a concert unable to
hear. In most cases their hearing returns shortly. Unfortunately,
permanent hearing loss from loud concerts is becoming increasingly
common. The situation can be even more serious for musicians,
because they suffer more frequent and prolonged exposure to loud
music than most people. It can also be more devastating for a
musician to lose his hearing, because his livelihood and passion often
leave with his hearing.

Sound levels at concerts can be in the range of 120 to 140 db, well
beyond the 100 db normally recognized as the threshold at which
short-duration exposure can cause hearing loss. The loss is caused by
damage to fragile tissue strands within the cochlea. These strands are
called hair cells and resemble tiny hairs. They move with the fluid in
the cochlea to stimulate the electrical impulses in the auditory nerve.
The hair cells become damaged in the presence of loud noise.

The mechanism of damage is much like the mechanism by which
constant walking on grass can damage it. A person walking on a lawn
occasionally doesn't damage the lawn, because the grass has a
chance to recover between tramplings. But if the grass is subjected to
frequent traffic, it soon loses its ability to spring back and becomes
permanently damaged. Damage to the hair cells occurs the same way.
The louder and more frequent the exposure to loud noise, the more
damage the hair cells sustain.

Fortunately, our ears often warn us when we have subjected them to
potentially damaging sound levels. Temporary hearing loss is one
indication; ringing in the ears is another. If you experience either of
these symptoms after exposure to loud sounds, it's an almost sure
indication of temporary damage that could become permanent with
repeated exposure.

For people who are unable or unwilling to remove themselves from
noisy situations, earplugs can help preserve hearing. Earplugs are
especially effective at reducing the intensity of high frequency sound,
which is what does the most damage to the hair cells. A 15 or 20 db
reduction in the intensity of high frequency sound can delay or prevent
hair cell damage.

Juliette M. Walker - Crown Community Academy



Now Hear This!

Juliette M. Walker        Crown Community Academy
751 E. 84st. Apt#2e         2128 S. St.Louis
CHICAGO IL 60619            CHICAGO IL 60623
(773) 488-3157            (773) 534-1680

Objective(s):

In this project, students will be able to describe how sounds are heard by the
human ear by creating a model of the human inner ear. This activity may be
utilized by grades 3 - 8.


Materials Needed:

Students may be placed into cooperative learning groups of 3.
 1long paper roll (used gift wrap rolls are perfect)
 plastic wrap        medium sized disc of foil rubber bands
 2cardboard paper discs doublestick tape             pink tissue paper
 flashlights        1 large box scissors       cardboard fork shape
(1 set of each item is needed for each group)

Strategy:

1. Students will create an eardrum by stretching a piece of plastic wrap across
  the end of the paper roll fixing it in place with a rubber band.
2. Students will create a set of ossicles with two cardboard discs and a fork
  shape of thin cardboard. This will be held together with doublesided tape.
3. Students will then attach a disk of shiny foil to one end of the roll, and
  will attach the other to the plastic wrap "ear drum" on the tube. This will
  complete the middle ear.
4. Students will then make an outer ear from a cone of cardboard with a hole
  at its end and will place it on the inside of the tube. Students may design
  their cone with pink tissue paper, for a more realistic look.
5. Students will then place the middle of the model of the ear on a box,
  leaving the ends of the rolls hanging off of the front and back.
6. Students will then shine a light onto the mirror and will ask a partner to
  to talk into the ear and watch for vibrations.
7. Have the students to watch the window of the ear. Have them describe how it
  responds to shouting, whispering, whistling etc.

Performance Assessment:

Students will be evaluated based upon their models, and oral explanations as
to how their ear works.

Conclusions:

This project works because the sound waves from the students voice makes the
plastic wrap vibrate. These vibrations are transmitted into the cardboard
"ossicles" and can be seen by watching the foil disc for movements. This is
a simple model of how the ear works.

References:

This project was adapted from the Encyclopedia of Science Projects written by
Pam Robeson, and Mick Seller (Shooting Star Press, 1994) (Aladdin Books, ltd,
1994)

searchText:
Waves


Objectives:

Students will be able to define, label and demonstrate the following vocabulary words: wave, wave motion,
longitudinal wave, transverse wave, pulse, crest, energy trough, amplitude, frequency, reflection,
Rarefaction, refraction and compression. Students will be able to state the properties that a medium must
possess in order that waves may be transmitted through it. Students will be able to tell the essential
difference between a longitudinal and a transverse wave. Students will be able to know how to make a
longitudinal or compress ional pulse and a transverse pulse. Students will be able to determine the time it
takes a pulse to travel down the rope or a slinky. Students will be able to understand that a wave is a
means of transmitting energy.

Apparatus Needed:

Marbles, grooved ruler or stick, hose or rope, large pan of water, cork, small stone, ripple tank, medicine
dropper, overhead projector, coil spring, meterstick, watch, slinky, string or fishing line, smooth pole or
stiff wire, curtain rings, movies

Recommended:

1. Place five or six marbles in a groove so that they touch each other. Roll another marble against the end
of the line of marbles. The vibration of waves will be transmitted through the line and the marbles on the
end will roll away. Roll two, then three and so on. Observe what happens.
2. Move the hose or rope up and down to make transverse waves. Drop the stone into the water. Observe
what happens.

3. Fill the flat pan about half full of water. Place the pan on an
overhead projector or tabletop. Fill a medicine dropper with water.
Allow one drop of water to fall into the center of the pan. Allow
another drop to fall near the edge. Notice what happens in each.
Sketch the pattern of waves that are seen.

4. Move a rope up and down. Describe and explain what kind of waves is observed. Cut equal-lengths of
string at least one meter long. Tie a curtain ring to one end of each string. Attach the free end of a piece
of string to every fifth coil of the slinky. Slip the curtain rings onto the pole [or wire], and then suspend it
from the ceiling. Observe: send a longitudinal pulse down the spring by pinching together several coils of
the spring and then releasing them. What kind of pulse is this? [Longitudinal or compress ional] What
happens to the shape of the pulse as it travels down the wire?
 Quickly pull the free end of the slinky to one side and then return it to its original position. What kind of
pulse is this? What happens to the shape of the pulse as it travels down the string? Determine the time it
takes a pulse to travel down the string. Change the amplitude of the pulse and again determine the travel
time. How does changing the amplitude affect the speed of the wave?
Change the medium by stretching the spring to a different length. Determine the speed of a pulse in this
new medium. How does changing the medium affect the speed of a wave?

Procedure
   1. Place the single slit slide in the end of the Hodson light box closest to the light source.

   A complete circuit is like a circle. No circuit will work if it has a break in it.

   A switch can be used to provide a break in a circuit.

LESSON 10 E&C                    BUILD A LIGHTHOUSE




         AIM OF THE LESSON


   During this lesson students will:
            Apply their understanding of simple circuits, batteries, copper wire and a
             globe to construct a lighthouse.
            Use conductors and switches to construct a lighthouse.
            Design a simple pressure switch for the lighthouse circuit.



         EQUIPMENT

Preparation

Safety

        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


Lighthouse features

      A lighthouse is a building that was made to guide ships. The most important part
       of a lighthouse is the light that it casts at night. Sometimes lighthouses guide
       ships to a port or harbour. Other times they guide ships away from a hazard.
       Sometimes they do both.
      At night, lighthouses guide ships with their light. All ships have a book, called a
       Light List, which tells them the characteristics of lighthouses. If a mariner saw a
       white light flashing every seven-and-a -half seconds, he could look it up and find
       out which lighthouse it is.
      During the day, lighthouses guide ships with a day mark. A lighthouse's day
       mark is simply its size, shape and colour.




Lighthouses in Western Australia


   A few of the well known light houses in WA include:
    Rottnest Island
    Cape Naturaliste, Dunsborough
    Cape Leeuwin, Augusta
    Fremantle North Mole (red)
    Cape Leveque
    Fremantle South Mole (green)

searchText:
Sound is Vibration


Objectives:

This lesson is designed for grade levels 1 - 3.
1. To understand that sound is caused by vibration.
2. To understand that sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
3. To understand that high pitched sounds are caused by more vibrations and low
  pitched sounds are caused by fewer vibrations.

Materials Needed:

plastic ruler(s), tuning forks of 2 or 3 different pitches, ping-pong ball
attached to a string with tape, boom-box-type radio, balloon filled with air,
paper plate, tiny pieces of torn paper, baggie filled with water, scissors,
several glass bottles of the same size, large container for water, styrofoam
cups, wire coat hangers, string (different types), wire cutters, pencils (with
wooden ball attached to the eraser end if possible), stopwatch, flower pots of
varying sizes attached to rope, long tubes of PVC pipe cut to different lengths
for different tones, xylophone, plastic straws, tape.

Strategy:

1. Ask children if anyone knows what a vibration is. Ask children to vibrate
their bodies. Write vibrate on board. Put a plastic ruler overhanging the edge
of a table; hit the ruler and watch it vibrate. Ask: "Can we see the vibration?
Can we hear the vibration? Can we feel it?" Show tuning fork; hit; listen;
touch vibrating tuning fork to ping pong ball attached to a string. Observe the
effect; ask same questions. Pass tuning forks around so children can experience
the sound and feel the vibration; note differences in pitch. Hold inflated
balloon in front of boom-box speaker with volume turned up loud. "Can you feel
the vibration? Where is it coming from?" Place small paper plate with tiny
pieces of paper on it on top of speaker. (Boombox must be turned so that
speakers are facing up.) Observe what happens to the papers. Explain that all
sounds are caused by something vibrating; sound is vibration, etc.

2. How do vibrations from tuning fork and ruler reach us as sound? The
vibrations cause waves to carry sound through the air. (You will perhaps need
to discuss waves, depending on age and experience of children.) "We know
sound
travels through air. Does it travel through a solid? Put your ear on the desk.
Tap the desk. What do you hear?" Try several such examples. "Does sound
travel through a liquid?" Get children to talk about experiences they have had
such as talking underwater in the bathtub or swimming pool. Can they hear
sound
under water? "Try putting a plastic baggie filled with water next to your ear.
Have another child speak loudly directly into the other side of the baggie. Can
we hear the sound through the water? Does sound travel through a solid, a
liquid, and a gas (air)? When was it the loudest?" (through the solid) "Why
do you think this may be true?" (The molecules in a solid are more tightly
packed, so the vibration can travel without being dispersed as it does in air.)

3. Show a child's xylophone or an autoharp. Strike a short bar, then a long bar
and ask children what they heard. Do the same for the lengths of PVC pipe.
(Hit the end of the pipes with the palm of your hand.) Make a kazoo out of a
plastic straw by flattening one end and cutting it into a triangular shape;
blow. As one person blows through the kazoo, another takes a scissors and snips
an inch or so off the end. Keep doing this and ask the students to notice
 what's happening to the sound as the straw gets shorter. Help them relate the
shortness of length to high pitch through a variety of such experiences.

4. Now allow the children to experiment and "play" with all the materials so
that they develop strong physical understanding of vibrations in all the ways
that have been presented. Have a set of 8 identical bottles and a container of
water and have them fill the bottles with varying amounts of water. See if they
can match the scale of the bottles to that of the xylophone. Give children the
opportunity to make a string phone or wire-hanger chime. (Tie a length of
string to each end of a wire coat hanger. Put the other end of each string in
your ears, tap the hanger against something like a desk. Listen for the ringing
through the string.)

Performance Assessment:

1. Children must: Arrange bottles with varying amounts of water in row
according to pitch. Explain the relationship between the amount of water and
the pitch. Tell what is vibrating. Blow across or just into the top of each
bottle and explain how the relationship between pitch and the amount of water in
the bottle changes. Hypothesize as to why this might be.

2. Make a stereo coat hanger as explained above. Tell how you might make one
with a higher pitch (shorter wire). Cut hanger with wire cutter to get
different lengths and different pitches.

3. Make a straw kazoo. Listen to its pitch. Have your partner cut off an inch
or two with a scissors while you are blowing. What happens to the sound? Cut
off another inch. What do you notice now?

4. Listen to the sound of each tuning fork. (Strike tuning fork on your shoe

title: Gamma ray
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Gamma ray 1 Gamma ray Gamma rays (γ-rays) are electromagnetic waves with the smallest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum.[1] They were discovered in 1900 by Paul Villard, and named in 1903 by Ernest Rutherford. Gamma rays are like x-rays, but the waves are smaller. Both gamma rays and x-rays are photons with very high energies, and gamma have even more energy. They are also a type of ionizing radiation. Gamma rays can travel through thicker materials than x-rays can. Gamma rays are produced by some types of radioactive atoms. Cobalt-60 and potassium-40 are two isotopes that emit gamma rays. Cobalt-60 is created in accelerators and is used in hospitals. Potassium-40 occurs naturally. Small amounts of potassium-40 are in all plants and animals. Gamma rays from potassium-40 each have an energy of 1460 thousand electron volts (keV). Gamma rays and X-rays can also be distinguished by their origin: X-rays are emitted by electrons outside the nucleus, while gamma rays are emitted by the nucleus.[2] Gamma rays in medicine Gamma rays can also go through the skin to kill cells, such as cancerous cells. Doctors can use radiation therapy machines which produce gamma rays in hospitals to treat people with some types of cancer.[] Doctors also use gamma rays to find disease. In hospitals, doctors can give patients radioactive medicine which emits gamma rays. Doctors can find some types of disease by measuring gamma rays which come from a patient afterward. You can also use gamma rays to sterilise (clean) hospital material.[] References [1] The electromagnetic spectrum is made of many types of waves that are like light, but you can not see all of them. [2] Feynman, Richard; Robert Leighton, Matthew Sands 1963. The Feynman Lectures on Physics, vol 1. USA: Addison-Wesley. pp2–5 ISBN 0201021161. title: Health Effects of Noise
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿Health Effects of Noise Noise Exposure Noise is perhaps the most common occupational and environmental hazard. As many as 30 million Australians are exposed to potentially harmful sound levels in their workplaces. Outside of work, many people pursue recreational activities that can produce harmful noise. Non-occupational sources of noise include chain saws and other power tools, amplified music, and recreational vehicles such as motorcycles. Some types of toys for children can produce sounds capable of causing permanent hearing damage. Common Sources of Noise Sound Loudness (dB) Gunshot (peak level) 140 to 170 Jet takeoff 140 Rock concert, chain saw 110 to 120 Diesel locomotive, stereo headphones 110 to 120 Motorcycle, lawnmower 90 Conversation 60 Quiet room 50 Whisper 30 to 40 Noise can be described in terms of intensity (perceived as loudness) and frequency (perceived as pitch). Both the intensity and the duration of noise exposure determine the potential for damage to the hair cells of the inner ear. Even sounds perceived as "comfortably" loud can be harmful. Sound intensity is measured as the sound pressure level in the decibel (dB) scale. Noise can cause permanent hearing loss at chronic exposures equal to an average of 85 dB or higher for an eight-hour period. The decibel scale is a logarithmic scale. A 3-dB increase represents a doubling of the sound intensity. Four hours of noise exposure at 88 dB(A) is considered to provide the same noise "dose" as eight hours at 85 dB and a single gunshot, which is approximately 140 to 170 dB, has the same sound energy as 40 hours of 90-dB noise. Health Effects When sounds are measured in decibels, the softest sounds we can hear are about 1 dB and extremely loud sounds are about 150 dB. Most people find sounds louder than 130 dB very painful. To reduce the risks of hearing damage, workers in noisy jobs are now required to wear protective ear muffs. The cabins of noisy machinery are insulated to reduce noise. Apart from deafness, another common hearing problem caused by too much noise exposure is tinnitus. This is when you hear a constant ringing sound in your ears.

title: Infrared
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Infrared 1 Infrared Infrared (IR) radiation is a type of electromagnetic radiation (a wave with electricity) . The wave is longer than light which humans can see and shorter than microwaves. The word infrared means below red. It comes from the Latin word infra (meaning below) and the English word red. (Infrared light has a frequency below the frequency of red light.) Red light has the longest wavelength that human eyes can see. Picture of dog in mid-infrared Infrared waves cannot be seen by the eye. The infrared wave is between 750 nm and 1 mm. People sense infrared as heat. Most remote controls use infrared to send the control signals. Telecommunications Before Bluetooth was invented, some computers, personal digital assistants, and mobile phones were using the infrared technology to send files to other devices. Bluetooth replaced infrared in the early 2000's. Infrared is limited by the need to have both devices in a "line of sight" with each other.[1] Infrared lasers are used to provide the light for optical fiber communications systems. Infrared light with a wavelength around 1,330 nm (least dispersion) or 1,550 nm (best transmission) are the best choices for standard silica fibers. Spectroscopy Infrared vibrational spectroscopy (IR spectroscopy) can be used to identify molecules by listing their chemical bonds. An IR spectrometer is a machine that shines infrared light from a set range of frequencies on a sample. It measures which exact light frequencies are absorbed by the sample. Each chemical bond in a molecule vibrates at a frequency which is characteristic of that bond. A group of atoms in a molecule may have multiple modes of oscillation caused by the stretching and bending motions of the group as a whole. If an oscillation leads to a change in dipole in the molecule, then it will absorb a photon which has the same frequency. The vibrational frequencies of most molecules correspond to the frequencies of infrared light. Typically, the technique is used to study organic compounds using light radiation from 4000–400 cm−1, the mid-infrared. The spectrometer records all the frequencies of absorption in a sample. This can be used to gain information about the sample composition in terms of chemical groups present and also its purity (for example a wet sample will show a broad O-H absorption around 3200 cm−1). searchText: 2019 Version Light and Sound Junior Science What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of wave form are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Particle movement in transverse and longitudinal waves Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. Sound travels in the form of longitudinal waves. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water or solid. Waves generated from Earthquakes can be transverse or longitudinal The waves generated from an earthquake travel through the ground as both longitudinal and transverse waves. Primary (or P) waves are longitudinal waves and move the fastest. They are similar to sound waves and can travel at 5000 metres per second through solid rock. Longitudinal waves can also travel through liquid and gas, travelling at the speed of sound through air. Secondary (or S) waves are transverse waves and can only travel through solids. They travel at nearly half the speed of P waves. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. Electromagnetic radiation travels as waves Light and other types of electromagnetic radiation from the sun and even further away stars travel through space in a vacuum – Light does not need matter or a medium through which to travel. Each particular type of electromagnetic radiation, including each different colour of light, has a unique fixed length of wave, called the wavelength (λ), that it travels in. GZ Science Resources 8 Types of Electromagnetic radiation Some objects, such as the sun, release large amounts of energy. The energy can be emitted from the energy source in the form of electromagnetic radiation and travels in electromagnetic waves. Light, radio waves and x-rays are all forms of electromagnetic 9 radiation. GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. A higher amplitude wave indicates a wave has more strength and that a light wave contains more photons, little packets of light energy. A nanometre is very small Small objects such as atoms, viruses and light waves need to be measured using very small units called a nanometre. A metre (m) can be divided into one thousand equal parts called millimetres (mm). If one millimetre is divided into a thousand equal parts then we have a micrometre (µm). If one micrometre is divided into a thousand parts then we have a nanometre (nm). A nanometre is one- billionth of a metre. Wavelengths can be measured in metres (m) or nanometres (nm). The type of electromagnetic radiation can be determined by its wavelength. 11 Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength . wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency ( f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency c Frequency = speed of light / wavelength λ f 13 Light energy is carried by photons The amount of energy in a wave depends upon the frequency of the wave. The energy of a photon can be calculated by multiplying the frequency by another constant called Planck’s constant (h). This constant is named after a famous German scientist called Max Planck who made many discoveries about light and how it also travels as particles called photons. A photon does not have mass like matter does, it only contains energy. Planck’s constant is 6.626 x 10-34 joules per second. This value is so small because a photon is so tiny but there are so many of them within a light wave. Structure and Function of the human ear Sound waves travel through the ear canal and cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the inner ear cochlea. The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells detect different wave frequencies and transmit this information to the brain using electrical impulses that move along the nerves. Audible range of humans and other animals Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see” without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long distances. Pitch and Loudness of sound Sound can be described by “characteristics” called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to frequency – the higher the frequency then the higher the pitch of the note (a single sound at a particular level). Loudness is related to amplitude – the higher the amplitude the louder the sound. Reflecting sound waves Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce off nearby objects, and some of them reflect back to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialized machines can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement. Total internal reflection When waves are going from a dense medium to a less dense medium they speed up at the boundary. This causes light rays to bend when they pass from glass to air at an angle other than 90º. This is refraction. Beyond a certain angle, called the critical angle, all the waves reflect back into the glass. We say that they are totally internally reflected. All light waves, which hit the surface beyond this critical angle, are effectively trapped. The critical angle for most glass is about 42 °. Fibre optics makes use of this so light rays can travel down a glass fibre that has curves in it. Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels perfectly straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays.. Gaze Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it— must enter the eye. An object that stops direct light rays creates a shadow. The shape of the shadow resembles the shape of the object. The shadow created when the Moon blocks the light from the Sun to the Earth is called a solar eclipse. The length of the shadow depends on the angle of the light source The length of the shadow formed on the ground depends on the angle that the light rays hit the object blocking the light. searchText: 794385 880110 0 0 Wavelength – the distance between one crest and the next crest, or one trough and the next trough on a wave. Colour – the light reflected off an object. For example, a red apple looks red because all the colours of white light are absorbed into the apple, except for red light which is reflected off it and passes into our eyes. Dispersion – white light being split into the seven different colours. Spectrum – the pattern of colours which make up white light. Speed of light – light travels at 300 000 kilometres per second. Reflection – the bouncing of light off a surface. Regular reflection – parallel rays of light that hit a smooth surface and are reflected parallel to each other. For example, mirror. Irregular reflection (diffuse reflection) – parallel light rays that hit a rough surface and are reflected in all directions. Example, newspaper. -523240 894080 0 0 Ray diagram – diagram that shows the incident ray and reflected ray off a surface. 859790 859155 0 0 Refraction – the bending of light that happens when light passes through one substance and into another. Transparent – Transparent materials allow all light to pass through it. Example, glass window. Translucent – Translucent materials let some light through. Example, tissue paper. Opaque – Opaque materials do not allow light to pass through them. They either block or absorb the light. Example, cardboard. Shadow – an opaque object blocking light from covering an area.

reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Microwave 1 Microwave A microwave is a kind of high-frequency radio wave. It is often used to cook food in a microwave oven. We can see waves travelling through water. There are many sorts of these waves, such as ripples, swell, tsunami, and even sound waves that we do not see, but we hear if our ears are under the water. Likewise, many different types of waves can travel through the air. We detect one type with our eyes as colours; we detect another type when it lands on our skin, as warmth; another type is called X-rays. Other types of these invisible waves are called microwaves. We cannot see them. They can quickly penetrate quite deep into materials that contain water, for example most food. The energy in these waves makes the water molecules vibrate faster, which means the water gets hotter. Although they can also heat some metals, there are materials, including many plastics, which they pass right through, without heating at all. Although many plastics used in bowls or cups will melt and get super-heated in microwave ovens. title: Radio wave
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Radio wave 1 Radio wave Radio waves make up part of the electromagnetic spectrum. These waves are packets of energy with differing wavelengths, similar to visible light waves, X-rays or Gamma rays, except longer. A radio wave, like other electromagnetic waves, is similar to an ocean wave or any other type of wave. Both types of wave have a hill and valley shape, repeating over and over. A wavelength is measured as the distance from the top of one crest to the top of its neighboring crest. While the wavelength of visible light is very very small, less than one micrometer and much less than the thickness of a human hair, radio waves can have a wavelength from a couple centimeters to several meters. Antennas designed to detect radio waves are usually similar in size to the wavelength they wish to detect. This is why many radio antennas (like those on cars) must be very long. If the antennas are not close to the size of the wavelength they do not usually do a good job of detecting the waves. Manmade radio waves have been used for a long time to send information, receive information, and to 'see' objects. Radar uses radio waves to 'see' distant objects by bouncing waves off an object and seeing how long it takes for the waves to return. Radar can even be used to find oil or see what chemicals are in soil. Radios also use these waves to send and receive information. Natural radio waves were first discovered in the 1930s by Karl Guthe Jansky, working for Bell Laboratories. Before his discovery, everyone thought only people could generate radio waves. Bell was detecting static on his radio channels, and had Jansky try to figure out where this static, or interference was coming from. Surprisingly, the interference was coming from space! This discovery eventually led astronomers to look at radio waves along with optical waves to find things in the sky. These radio astronomers use giant Radio telescopes, shaped like satellite dishes, to gather and analyze the waves. Uses Radio waves are used for many things today. They broadcast radio and television, communicate with satellites, let mobile phones communicate with each other, make radar systems, and allow computers to share information without wires. searchText:
Refraction
 Aim: To observe the relationship between angle of incidence and refraction


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Ray box
                                                         Filament bulb – risk of burns
• Single slit plate
                                                         Handle with extra care. Rinse any
• Lab pack (if needed)                                   burns under cold running water for
                                                         10 minutes and inform the teacher immediately.
• Protractor

• Pencil and ruler

• Paper




                Figure 1. Set-up



                                                                 Figure 2. Measurements


Method:
Step 1: Place the glass block flat in the middle of the paper and draw around it.

Step 2: Direct the light from the ray box onto one of the longer sides of the glass block, at a diagonal
angle.

Step 3: Trace over the ray as it leaves the ray box and enters the glass box (the incidence ray). You can
tidy up the line with the ruler afterwards.

Step 4: Trace over the ray as it leaves the glass block on the other side (the emergent ray). You can tidy
up the line with the ruler afterwards.


                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                                                 Refraction

Step 5: Remove the glass block and join the incidence and emergent rays with a straight line.

Step 6: Use the ruler and protractor to mark normal lines at the point where the incidence ray enters
the glass block, and the point where the emergent ray leaves the glass block.

Step 7: Measure the angle of incidence (A), angle of refraction (r) and angle of emergence (B). Record
these in the table.

Step 8: Repeat steps 1 to 7 for at least four different angles of incidence.


Results:


      Angle of Incidence                 Angle of Refraction                   Angle of Emergence




Questions:

1. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.

2. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of emergence.

3. What is the name of the type of wave by which light is transmitted?

4. Explain refraction in terms of density and wave speed.



                                                 Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of refraction; A > r.

2. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal.

3. Transverse wave (electromagnetic spectrum wave).

4. The velocity of the light wave is decreased as it enters a denser medium (the glass block). As
   it enters at an angle, the ray is ‘bent’ (refracted). When the light ray emerges into the original
   medium again (air) it resumes the same velocity and angle as before it entered the glass block.

Science in the news – living ear grown in lab

Teaching notes

This task can be used when covering cells, tissues and organs with GCSE students or high achieving
KS3 groups.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘Living ear grown in lab’. Further information
and web links can be found at http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/08August/Pages/Artificial-ear-grown-in-
lab.aspx.
All links were available at the time of publishing.


Starter
As an interesting stimulus show the class the famous image of a human ear grown on a mouse's back
(http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/1949073.stm). You may also like to show them a video
(http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHHe_q3DNas).
Ask the students to discuss in pairs why they think scientists have done this and feedback their ideas.
Explain that some people have lost ears through injury or because they were born without them (you
might like to show a suitable image at this point) and this kind of research is helping to work out ways
of building human tissue in the lab to help such people. It is called tissue engineering. The image
shown at the start shocked the world when it was released in 1997. Since then, tissue engineering is
making progress and the same team have recently announced improvements to the human ears they
are engineering.


Main
Students complete Task 1. If you have access to microscopes and slides with cartilage then students
could use them to take a look at some cartilage and draw what they observe.
Go through the answers with the students:


Answers

2. Cartilage is a tissue because it is made up of one type of cell (chondroblasts). The ear is an organ
   because it is made up of several different tissues all working together to perform a function.
3a. Cartilage in the outer ear contains mostly elastin in its extracellular matrix so it is flexible.
3b. The cartilage that makes up the rings around the trachea contain mostly collagen so it is strong
    enough to hold open the trachea so air can pass through.
4. Titanium was used because it is lightweight so the ear would be light enough to wear and also it is
   non-reactive. This is important so it does not react with the cells.
5a. The rat's immune system would have attacked the foreign cartilage cells and rejected the ear if it
    had a functioning immune system.
5b. If the ears are to be used in humans then the patient's immune system would have to be
     suppressed or the ear would be rejected. With a weak immune system the patient would be at
     risk from infections.
5c. To avoid this problem the replacement ear would have to be made using the patient's own
    cartilage cells.

Then ask students to work in small groups to complete Task 2. They should cut out the cards and use
the information to answer the question: 'How close are we to building replacement outer ears?'

Ask students from each group to read out their statement. Discuss with the class what steps the
researchers need to take next.



Plenary
Discuss with the students the need for scientists to develop techniques to build other replacement
body parts such as whole organs. Talk about why this is more complicated and why. For example,
organs are made up of many tissues working together, they require a blood supply and connection to
the nervous system.
Ask the students to consider the question: 'How close are we to building replacement organs?' Ask
them to stand in a line to form a continuum to show where they think we are in this endeavour.



Homework idea
Ask the students to do some research into other teams that are working in the field of tissue
engineering and summarise their work in their own words. For example, another recent news story
reported that a team have grown a miniature human brain (see http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-

Questions:
 1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?

 Answers
1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current remains the same / unchanged in a series circuit.

2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current is shared between the number of branches / bulbs in the parallel circuit.

3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage is shared between the bulbs in a series circuit.

4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage remains the same for all bulbs in a parallel circuit.

5. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the current of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a series circuit has no effect on the current, whereas in a
   parallel circuit the current is shared between the branches.

6. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the voltage of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a parallel circuit has no effect on the voltage supplied to each
   bulb, whereas in a series circuit the voltage is shared between the bulbs.

searchText: ﻿SERIES AND PARALLEL CIRCUITS There are two basic arrangements of components in a circuit. Series Circuits The resistors are added end-to-end so that the whole current flows through each resistor in turn. • There is only one path for the current through the circuit. • If one component stops working, they all stop working. • Resistance increases with more components added. Parallel Circuits The resistors are on separate branches, and the current splits up to flow through each branch, depending on its resistance. • Current splits up - there are multiple pathways. • If one component is turned off, the others keep working. • Resistance decreases for more and more resistors connected in parallel.

subject: Science
searchText: Sources of Light We can see most objects because light bounces off of them into our eyes. However some objects are a source of light as they are luminous . This means they produce their own light eg the sun or a torch. Objects that do not produce their own light eg the moon or people, are non-luminous . They require light from another source to be seen. Non-luminous objects can be classified into 3 groups: Transparent – Light can trav el through it easily without any interference eg glass, air, water Translucent – Some light is transmitted but some is absorbed. Vision is interfered with eg frosted glass. Opaque – No light is transmitted eg people, wood and metal. When ever light is prevented from hitting a surface by an opaque object a shadow is formed.

title: Static Electricity
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿ Lesson 2 e&c DANCING WITH STATIC­­­­­­­­­­­­­­ AIM OF THE LESSON During this lesson students will: • Describe how a transfer of energy from one material to another can create static electricity. • Name some examples of static electricity. EQUIPMENT Per Class • 1 foam cup filled with water • 1 compass or sharp object • 5 tea bags • a variety of materials eg nylon; wool; fur; silk; paper; cotton; rubber; chux; stockings; polyester; plastic; sponge ( a few of each is best) Per Group • 2 balloons • 1 plastic comb or plastic pen cover • 1 ball of wool (not acrylic) or piece of wool cloth • 1 empty soft drink can • 5 or 6 styrofoam balls/ packing foam/ beans out of bean bag or puffed wheat Preparation • Collection of materials to test (Students could bring in one each and could be a piece of clothing as they do not need to be cut). Safety ▪ Nil Background Information for teachers Electricity ◦ The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber – electron. ◦ Electricity is a form of energy that is used in many ways in daily life. ◦ Electricity can be observed in the natural environment – eg lightning. ◦ All matter is made of small particles called atoms. ◦ Within atoms are tiny particles called electrons which are negatively charged. Static Electricity • When materials come in contact with each other electrons may be transferred from one material to the other. • This causes a build up of charge which is called static electricity. • If a substance picks up electrons it becomes negatively charged. • When materials have different charges they attract each other. When they have similar charges they repel. • When there is a very big difference between these charges, when the objects come in contact they produce a spark. • By rubbing certain objects together they become charged with electricity. • Wool cloth and human hair readily give up electrons. • Humid weather reduces the effectiveness of static electricity. • When students rub materials on their hair it is best if the hair is fine and dry with no gel or hair spray. Electric Shocks • If you rub your feet on a carpet, your entire body can become charged. • The excess electrons in your body need to go somewhere. Therefore, when you touch something that is not charged (like a large piece of metal) it absorbs the extra electrons suddenly. • The electrons flow quickly through the tip of your finger into the object you touch with a ZAP! • The flow of electrons might be great enough for you to see a tiny spark and hear a snapping sound. Balloons • A balloon rubbed with a wool cloth becomes negatively charged. • When this balloon is held above some foam balls, the neutrally charged balls become positively charged and leap upward to cling to the balloon. • After several minutes, some of the electrons may drain off the balloon onto the balls. This will cause the balls to become negatively charged and be repelled by the balloon. When this happens they may actually leap off the balloon and back to the table. • The repelled foam balls may then transfer their excess electrons to the table after a few minutes and once again leap toward the balloon. Activities • After the Styrofoam clings to the balloon, students who are patient and wait several minutes may see some of the Styrofoam leap forcibly away from the balloon back to the table. • Students who observe very closely will notice that the same grains of tea will alternately leap toward and away from the comb. Investigating Scientifically • Prediction: what you think may happen in an experiment based on your experiences. Lesson Outline 1. Introduction (Engaging Students) Demonstration • Fill a foam cup with water. • Ask a student to rub a plastic comb with a ball of wool or their hair for 10 secs but do not put the comb down. • Use a compass to put a tiny hole in the bottom of the foam cup to produce a very fine stream of water ( a tap is better if available). • As soon as the water starts to flow hold the charged comb next to the stream of water without touching it. The comb should cause the stream of water to bend towards it. The comb is attracting it like a magnet. Transfer of energy or electrons. Getting a shock when stepping out of a car. Combing hair causes unusual attractions. Turning the TV off sometimes causes a zap and shock. Lightning. Clothes out of the dryer cling together. 2. Activities and Strategies • Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity as a class. • Discuss what is meant by a prediction. Students write a prediction for each activity. • Students conduct the activities on the handout. 3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate) Opposite charges. Like charges. Electrons moving from one material to another. Static electricity is through the air. Other electricity travels in wires. 4. Reflection • In groups, students share one idea that summarises what they have learnt about static electricity. • These could then be shared with the class. • Students to write a conclusion. Extension Activities • Investigate a range of other materials found in the classroom to see if they attract or repel other materials e.g. plastic rulers, erasers, pencil cases. Record your results in a table. Links to other learning Areas • Write a poem about lightning. • Design a bookmark using lightning or static electricity as the focus. • Research about Benjamin Franklin who flew a kite in a lightning storm. • Write a story about a lightning storm. • Make up a crossword puzzle or word sleuth that includes the types of materials you have used in this lesson. • Find out if we see lightning or hear thunder first and why this is so. ACTIVITY 2 DANCING WITH STATIC Aim (What are we going to find out?) Equipment (What do I need to complete the task?) Method (How is the task to be done?) Results (What did I observe?) No Method Prediction (What I think will happen) Observations (What I saw) 1 Rub a balloon with a ball of wool and hold the balloon over a friend’s hair. 2 Rub two balloons with a ball of wool and then hold the balloons side by side. 3 Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near some small torn up pieces of paper. 4 Rub a balloon on a ball of wool, see if you can get it to stick to the wall. 5 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and bring the balloon close to the foam balls. Wait to see what happens. 6 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it above ¼ teaspoon of tea leaves on your desk. Wait to see what happens. 7 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it next to an empty soft drink can which is on its side on a flat surface. • Rub a plastic comb or a plastic pen cover with a selection of materials. • After rubbing each material hold the comb near some foam balls. • Record the material you used and your observations. No Material Observation (attracted or repelled the foam balls) 1 2 3 Conclusion (What did I learn about static electricity?)

searchText:
Taboo – circuit symbols
Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

 1. Students work in teams

 2. Each team needs a set of cards.

 3. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
    and then describes the symbol and keyword at the top of the card without
    using the words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is
    described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes
    with’ and no gestures or sounds. The rest of the team guess the keyword
    and/or draw the symbol.

 5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
    opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
    next word.

 6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words/symbols
    as possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next
    team.

 7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
    point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term and
symbol.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research the keywords and symbols.

Attach your equipment to the mat using masking tape. Follow the instructions and record your results

searchText:
Topical science - healing light
Task
Read the following article and answer the questions.

       Imagine a vivid red light.
       Now think of a time when you were younger and hurt yourself; perhaps you fell
       over and grazed your knee, or scalded yourself whilst helping in the kitchen.
       Imagine simply shining a red light on the injury and the wound healing more
       quickly than usual! This really does work. Not in seconds or hours, that still only
       occurs in science fiction, but shining a certain type of red light onto a wound
       does speed up healing time.
       The light in question is deep red (close to the infra-red part of the
       electromagnetic spectrum). It has a wavelength of 670 nanometres and it
       causes the mitochondria in cells to release more energy (ATP).
       How does it do this?
       At first, scientists speculated that the red light affected the enzymes found in
       mitochondria by speeding up their activity.
       However, the most recent research reveals that it is water which is affected by
       the red light. Water seems to become less viscous (sticky) under this
       wavelength of light.
       The light causes each water molecule to move slightly further away from its
       neighbour, making water 'runnier'. Cells are full of water and it seems enzymes
       in mitochondria work more easily when they are surrounded by water which is
       more fluid.
       Scientists are investigating how this effect could be used to help heal skin
       wounds and burns. It may also be used to help treat some cases of infertility in
       males.



Questions

  1. What are mitochondria?
  2. What is the role of mitochondria in cells?
  3. Describe what you know about infra-red light.
  4. Would the deep red light described in the text be
     visible to our eyes? Can you explain your answer?
  5. Is this light safe to use in this way?
  6. What does 'viscous' mean?
  7. Think of six liquids you might find at home.
     List them in order of viscosity.
  8. Draw a diagram to show the effect of shining
     deep red light on water molecules.

searchText: Ultraviolet 1 Ultraviolet Ultraviolet is the part of the spectrum shown on the left side of the picture above as black—because humans cannot see light of such short wavelength (or high frequency). Many animals such as some insects, some reptiles, crocodiles, salamanders, and small birds can see things that reflect this light. The name 'ultraviolet' uses the ancient Latin prefix ultra-, which means 'behind', 'beyond', or 'far'. Ultraviolet is beyond the visible violet light in terms of frequency, wavelength, and energy. Its wavelengths are between about 10 nanometers (nm) about 400 nanometers. UV is a common abbreviation of ultraviolet, mainly used in technical contexts. Frequency and wavelength are closely related. The equation that shows this relationship is: ν = c/λ (nu, i.e. frequency = speed of light ÷ lamda, i.e., wavelength), so saying that something has a short wavelength is equivalent to saying that it has a high frequency. Ultraviolet radiation Ultraviolet light can damage or kill cells. Any electromagnetic radiation (light) that has a wavelength shorter than 450 nm may cause trouble. Therefore humans that live in places with more ultraviolet light have adapted by getting darker skins. Pigments absorb the ultraviolet radiation, so it does not get through the skin to kill or injure cells inside. Injury to the skin by ultraviolet is called "sunburn." The only difference between violet light and ultraviolet light is the wavelength (or the frequency). The only difference between ultraviolet light and x-rays is also the wavelength or frequency. Ultraviolet is beyond violet, x-rays are beyond ultraviolet, and cosmic rays are beyond x-rays. Cosmic radiation can also be called gamma rays, or gamma radiation. Technically, electromagnetic waves with a frequency of 789 terahertz or more are called ultraviolet. This corresponds with a wavelength from 380 nanometers down to approximately 5 nanometers. A single light quantum or photon of ultraviolet Indoor tanning device carries an energy around some 3.26 electron volt. The higher a photon's frequency, and so the shorter its wavelength, the more energy a photon carries. Ultraviolet 2 Although the air of the Earth is transparent to a broad range of ultraviolet, some ultraviolet sunlight is absorbed at a very high altitude by the ozone layer. Recent and ongoing destruction of ozone in high altitudes caused by human influence—mostly by industrial chemicals and air travel—has greatly increased the amount of ultraviolet light reaching the Earth's surface. This, in turn, has increased the risk of skin cancer to mankind, and this risk will only increase with time unless the ozone layer is better protected. Ultraviolet wavelengths less than 200 nanometers, X-rays, and gamma rays, are collectively called ionizing radiation since the energy in any such light quantum is high enough to 'kick' an electron out of an atom. This is why these kinds of radiation are dangerous to life. Ordinary glass does not let radiation through if its wavelength is less than 200 nanometers, so it acts as a shield against the more dangerous range of ultraviolet light, but some special sorts of glass do not shield as well, including many car windows. One use for ultraviolet radiation is tanning. Use of tanning devices can cause skin cancer because ultraviolet goes through the skin and causes destruction to cells causing sunburn. Because of the destructive power of ultraviolet light, it can be used to kill germs. Sunlight is a powerful disinfectant. Ultraviolet lamp An ultraviolet lamp is one that emits light mostly at a frequency higher than violet, called ultraviolet. These lamps are often used to kill microbes (germs). They can be very powerful, so the people who work around them when they are turned on may need to wear protective glasses and keep their skin covered to avoid injury. In the laboratory pictured, ultraviolet lights are turned on when the workers are gone so that anything on the table surface will be killed. Besides ultraviolet light, which makes up most of the light produced by these lamps, there is also a little violet and blue light. So people can easily tell when the ultraviolet lamps are turned on. searchText: ﻿VOLTAGE, CURRENT AND RESISTANCE Voltage / Potential Difference (V): provides the energy to drive electrons around a circuit. Measured in - volts (V) Current (I): a measure of the rate at which charge (electrons) flows in a circuit. Measured in - Amperes (A) Resistance (R): a measure of the difficulty electrons have in moving around a circuit. Measured in - Ohms () Voltage equals current times resistance V = IR The resistance of a wire is dependent on the following. • Type of material used. e.g. Copper has a lower resistance than nichrome wire. • Diameter of the wire. e.g. Thin wire has a greater resistance than thick wire. The filaments in globes are very thin to give them high resistance which makes the metal get very hot and glow. • Length of the wire. e.g. Long wire has more resistance. Rheostats (variable resistors) used to control fans and lights have the wire wound around a non-conductor to save space.

 What is Energy? (Revision)                     Energy is what causes things to change.
 There are many different types of energy. Here are just a few:

 Type of Energy              Changes Caused by this Energy
 Kinetic (in moving objects) Change in position because object is moving.
 Potential (stored)          Only causes changes when released in another form.
 Heat                        Change in temperature. e.g. a stove causes food to get hot.
 Light                       Nerve changes in your eye which allow you to see things,
                                     or chemical changes in the film in a camera.
 Sound                       Vibrations in your ear which allow you to hear.
 Electrical Energy           Can cause a light bulb to glow and produce light,
