searchText: ﻿ HAND-ME-DOWN GENES An Introduction to Genetics Program 2: Family Patterns Written by Jan Rosenberg BEd Edited by David Brown and Stewart Jackel Teacher Notes Following many requests from teachers, these notes have been printed on A4 size sheets for easy photocopying. 111A MITCHELL STREET BENDIGO VIC 3550 TELEPHONE (03) 5442 2433 FAX (03) 5441 1148 Produced by ROD REES for VEA ,1997 Duration: 28 minutes This program is protected by copyright laws both in Australia and overseas. The penalties for unauthorised copying of this program include a $50,000 fine for individuals and a $250,000 fine for institutions. Program 2: Family Patterns The two part program HAND-ME-DOWN GENES introduces basic genetic concepts for years 9 & 10 science. In particular the programs support the following curricula: National Curriculum - Middle school science Victorian Curriculum - CSF Life and Living strand Level 6 NSW Curriculum - Middle school science - 9 & 10 GENERAL INTRODUCTION Almost every week there are news items of discoveries or new applications of genetic science. Genetically engineered crops and food plants, methods for detecting genetic disorders in embryos, cloned animals and plants, trials of genetic based treatments for life threatening conditions, and the production of many important drugs are just a few. It is important for students to gain a sound understanding of genetics so they can appreciate the impact of these developments and the science behind them. These programs are designed for middle school science students and cover the fundamental ideas needed to understand how genes work and how human characteristics are inherited. They are based on the latest research in genetics and presented in such a way that students will find interesting and comprehensible. The latest in computer generated graphics and film footage of young people discussing their genetic conditions provide engaging examples of the ideas that underpin the programs. USING THE PROGRAMS • The programs offer explanations of the fundamental principles of genetics. The material is logical and dense and therefore lends itself to use in contained segments rather than in a single viewing. • The programs could provide the basis for designing a whole unit of work around each of the main themes - in program 1: (1) How genes work in program 2: (2) Family patterns: inheritance (3) Genetic disorders Program 2: FAMILY PATTERNS Introduction: When you get together for a family photo what do you notice? See how some of the family are very similar....but in the same moment, see how each is very different from each other! Why aren’t brothers and sisters identical? And, how come some siblings ARE identical in everyway? How do we explain the sameness and diversity of family patterns? These are the fundamental questions examined by Program 2 of HAND-ME-DOWN GENES. A recap from Program 1: How Genes Work We have long known that some human conditions “run in families”. Like eye colour, blood group and many other characteristics, they are inherited - controlled by factors called genes. In recent years, geneticists - scientists who research inheritance- have deciphered the code system of genes and how it controls the production of all the different proteins essential for our bodies to grow and function. Program 1 describes and explains the amazing biology at work in this process with particular emphasis on DNA and the role of cell division, mitosis. Because of the duplication through mitosis, all the billions of cells in our body carry the same set of chromosomes and exactly the same alleles. The one exception is in the sex cells. The start of inheritance: The formation of Sex Cells The program highlights how when the body produces sex cells - what are known as the gametes, the cells which form sperm in males and eggs in females - the cell division process undergoes a further development from mitosis. Sex cells divide twice, first by mitosis but then, on a second division the chromosomes are not duplicated leaving resultant cells with half the number of original chromosomes. These go on to form sperm and eggs, or gametes, the reproductive building blocks on which each individual human being is formed. This particular secondary cell division of the sex cells is called meiosis. The difference between meiosis and mitosis, and the function performed by this differential, is clearly explained and illustrated by the animated graphics and precise narration. The Purpose of Meiosis: So, asks the program, why should the sex cells be different from the other body cells? Well, the ultimate grand purpose is to produce new individual human beings! Here is the basis of our individual difference and the our uniqueness. The moment of conception, when the egg is fertilised by the sperm, is the only time in our life cycle when two cells combine to form one cell with equal number of chromosomes from each parent. Biologically then, it is indeed a wondrous moment. Most human body cells contain 46 chromosomes or 23 pairs. As the gametes of each sex contain only 23 chromosomes fertilisation is necessary to restore the new cell to a total of 46 chromosomes. Once the egg is fertilised and has its full compliment of chromosomes it begins to grow and divide by mitosis. Next question: Why differences? Basic logic raises the next question: if chromosomes combine from the same two parents, why do children in a family show all kinds of genetic differences? And why are some male and some female? Answer: its all in your hand-me-down genes ... different eggs and different sperm must carry different genetic information. The program goes on to tell this part of the story starting with the way our sex is determined the sexing instructions are carried in chromosomes. Here the animated graphics clearly show how we X and Y chromosomes are split during meiosis and how the lottery leaves us with XX or XY. Sometimes, as we see later in the program, there are other mutant variations of this. In addition we see that the chromosomes of the two parents can be reshuffled in many ways which means the games of both can carry many combinations of chromosomes . This extra dimension of ‘the lottery’ is the simple explanation of why the children of the same two parents show genetic differences. There is one exception: identical twins, where a fertilised egg splits and two babies develop carrying exactly the same genetic information. They will be of the same sex and be truly identical. Not so for fraternal twins who are totally different individuals who develop from two fertilised eggs which developed at the same time in the womb. Inheritance of Genetic conditions - Recessive and Dominant: The remainder of the program focuses on describing and explaining a variety of “genetic conditions” where there has been a hic cup in the system and how these mishaps are inherited within families. First we meet Madelaine, who has inherited cystic fibrosis where the absence of a particular protein in her system results on respiratory disorders. The protein is absent because of a mutant allele carried by both parents. But neither parent has the condition because they have at least one normal allele as well as one mutant version. They are “carriers”. For this reason Cystic Fibrosis is called a recessive condition. Madelaine inherited one mutant allele from both parents and therefore the condition is expressed. In contrast, Huntington disease, a disorder of the nervous system that appears late in life, is known as a dominant condition because it only requires one mutant allele for the condition to take effect. In both these cases, a study of the family pedigree or pattern of genetic inheritance can tell us a great deal about the pathway of the condition and can help us predict when some conditions will occur. The program highlight some of the current research taking place by geneticists using the study of family patterns to extend our knowledge of inherited characteristics. The case of Oliver, who has achondroplasia, underlines the fickle role of chance in the development of mutations. Achonroplasia is a dominant condition yet neither of Oliver’s parents have the condition. How could this be? The explanation appears to be that a chance event during meiosis causes a slight change in the base code sequence throwing out the coding for creating a particular protein. This protein is crucial to long bone growth. So, due to a chance “spelling error” in the base coding Oliver lives with short limbs. The program explores other forms of genetic conditions such as different eye colours and Down Syndrome where the mishap - an extra chromosomes on chromosome 21 - arises from an unusual event during meiosis when the egg is formed in the mother. Mutant variation in the distribution of the sex coding X chromosome in the mother can lead to Klinefelter Syndrome in boys where there is an extra X chromosome (XXY). In the case Turner Syndrome in girls there is an X chromosome missing leaving the child with an XO pair. In both cases stature and fertility are affected. But, as an optimistic comment of the state of this science, the program subtly draws our attention to how new treatments, such as hormone therapy, are being used to successfully counteract these impacts of genetic chance. AFTER THE PROGRAM STUDENT ACTIVITIES 1. Create your own genetics crossword Create clear definitions of these genetic terms in your own words and use them to create your own crossword puzzle. Test your puzzle with other students. Chromosomes Genes Gametes Fertilisation Inheritance Ribosome Allele Sperm Egg Geneticists Mitosis Meiosis Mutation Recessive condition Dominant condition 2. Seeing How it Works: a) Role play cell division in meiosis. Everyone can participate by forming nucleus and cell membranes as well as representing the dividing chromosomes. b) Photocopy and enlarge the table on the following page. Cut the table into separate squares and jumble up the pieces. In groups ask s

searchText: A New Paper Reveals The Amazing Evolution of The Human Face CARLY CASSELLA 22 APR 2019 The human face is unique yet universal, mechanical yet expressive, modern yet ancient. For over 4 million years, our features have slowly morphed into what we see today in the mirror, a brief stop on the way to who knows what. From early hominins to modern Homo sapiens , a new review written by leading experts traces the history of the human face across millions of years, as landscapes, climates, and cultures come and go. Like many before them, the international team agrees that diet and climate were important factors in shaping the human face. Still, there's another element they think is too often overlooked: social necessity. "We know that other factors such as diet, respiratory physiology, and climate have contributed to the shape of the modern human face," says anatomist Paul O'Higgins from the University of York, "but to interpret its evolution solely in terms of these factors would be an oversimplification." Using facial skin, bones, and muscles, modern humans can signal more than 20 different categories of emotion to one another. And that's not something we could always do. As the human face evolved over millennia, it went from a stiff mask to an easily-manipulated mug: "a short-faced cranium with a large globular brain case," as the authors put it . With the dawn of a smooth forehead, our eyebrows were officially unleashed with plenty of room for movement; at the same time, our faces grew smaller and more slender , allowing for subtle emotions like recognition and sympathy. Suddenly, there were more opportunities than ever before for gestures and non-verbal communication - a vital step if humans were to establish and maintain large social networks. "We think that enhanced social communication was a likely outcome of the face becoming smaller, less robust, and with a less pronounced brow," says one of the authors, Rodrigo Lacruz , a craniofacial biologist at New York University. "This would have enabled more subtle gestures and hence enhanced non-verbal communication." It's doubtful that social communication could have reshaped the modern human face all on its own, but the authors think it should at least be included in leading theories. Diet, for instance, is one of the most cited factors in explaining our facial shape. Unlike modern humans, early hominins ate tough plant foods, tearing through them with their teeth alone. As such, they needed large jaw muscles, and these massive attachments required broad and deep faces. In the past 2 million years, however, humans have started using tools to break down and cut our food. And as we've learned to process and cook it, our faces have begun to shrink . ( Lacruz et al., Nature, 2019) "Softer modern diets and industrialised societies may mean that the human face continues to decrease in size," says O'Higgins. "There are limits on how much the human face can change however; for example, breathing requires a sufficiently large nasal cavity." It's a trend that's been going on for some 100,000 years, and with climate change becoming an ever-growing problem, it too could be affected. With temperatures increasing, the authors say it could change our appearance. If climate predictions are correct, they argue we might expect changes in our nasal cavities, which help warm and humidify air before it enters our lungs. "We are a product of our past," says human evolution expert William Kimbel from Arizona State University. "Understanding the process by which we became human entitles us to look at our own anatomy with wonder and to ask what different parts of our anatomy tell us about the historical pathway to modernity." This study has been published in Nature Ecology and Evolution . https://www.sciencealert.com/here-s-how-the-human-face-evolved-to-look-the-way-it-does

searchText: HUMAN FEET ARE STRANGE Humans, along with familiar species such as orangutans , gorillas, lemurs, baboons, and chimpanzees, are primates. Among living primates, modern humans are most closely related to chimpanzees. The two species shared a common ancestor that lived about 6–7 million years ago. One of the traits that distinguish humans from all other primates, including chimpanzees, is the way we walk. Chimpanzees are primarily quadrupedal, which means that they walk on four limbs. Chimpanzees move with their hands turned under so that their knuckles make contact with the ground, which is why they are also described as knuckle-walkers. Humans, on the other hand, are bipedal, meaning that we walk on two legs. We walk with our feet close together and directly underneath our hips, enabling us to balance on one leg while the other leg swings forward. Chimpanzees can walk on two legs only for short distances. Because their feet are not directly under their hips, they sway side to side to help maintain balance when walking on two legs. Because humans are the only primate to walk on two legs, bipedality most likely evolved in the lineage that led to humans. When did this human trait first evolve? The “Human Feet Are Strange” activity will help answer that question. Part 1 focuses on observing modern human footprints and what we can infer from them. In Part 2, you will make observations and inferences from a portion of the Laetoli trackway, a trail of footprints th at were made in what is now East Africa about 3.6 million years ago! You will compare human feet and chimpanzee feet to the footprints in the Laetoli trackway, to determine whether those footprints were more human-like or chimp-like. Carefully analyze the two sets of footprints made in class. Consider the following questions when making your observations: • Is the big toe pointed in the same direction as the stride? • How far apart are the left and right feet? • How long is the stride? • Where was most of the weight placed on the foot? How can you tell? Write your notes below. 4. What are the similarities and differences between the two sets of footprints? Similarities Differences 5. If you hadn’t seen the footprints as they were being made, what could you infer about how they were made or who made them? What observations did you base your inferences on? What couldn’t you infer? List below the observations and inferences. Unlike the fossils of bones, which are referred to simply as fossils, fossil footprints are referred to as trace fossils. They provide indirect evidence of past life. Fossils of Australopithecus afarensis, the same species as the famous “Lucy” fossil, have been found near the Laetoli footprints. Had A. afarensis made the footprints at Laetoli ? 7. searchText: Short Film Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans Educator Materials IN-DEPTH FILM GUIDE DESCRIPTION Paleontologists have studied the fossil record of human evolution just as they have done for that of other major transitions—including the transition from fish to tetrapods and dinosaurs to birds. The short film Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans highlights the most important hominid fossil discoveries of the past 50 years and the insights they provide into human evolution, focusing on three key traits: bipedality, tool use, and larger brains. KEY CONCEPTS A. The fossil record details the history of life on Earth, including transitions from one major group of animals to another. B. DNA evidence indicates that the human lineage split from that of our closest relative, the chimpanzee, about 7 million years ago—a timing that is consistent with fossil evidence. C. Traits that distinguish modern humans from modern chimpanzees include bipedality (the ability to walk upright on two legs), extensive tool use, and larger brains. Fossil evidence provides information about when and where each of these traits evolved. D. Tracing the evolution of distinct traits shows that, like other major transitions, the evolution of humans from quadrupedal apes occurred in distinct phases. E. Fossil evidence reveals that bipedalism arose over 4 million years ago and predates tool use and the evolution of larger brains by at least a million years. F. Fossils also provide evidence about the environment in which a species lived. For example, bipedalism evolved when our human ancestors were still living in forests and climbing trees. G. Finding and identifying fossils is difficult and time-consuming work. Almost every individual that lived on Earth left no fossil evidence of its existence. BACKGROUND It wasn’t until the publication of The Descent of Man in 1871, 12 years after On the Origin of Species, that Charles Darwin wrote about the evolution of humans. In The Descent of Man, he hypothesized that humans and modern apes share a common ancestor that lived in Africa. He predicted that fossil evidence would one day be found in Africa to support his hypothesis—and he was right. The film Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans explores several key fossil discoveries from Africa and what they reveal about human evolution. What Are Humans? Humans, along with familiar species such as lemurs, gibbons, and chimpanzees, are primates (Figure 1). Primates are hundreds of species that form a mammalian order, characterized by many traits, including forward-facing eyes, generalized teeth, collarbones, and nails instead of claws on their fingers and toes. In the film, Dr. Sean Carroll explains that members of our own species, Homo sapiens, are distinguished from other primates by three primary traits: large brains, bipedalism, and tool use. These traits must have evolved after the lineage leading to modern humans split from the one that would eventually split into modern chimpanzees and bonobos, our closest living relatives. www.BioInteractive.org Published July 2015; Revised October 2016 Page 3 of 14 Short Film Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans Educator Materials Scientists have examined the fossil record to understand when and where these three distinctly human characteristics evolved. The film describes fossils of species that were either side branches of our immediate family tree or ancestors on the evolutionary lineage that led to modern humans (Figure 2). In the film, these species are referred to as hominids (the nontechnical form of the zoological family name Hominidae). As used in the film and in this guide, “hominid” is synonymous with the alternative term “hominin,” increasingly used in the scientific literature and many textbooks. Figure 1. The Primate Family Tree. Humans belong to the primate order, and Darwin had observed that humans shared many similarities with the African great apes. DNA studies have since shown that chimpanzees and bonobos are humans’ closest living relatives; we shared a common ancestor with them about 7 million years ago. The Earliest Fossil Finds “On July 17, at Olduvai Gorge in Tanganyika Territory, at site FLK, my wife found a fossil hominid skull, at a depth of approximately 22 ft. below the upper limit of Bed I.” This is the first line in a now-famous paper written by Dr. Louis Leakey and published in the journal Nature in 1959 announcing the discovery of the 1.76-million-year-old Zinjanthropus boisei (today classified as Australopithecus boisei or Paranthropus boisei). For three decades, the Leakeys had been searching for evidence of human evolution in the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, but they found only stone tools. Finally, they thought they had the toolmaker. In the Nature paper, Dr. Leakey proposed that this species was “the oldest yet discovered maker of stone tools,” but later finds would soon cause him to rethink this inference. www.BioInteractive.org Published July 2015; Revised October 2016 Page 4 of 14 Short Film Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans Educator Materials The Leakeys concluded that Zinjanthropus was the toolmaker because the skull was found with stone tools in the same layer of sedim

searchText: Incomplete Dominance Definition: Incomplete dominance is a form of intermediate inheritance in which one allele for a specific trait is not completely expressed over its paired allele. This results in a __________ phenotype in which the expressed physical trait is a _____________ of the phenotypes of both alleles. Unlike in complete dominance inheritance, one allele does not dominate or mask the other allele. Incomplete dominance occurs in the polygenic inheritance of traits such as eye colour and skin colour. 5934710 357505 0 0 INCOMPLETE DOMINANCE IN SNAPDRAGONS Example: 6029960 990600 0 0 Incomplete dominance is seen in cross-pollination experiments between red and white snapdragon plants. In this monohybrid cross , the allele that produces the red colo u r (R) is _____ completely expressed over the allele that produces the white colo u r (r) . The resulting offspring are all pink. The genotypes are: Red (RR) X White ( rr ) = Pink ( Rr ) . Use a Punnett square to demonstrate that all the offspring from this cross would be pink. 6034405 212725 0 0 Use aPunnett square to show what would happen if plants from the first filial generation were allowed to cross: Write out the ratio of genotypes: Write out the ratio of phenotypes: Show what would happen if the firs filial generation is allowed to cross pollinate with true breeding red plants: Show what would happen if the first filial generation is allowed to cross pollinated with true breeding white plants: In incomplete dominance, the intermediate trait is the _________ zygous genotype . In the case of snapdragon plants, the pink plants are heterozygous with the ( Rr ) genotype. The red and white plants are both ________ zygous for plant colo u r with genotypes of (RR) red and ( rr ) white . POLYGENIC TRAITS Polygenic traits are determined by more than one gene and by interactions among several alleles . The genes contributing to these traits equally influence the phenotype and the alleles for these genes are found on different chromosomes . The alleles have an additive effect on the phenotype resulting in varying degrees of phenotypic expression. Individuals may express varying degrees of a dominant phenotype, recessive phenotype, or intermediate phenotype. Those that inherit more dominant alleles will have a greater expression of the dominant phenotype, while those that inherit more recessive alleles will have a greater expression of the recessive phenotype. Those that inherit various combinations of dominant and recessive alleles will express the intermediate phenotype to varying degrees. Height, weight, eye colo u r, and skin colo u r are examples of polygenic traits.

searchText: ﻿ INTRODUCTION TO GENETICS • Genetics is the study of heredity, that is, how such as eye colour are inherited from to offspring. • Genes are the chemicals in the nuclei of cells that determine the characteristics that are inherited. Each human has thousands of genes in the nucleus. Genes are made of (deoxyribonucleic acid). • Chromosomes are fine thread-like structures in the of all body cells. Genes are situated on chromosomes. • Numbers of Human Chromosomes – Human body cells (somatic cells) have 23 pairs or chromosomes. Human (sperm and egg) have only 23 chromosomes. • Homologous Chromosomes – Homologous chromosomes is the name given to the of chromosomes in body cells. • Human Sex Chromosomes – Of the 46 chromosomes in human body cells, 1 pair or 2 sex chromosomes only determine whether a person is male or . Human females have 2 X-shaped sex chromosomes ( ). Human males have 1 X-shaped and 1 Y-shaped chromosome (XY). • Autosomes are the 22 pairs or 44 chromosomes in human body cells. ALLELES • Genes are made of DNA. Genes help us to make (e.g. muscle protein, hormones, enzymes, antibodies, skin collagen, hair keratin) that will determine certain characteristics we inherit. • For a specific characteristic (e.g. eye colour), there may be one or more types (e.g. blue, brown) that may be determined by slightly different variations of the DNA in the . These are called alleles. For example, in eye colour, there may be brown eye colour determined by a gene or allele B, or for blue eye colour, it is determined by a slightly different gene or allele b. MULTIPLE ALLELES • For a particular characteristic, there may be more than 2 alleles. For example, in Blood Type, there are 3 alleles – A, B and O.) GENOTYPES AND PHENOTYPES • Each characteristic (e.g. eye colour) is determined by a of genes/alleles. One of those genes came from the via sperm, and the other came from the mother via . • Genotype is the pair of genes/alleles written in letter form (e.g. BB). • Phenotype is the characteristic that appears as a result of that genotype (e.g. brown eyes). • Example 1 – Eye Colour in Humans GENOTYPE PHENOTYPE BB Brown-eyed person Bb Brown-eyed person bb Blue-eyed person • Example 2 – Height in Pea Plants GENOTYPE PHENOTYPE TT Tall pea plant Tt Tall pea plant tt Short pea plant • Homozygous (or Purebred) – The genotype for the characteristic has the same genes/alleles (e.g. BB, bb). • Heterozygous (or Hybrid) – The genotype for the characteristic has different genes/alleles (e.g. Bb). • Wild-type - The most common phenotypes in a population are called the wild-type. These may be dominant (e.g. brown eye colour) or (e.g. green pea colour). MENDEL'S LAWS • Gregor Mendel (1822-1884) was an Austrian monk whose work with pea plants laid the foundation for genetics. • Principle of Segregation states that the alleles of a gene separate when gametes (sperm or ) are formed. Each receives one or the other allele. • Principle of Independent Assortment states that the segregation of alleles of one gene is independent of the segregation of alleles of another gene during gamete formation. SEX DETERMINATION • Because the sperm or egg will contain only of the genes and chromosomes of a person, then each sperm could contain either an X or a Y chromosome. Each egg contains either an X or the other chromosome. • To have a , the sperm from the father and the egg from the mother must both contain X chromosomes. • To have a , the father’s sperm must have a Y chromosome to join with the mother’s egg that has an X chromosome. • It is the who determines the sex of a child.

searchText: ﻿Chapter 1 DNA and genetics extra worksheet 1:Karyotypes It is possible to isolate some cells from a developing fetus and photograph the chromosomes in the cells. Scientists use the photograph to create a karyotype and from this they can identify genetic abnormalities. To create a karyotype, the photograph is cut up and individual chromosomes are arranged into homologous pairs according to their size, as shown in Figure 1. Homologous pairs are chromosomes with the same genes for particular characteristics at the same location along the length of each chromosome. The pairs are numbered for ease of identification. The karyotype that is produced can provide information about the developing foetus. Questions 1 Identify the karyotype that matches the description of the following three syndromes. Karyotype Description of Syndrome Klinefelter’s syndrome: Male with an extra X chromosome (genotype XXY). Down syndrome: Extra copy of chromosome 21. Turner’s syndrome: Absence of a Y or second X chromosome (genotype XO). 2 Create your own karyotype by cutting up the mixed up picture of chromosomes and then matching the homologous pairs of chromosomes. Glue them in the space below, and then answer the questions. a State the number of homologous pairs of chromosomes in Figure 2. b Deduce whether this set of chromosomes came from a male or a female. c Justify your response.

searchText: Teacher Guide: What is DNA? DNA Extraction from Kiwifruit Adapted from the office of Biotechnology, Iowa State University Introduction DNA is present in the cells of all living organisms. This procedure is designed to extract DNA from kiwi in sufficient quantity to be seen and spooled. This activity is ideal for students to work in pairs, but each student will have a tube of DNA at the end. Some questions to get you thinking about the lab: One way to purify a molecule is to get rid of everything but that molecule. If we want to isolate DNA from kiwifruit, what do we have to get rid of? All parts of the cell besides the DNA, i.e. cell wall (kiwi is a plant, after all), cell membrane, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum, vacuoles, lysosomes , nuclear membrane, etc. What materials would you use to do that? Something to mush the cells (blender or your hands), something to destroy membranes (soap dissolves them), something to get rid of proteins and carbohydrates (salt causes them to precipitate), something to separate insoluble cell stuff from soluble DNA, and something to help get the DNA (alcohol precipitates it). What can we do with the DNA once weÕve purified it? Use it in DNA fingerprinting (solve a crime, see a genetic defect), put it into another organism to give it specific traits (this is called transformation or genetic engineering), other? Materials ziplock bags (1 per student pair) jar or beaker that fits strainer or funnel (1 per 10 students) strainer or funnel (1 per 10 students) cheese cloth (cut to cover the funnel) ice water bath (a large mixing bowl works well) (1 per 4-6 students) extraction solution (1 tube of 20 mls per student pair) kiwifruit (cut into 12 pieces, each student pair needs 6 pieces) cold 95% ethanol or isopropanol (2-3 mls per student) small test tubes (1 per student) Extraction solution recipe: For one liter of the extraction solution, mix 100 ml of shampoo ( eg Suave Daily Clarifying Shampoo, many shampoos will work, but do not use shampoos with conditioner or baby shampoo) and 15 g of table salt (iodized or non-iodized both will work). Add water to make a final volume of 1 liter . Dissolve the salt by stirring slowly to avoid foaming. Measure 20 ml of solution for each pair of students. Protocol - These are the directions for each pair. Get 4 pieces of kiwi and put them in a ziplock bag. Add 20 ml of extraction solution to the ziplock bag. Make sure the bag is closed without much extra air. Mush the kiwi thoroughly but carefully so the bag doesnÕt break, for about 5 minutes. What does mushing the kiwi do? Breaks the cell wall What do you think the extraction solution is? What does it do to the kiwi? Soap will cause the solution to bubble so students should be able to guess what's in here. The soap destroys the cell and nuclear membranes, allowing the DNA to get out. There is also salt in the extraction solution, which causes the proteins and carbohydrates to precipitate, while the DNA remains in solution. Cool the kiwi mixture in the ice bath for a minute. Then mush the kiwi more. Cool, then mush. Repeat this several times. Why do we cool the mixture? Cooling protects the DNA. There are DNases (enzymes that destroy DNA) in the cell's cytoplasm. The DNA is usually protected from DNases by the nuclear membrane, but that is destroyed by the soap. Cooling slows down the DNases , just like it would any enzymatic reaction. DNases are in our cells to protect us from foreign DNA (like viruses). Filter the mixture through the cheesecloth. All the groups can combine their mixtures at this point, to filter together. What is being filtered out? What is going through the filter? Students can usually see the seeds being filtered out. Most of the cell parts and the precipitated protein and carbohydrate are also being filtered out at this point. Dispense approximately 2 ml of kiwi solution into each test tube, one for each student. Being careful not to shake the tubes, add approximately 2 ml of cold 95% ethanol to each tube. What do you think the ethanol does? Why do we want it cold? We don't have to worry about the DNases at this point, because hopefully they've mostly been filtered out. What we are most concerned about is precipitating (or solidifying) the DNA. The colder something is, the more likely it will precipitate or solidify. Cooling the alcohol just increases the amount of DNA that precipitates. Take a look at your tube. What do you see in the top portion of the liquid? You can actually pick up the DNA at this point, using a toothpick, wood pencil, or glass stirring rod.

searchText: Meiosis notes Gametes each contain only 23 chromosomes and are described as being haploid . When the gametes combine during fertilisation the resultant zygote has 23 pairs of chromosomes and is diploid . In this way the traits of both parents are inherited. right 8890 0 0 Meiosis only occurs in the gonads of organisms which reproduce sexually. Essentially after the initial replication of the DNA in the parent cell, it then undergoes two separate divisions producing four daughter cells, each with half the amount of DNA that was present in the parent cell. In males s permatogenesis happens continuously in the testis for most of a man’s adult life and produces the male sex cell known as sperm. Millions of sperm are produced each day. As you can see from the diagram, half the sperm produced will contain an X chromosome and half will contain a Y chromosome. 4524375 247015 0 0 Oogenesis or the production of female sex cells known as eggs or ova, happens in the ovaries. Women are born with all the eggs that they will ever have already stored in their ovaries and each month one egg matures and is released so that it is available for fertilisation to take place. Despite going through the same processes as sperm during meiosis each parent cell only produces one viable egg cell, the others become polar bodies and are absorbed by the body. Unlike men who have XY sex chromosomes, the sex chromosomes in women are referred to as XX. Therefore every female gamete can only carry the X chromosome. searchText:
Modelling DNA and chromosomes
This craft based activity is fun and many useful observations and questions can
arise from it.

Students make two simple models:

      One is a paper ladder to represent a short length of the DNA molecule
       and is used to show the helical structure and illustrate the notion of a
       gene(s).

      The second is a paper chain which represents a chromosome. It is used
       to show how the long, thin DNA molecule shortens and condenses as it
       coils up to form a chromosome.

You will need:
      lined a4 paper
      scrap paper
      scissors
      sticky tape.


Ladder instructions

Cut one A4 sheet in half lengthways.
Take one piece and fold in half, lengthways. If the paper is lined it's helpful to
have the margin on the outside so it is visible.
Start at one end and cut out a block two lines deep, cutting from the fold along
a line and up to and along the margin.
Move along the sheet a distance of two lines. Leave these intact and cut out a
block of the next two lines, up to the margin.
Continue up the length of the sheet, removing about 8 blocks.
Opening the sheet will reveal a ladder.


Paper chain instructions

Simply make a long paper chain. Get students to make sections and then join
them together to make one long chain.
Use scrap paper or coloured paper, each link should be about 1-5 cm wide

Show students two or three 3-D animations of DNA molecules. Mute the video
so students are not overwhelmed with keywords.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019         33948                               Page 1 of 3
                                                Modelling DNA and chromosomes
Using the ladders

Below are some suggestions for questions and things to do with the ladders.

1. What does the ladder represent?

2. Students can colour sections, three or four rungs long, to represent individual
   genes. Students then have a go at twisting their ladders. How well does this
   show the structure of DNA compared to other models and diagrams they
   have seen?

3. The rungs of the ladder usually collapse so the helix is difficult to see – how
   can they solve this? (Students may suggest things like using short strips of
   sticky tape to reinforce each rung and joined two or more ladders together).

4. Some 3-D animations show the DNA molecule 'unzipping' and two new
   strands forming. How could they use their ladder models to illustrate this?


Using the paper chains

Below are some suggestions for questions and things to do with the chains.

1. What does the chain represent?

2. Which parts might be said to model genes?

3. Are the ladder and the chain actually showing the same thing?

4. Which is a more accurate model of the double helix? Why?

5. Now, twist the chains. (Hopefully, each link is stuck together firmly). What
   happens to the chain? Show a 3-D animation which illustrates this.


Further questions

1. If you had a giant model cell, where would you put the ladder or chain you
   have made?

2. When would you coil up the chain to show the formation of a chromosome?

3. When would you open up your ladder to create two copies of the DNA
   molecule?




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019        33948                              Page 2 of 3
                                               Modelling DNA and chromosomes
Suggested answers

Using the ladders

1. What does the ladder represent?
   A short length of DNA molecule; DNA with a couple of genes; double helix
   structure of DNA

4. Some 3-D animations show the DNA molecule 'unzipping' and two new
   strands forming.
   How could they use their ladder models to illustrate this?
   They could cut them up the middle of the rungs and new T-shaped pieces of
   paper added to make two new ladders

Using the paper chains

1. What does the chain represent?
   A single chromosome and how it becomes more visible under microscope
   when it coils up.

2. Which parts might be said to model genes?
   Each link of chain.

3. Are the ladder and the chain actually showing the same thing?
   Ladder represents a small section of the chain.

4. Which is a more accurate model of the double helix? Why?
   Ladder shows the 'backbone' of DNA molecule and cross-pieces. Chain has
   links which pass through one another.

5. Now, twist the chains. (Hopefully, each link is stuck together firmly). What
   happens to the chain?
   Shortens; thickens

Questions

1. If you had a giant model cell, where would you put the ladder or chain you
   have made? Inside the nucleus

2. When would you coil up the chain to show the formation of a chromosome?
   When cell is preparing to divide.

3. When would you open up your ladder to create two copies of the DNA
   molecule?
   During process of cell division when chromosome is making a copy of itself

searchText:
Modelling variation activity
Teaching notes
In this activity, students make simple 'organisms' from different materials.
Working in pairs, they use the same material to make a population of
organisms by following very simple rules.
When they have made their population they study each individual and note
down any differences between them. This reveals variation within the
population.
Students look at the differences and try to decide what environmental change
these particular individuals may be better adapted to.

Keywords
Adaptation, offspring, population, reproduce, species, survive, variation
(continuous and discontinuous variation).
The idea is to demonstrate how variation within a population may help
individuals of the same species survive when the environment changes.
As an extension it can be used to illustrate continuous and discontinuous
variation.

Activity
1. Choose an organism from the following suggestions for students to make.
   Give them a certain amount of time to make their population e.g. 60
   seconds. Challenge students to make them as identical as possible.

Organism 1
Work in pairs (to represent parents and shows that variation occurs even
amongst offspring who share the same parents).
Using modelling dough, students make as many pea-sized balls of dough as
they can in the given time.
Organism 2
Cut out very simple winged shapes from paper strips folded in half. The shapes
should be no larger than 2 cm2 when opened out.

Organism 3
Using the back of a pair of scissors, paper-curl (pre-cut 1cm wide strips from
width of A4 sheet) paper strips.
2. Next, they decide broadly which habitat their organisms live in.
    Are they herbivores, carnivores or omnivores?
    Are they a prey species for other organisms?
    Are they camouflaged?
    Are they nocturnal?
    Do they hibernate?
When they have their population they carefully study each individual and make
a note of any differences such as size, shape, smoothness, colour. Can they
group them?
Now, they decide an environmental change which might favour the more
unusual individuals.

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019       34808                                 Page 1 of 3
                                                     Modelling variation activity
E.g. Small pea shapes may survive better should there be a shortage of food in
their habitat; darker peas may have an advantage if the climate becomes
wetter and more cloudy.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2019      34808                             Page 2 of 3
                                                       Modelling variation activity
Extension - continuous and discontinuous variation
Students decide which forms of variation in their population can be described
and measured by using numbers and units and which can only be described
using words and the number in each category tallied.
They can collate their data and share with other pairs who made the same
creature.
Bar charts and histograms can be drawn.
Discuss the differences in bar charts and histograms e.g. bars are not touching
on the chart because the categories are quite separate and distinct
(discontinuous variation) whereas a histogram shows continuous variation and
the bars are touching.
Discuss how charts can be used to show which part/proportion of a population
shown on the graph may survive to pass on genes to its offspring, should a
particular environmental change occur.
Discuss the effects of rapid changes in climate on species in evolutionary
terms. There may not be sufficient variation in a population to allow it to adapt
to a decrease in precipitation, for example.
To stimulate discussion, there are video clips available showing penguins which
breed on the rocky shores of South Africa. Due to rising sea temperatures the
fish stocks that they feed on are moving further away from the shore making
harder for the penguins to feed. The population has declined by 60% since
2004.

Science in the news – the abominable snowman’s DNA

Teaching notes

This task can be used when learning about classification and evolutionary trees with
GCSE students.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘The abominable snowman's
DNA'.
Further information can be found at (links all available at time of publishing):
http://www.theblaze.com/stories/2013/10/17/mystery-solved-dna-test-finds-reasonable-
explanation-for-identity-of-abominable-snowman/


Starter

To add an element of mystery to the lesson, show the class a video or an image of a
possible abominable snowman, or yeti, sighting:
http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zZFHxqesLo4
http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-2278024/The-clearest-sighting-Yeti--elaborate-
hoax-schoolboys.html
Discuss with the students if they think these sightings are real and what they think a yeti
might be.
Then ask them to discuss in pairs what evidence would they need in order to prove that
yetis exist. Suitable answers might be samples of fur, footprints, good quality photographs
or video.
After hearing their feedback, discuss how their ideas could prove the existence of the yeti
and also its limitations. For example, if some fur was found, how could it be proved that it
belonged to a yeti?


Main task

Inform students that an Oxford University Professor has collected what could be evidence
for the existence of the yeti and their task today is to analyse it.

 He has extracted some DNA from two hair samples found in two different mountainous
areas where yetis are thought to live and worked out the DNA sequence. He has found
they are exactly the same, so from the same species, but are they from the yeti?

 Ask students to work in small groups and hand out each group a paper copy of the 'yeti'
DNA sequence. Also give them copies of 'human', 'gorilla', 'polar bear' and 'brown bear'
DNA sequences which should be photocopied onto acetate. They should follow the tasks
given on the worksheet. Students place the acetate copies on top of the 'yeti' sequence
and also on top of each other to compare them and help them to answer the questions.
The matching sequences are shown at the end of the resource.
© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2013              22037                                 Page 1 of 13
                             Science in the news – the abominable snowman’s DNA
 Go through what they have found. They should have seen that the polar bear and the
brown bear are most closely related (they share seven sequences). The human and
gorilla share three sequences. The mystery animal is equally related to both the polar
bear and brown bear which suggests that it would be a bear-like creature and not human
looking as many 'sightings' of the yeti suggest.
Explain that this is a simulation and in real life the DNA sequences would be much longer
(thousands of bases long) which makes the comparison more accurate.
 Tell the students that the professor also sequenced DNA from an ancient bear and found
a 100% match to the mystery animal - so it looks like the yeti could be a species that was
thought to be extinct.
 Introduce the idea of common ancestors. They would have seen from the DNA
sequencing task that all the animals have one sequence in common which suggests that
they all share a common ancestor. Display a mammalian evolutionary tree
(http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:An_evolutionary_tree_of_mammals.jpeg) which
shows the orders of Primates (apes belong to this order) and Carnivora (bears belong to
this order). Ask the students to place the common ancestor of these two orders on the
evolutionary tree.

 Display a bear evolutionary tree
(http://bix.ucsd.edu/bioalgorithms/downloads/bookfigs/fig.10.7.pdf) and ask the students to
place where they think the ancient bear, and therefore the 'yeti', goes.


Plenary

Ask the students to read the article from The Week magazine for further information and
then discuss in pairs:
      If this is a species that we thought was extinct, why haven't we discovered it before?
      Can we be sure that this is the 'yeti' that people have claimed to have seen. Why?
       What further evidence is needed?
      Why is it important that the professor publishes his findings in a scientific journal?


Homework idea

Ask the students to use ideas about natural selection to write an explanation of either:
How the brown and polar bear evolved from this ancient ancestor
or
How the ancient bear may have evolved to become the human-looking 'yeti'

Spaghetti Worms Natural Selection
 Aim: To model natural selection in the environment.

Equipment:
• 20 pieces of coloured spaghetti                       Safety Information
  (10 each in two colours)                              Pasta – possible chemical
                                                        contamination
• Ruler
                                                        Do not consume anything made in or for
• Scissors
                                                        laboratory use.
• A quiet grassed area




Method:
Step 1: Measure ten pieces of the first colour of spaghetti and cut to an equal length.

Step 2: Measure ten pieces of the second colour of spaghetti and cut to an equal length as the first
coloured spaghetti.

Step 3: Take the 20 pieces of spaghetti (with your teacher’s permission) out to the chosen area on
the field.

Step 4: Using a random method, throw the spaghetti into the grass. Make sure you know where it has
landed (you might sketch a diagram).

Step 5: After 24 hours return and count the spaghetti. Record your observations into the table.

Step 6: Repeat set 5 another 4 times.


  Often organisms of the same species have some differences. These differences are called variation.
  Most variation is a result of mutation in the genetic information of the organism. Sometimes the
  particular characteristic which is varied can be an advantage and helps the organisms adapt and
  survive in their environment.

   One colour will offer greater camouflage in the grass, making them less visible to predators

searchText:
Answer Key for Strawberry DNA Lab

Part I: Questions

1. What was the purpose of mashing up the strawberry?

To break down the cell wall, cellular and nuclear membranes.

2. What does the extraction buffer do? (Hint: Extraction buffer contains soap. What does soap
   do when you wash your hands?)

The extraction buffer helps to release the DNA from the surrounding cell components of the
crushed strawberry.

3. What does the filter do?

The filter removes the larger particles from the solution, such as seeds, pith, etc., allowing only
the smaller cell components such as the DNA, proteins, etc. to filter through.


Questions Parts II and III:

1. What happened when you added the filtrate to the alcohol?

The DNA precipitated out of the solution.

2. What did the DNA look like?

The DNA looked like white, thin fibers wadded up together forming a clump.

Analysis:
3. What does DNA look like?

The DNA will look like a white, cloudy or fine stringy substance.

4. A person cannot see a single cotton thread four classrooms away. But if you wound
   thousands of threads together into a rope, it would be visible at the same distance. How is
   this statement an analogy to our DNA extraction?

DNA is not visible as a single strand to the naked eye, but when thousands of threads of DNA are
present, you will be able to see the large groups of threads of DNA.

5. Is DNA found in all living or once living cells?

Yes, DNA is present in all living and once living cells. Scientists can use DNA from mummies or
seeds that are thousands of years old and identify the genetics of those plants and animals
using their DNA.
 6. Since the strawberries were once living, and we extracted DNA from them, what does this
   mean about the foods you eat?

All the foods we eat that come from plants and animals that contain DNA. DNA has been
consumed on a daily basis since the beginning of time and is completely safe to eat.


7. Look at the plant cell pictured on page one of the lab handout. Remember that genes are
   found on chromosomes, and genes control traits. Give at least two examples of traits that
   are expressed in the strawberry.

Examples: Color, size and sweetness.

Variation and identical twins
Task – version A

Read the description of a pair of identical twins.


 Mateo and Felipe are identical twins. Mateo is five minutes older than his
 brother. Today is their 30th birthday.
 'Feliz cumpleaños, big brother.' Felipe can speak fluently in both Spanish and
 English. Mateo only speaks English but with a strong Scottish accent which
 sometimes confuses his brother.
 When they were very young, family circumstances forced the boys apart.
 Mateo went to live with his father, a football coach, in Edinburgh, Scotland,
 whilst Felipe remained with his grand-parents on the family olive farm in
 Andalucia, Spain.
 Both young men have dark brown eyes and black hair. Mateo's hair reaches
 his shoulders and Felipe's is very short. They have a wide gap between their
 two front teeth.
 When he was a toddler, Felipe used to roll up his tongue and poke it out at his
 grand-mother's parrot, Loro, which he did not like. Mateo broke his leg when
 he was eight and learnt from the doctor that his blood group was O+. In
 Andalucia, when Felipe was told about the accident he decided to send his
 brother a keyring carved in the shape of a bull. Whilst wrapping the present,
 he noticed his fingerprints on the sticky tape and wondered for a moment, if
 they were identical to Mateo's.
 When he was seventeen years old, Mateo applied to do sports science at
 university. He was amazed to learn that Felipe had chosen to do the same
 course in the same city! They decided to share a flat with two friends. At first,
 their friends had no problem telling the twins apart as Felipe had very dark
 skin whilst Mateo's face was pale. Felipe was also one centimetre taller than
 his brother.
 The friends soon decided to join a gym. They were very competitive! It was
 discovered that Felipe had a greater grip-strength than his twin and could
 work out for longer on the rowing machine. But Mateo always beat his brother
 on the squash court.
 Today, they both support Manchester United and like to wear beanies when
 it's cold. Mateo won't admit, even to his twin, that he is afraid of birds. Felipe
 regularly plays the guitar and their grand-parents describe him as 'the
 musical one'. Mateo doesn't play any instruments but he does sing opera and
 Ed Sheeran songs very loudly in the shower!


When you first see identical twins, they can be hard to tell apart. This is
because much about the human body is controlled by genes and identical
twins have identical genes.

As well as (usually) having the same birthday, they also share the same
physical features, such as eye colour.

But, as you have read, Mateo and Felipe are not exactly the same. How people

live and their environment, will alter the effect of their genes.

Have 5 different colours ready (they don't have to be identical to those listed
below). Choose pens or pencils which make a thin line. These will help you
draw around the words you select so you can still read them easily.

Pink – circle all the physical features the twins have. Now draw a table with
two columns, one for Mateo and the other for Felipe. Record all their physical
features.

Green – In your table, circle the physical features which are different in both
boys.

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    Brown - circle the coincidences.
    Orange – circle the other skills and attributes they have between them.
    Draw a second table with two columns and list all the orange-circled words.
    Blue - In both tables, circle any physical features and skills which can be
    easily measured.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be

5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins

Discussion points

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
    These features are controlled by their genes and their genes are identical.

2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    These have been affected by their environment: hair can be cut; skin tone
    is affected by exposure to sunlight and Mateo lives in Scotland whilst Felipe
    spent his childhood in Spain; grip-strength depends on practice – Felipe has
    lived on a farm and may have helped out, making his grip stronger. This
    may also have given him greater endurance. Mateo may be better at
    squash because this indoor sport is one which can be done regularly in a
    colder, wetter climate.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
    Eye colour; hair colour; tongue roll; blood group; fingerprints; skin colour

4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be
   easily compared. What units would you use to measure the other blue-
   circled features and skills?
    Hair length – cm; gap between teeth – mm; height – m and cm; grip-
    strength – Kg, N or mmHg (often with a dynamometer); work-out – hours,
    mins, sec; squash – no unit as such just number of winning games.

5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins
   share and what is your evidence for your conclusion?

    sports possibly due to their different exposure to physical activity when
    young; also father is a football coach, so they will have inherited and share
    some of his genes. Both like football but why the same team? Is this simply
    a coincidence?
    May both have a fear of birds – Felipe 'did not like' the parrot; Mateo doesn't
    admit his fear of birds.
    Both may be equally musical as one plays guitar and other sings opera with
    confidence.

6. Which features or skills do you judge to have an equal genetic and
   environmental influence? Explain why you think this.
    Language – humans genetically predisposed to communicate with
    language.
    Type of language and accent – result of environment.
    Musicality – genes may complement each other to bring about a strong
    musical potential.
    Instrument and skill – heavily dependent on environment.
    Sporting ability – as above.

dating
1   A carbon containing compound produced by a living thing.

2   Carbon-14 is formed high in the atmosphere by cosmic rays (radiation
    from the Sun) changing nitrogen atoms into carbon-14 atoms.

3   The radioactive carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in photosynthesis
    and made into sugar and later into other organic compounds in the plant.

4   When the plant is eaten by animals, the radioactive carbon atoms become
    part of the animal’s body tissues.

5   5730 years old.

6   About 11 460 years old.

7   Rock cannot be dated using carbon-14 dating unless it contains material
    that was originally part of a living organism (such as coal). Few rocks are
    of organic origin or contain any organic materials such as oil.

   Neutralisation Reactions: Hydroxides and Oxides
A neutralisation reaction occurs when an acid reacts with a metal hydroxide or
metal oxide to form water and a salt.

The water comes from the reaction between the H+ in the acid and the OH-
produced by dissolving the hydroxide or the oxide in water. The salt is made
from whatever is left.

balance the equation.

            Hydrogencarbonates (HCO3-1)
A neutralisation reaction occurs when an acid reacts with a carbonate or a
hydrogencarbonate to form water, carbon dioxide and a salt.

formed when the carbonate or hydrogen carbonate dissolves. The carbon

searchText:
Acid Rain
What is Acid Rain?

Acid rain is a result of air pollution. When any type of fuel is burnt, lots of different
chemicals are produced. The smoke that comes from a fire, or the fumes that come out
of a car exhaust don't just contain the sooty grey particles that you can see - they also
contain lots of invisible gases that can be even more harmful to our environment.

Power stations, factories and cars all burn fuels and therefore produce polluting gases.
Some of these gases (especially nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide) react with the
tiny droplets of water in clouds to form sulphuric and nitric acids. The rain from these
clouds then falls as very weak acid - which is why it is known as "acid rain".

Rain is always slightly acidic because it mixes with naturally occurring oxides in the air.
Unpolluted rain would have a pH value of between 5 and 6. When the air becomes
more polluted with nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide the acidity can increase to a pH
value of 4. Some rain has even been recorded as being pH 2.

Vinegar has a pH value of 2.2 and lemon juice has a value of pH2.3. Even the strongest
recorded acid rain is only about as acidic as lemon juice or vinegar and we know that
these don't harm us - so why do we worry about acid rain?

The Effects of Acid Rain

Acid rain can be carried great distances in the atmosphere, not just between countries
but also from continent to continent. The acid can also take the form of snow, mists
and dry dusts. The rain sometimes falls many miles from the source of pollution but
wherever it falls it can have a serious effect on soil, trees, buildings and water.

Forests all over the world are dying, fish are dying. In Scandinavia there are dead lakes,
which are crystal clear and contain no living creatures or plant life. Many of Britain's
freshwater fish are threatened; there have been reports of deformed fish being
hatched. This leads to fish-eating birds and animals being affected also. Is acid rain
responsible for all this? Scientists have been doing a lot of research into how acid rain
affects the environment.

Forests

It is thought that acid rain can cause trees to grow more slowly or even to die but
scientists have found that it is not the only cause. The same amount of acid rain seems
to have more effect in some areas than it does in others.

As acid rain falls on a forest it trickles through the leaves of the trees and runs down
into the soil below. Some of it finds its way into streams and then on into rivers and
lakes. Some types of soil can help to neutralise the acid - they have what is called a
"buffering capacity".

Other soils are already slightly acidic and these are particularly susceptible to the
effects of acid rain.



Acid rain can effect trees in several different ways, it may:
 • dissolve and wash away the nutrients and minerals in the soil
which help the trees to grow.

• cause the release of harmful substances such as aluminium into the soil.

• wear away the waxy protective coating of leaves, damaging them
and preventing them from being able to photosynthesise properly.

A combination of these effects weakens the trees which means that they can be more
easily attacked by diseases and insects or injured by bad weather. It is not just trees
that are affected by acid rain, other plants may also suffer.

Lakes and Rivers

It is in aquatic habitats that the effects of acid rain are most obvious. Acid rain runs off
the land and ends up in streams, lakes and marshes - the rain also falls directly on
these areas.

As the acidity of a lake increases, the water becomes clearer and the numbers of fish
and other water animals decline. Some species of plant and animal are better able to
survive in acidic water than others. Freshwater shrimps, snails, mussels are the most
quickly affected by acidification followed by fish such as minnows, salmon and roach.
The roe and fry (eggs and young) of the fish are the worst affected, the acidity of the
water can cause deformity in young fish and can prevent eggs from hatching properly.

The acidity of the water does not just affect species directly, it also causes toxic
substances like aluminium to be released into the water from the soil, harming fish and
other aquatic animals.

Lakes, rivers and marshes each have their own fragile ecosystem with many different
species of plants and animals all depending on one another to survive. If a species of
fish disappears, the animals which feed on it will gradually disappear too. If the extinct
fish used to feed on a particular species of large insect, that insect population will start
to grow, this in turn will affect the smaller insects or plankton on which the larger insect
feeds.

Buildings

Every type of material will become eroded sooner or later by the effects of the climate.
Water, wind, ice and snow all help in the erosion process but unfortunately acid rain
can help to make this natural process even quicker. Statues

title: Acids and Bases
subject: Science
searchText:
An acid is classed as a substance that produces H+ ions
when it is dissolved in water.

Some acids just split into separate ions for example
Hydrochloric (HCl) and Hydrofluoric (HF) acids.

HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)


Other acids are made from the reaction of a non-metal oxide
with water when it dissolves. Some of these are carbon dioxide
(CO2), nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and sulphur trioxide (SO3).

SO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq) ↔ 2H+(aq) + SO4-2(aq)

The double headed arrow (which should be two arrows on top
of each other) shows that the reaction goes both ways.


A base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions (OH-
-
 ) when it is dissolved in water.

Metal hydroxides will separate into ions in water.

NaOH(aq) → Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)


Other bases react with water to produce the hydroxide ions

Metal oxides
CaO(s) + H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq)

Metal carbonates
CaCO3(s) + H2O(l) ↔ Ca2+(aq) + OH-(aq) + HCO3-(aq)

Metal hydrogencarbonates
NaHCO3(s) + H2O(l) ↔ Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) + H2CO3(aq)

Ammonia
NH3(g) + H2O(l) ↔ NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)
 None of the exercises ask you to show how the hydroxide ions
are formed, however it is good to be aware of what happens as
you will use it later.

Exercise 37: Acids and Bases
This is just asking you to either name or write the formula of
the compound and then classify it as an acid or a base.

If you use the examples you should be ok with this part.



Reactions of Acids and Bases

Acids and bases react in predictable ways. For example, an
acid and a hydroxide will always combine to form water and an
ionic salt. The ionic salt is formed from the left over reactants.

There are four common types of acid/base reactions.

1. Acid + Hydroxide → Water + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide → Water + Sodium
chloride
     HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → H2O(l) + NaCl(aq)

2. Acid + Oxide → Water + Salt
Eg. Nitric acid + Calcium oxide → Water + Calcium nitrate
     2HNO3(aq) + CaO(s) → H2O(l) + Ca(NO3)2(aq)

3. Acid + Carbonate → Water + Carbon dioxide + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Calcium carbonate → Water + Carbon
    dioxide + Calcium chloride
     HCl(aq) + CaCO3(s) → H2O(l) + CO2(g) + CaCl2(aq)

4. Acid + Hydrogencarbonate → Water + Carbon dioxide
   + Salt
Eg. Nitric acid + Sodium hydrogen carbonate → Water +
    Carbon dioxide + sodium nitrate
     HNO3(aq) + NaHCO3 → H2O(l) + CO2(g) + NaNO3
 Another important reaction of acids which is not covered in this
section is the reaction of acids with metals

Acid + Metal → Hydrogen gas + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Magnesium → Hydrogen gas +
Magnesium chloride
    2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → H2(g) + MgCl2(aq)

Exercise 38: Neutralisation
For this exercise, you need to use the general reactions to
predict what will be formed in the reaction.

For the first one, you are adding acid to a metal hydroxide,
which always produces water and a salt. You need to finish the
word equation first, write the symbol equation, and then
balance your symbol equation.

Sulphuric acid + Potassium hydroxide → Water + Potassium
sulphate

H2SO4(aq) + KOH(aq) → H2O(l) + K2SO4(aq)

Then balance

H2SO4(aq) + 2 KOH(aq) → 2 H2O(l) + K2SO4(aq)

Title: Discovering Acids and Bases
WHAT ARE ACIDS AND BASES?
Acids and bases are two kinds of special chemicals. Almost all liquids
are either acids or bases, which is determined by the type of ions in
them. An acid has many hydrogen ions, and splits apart in water to
release these hydrogen ions. On the contrary, bases have hydroxide
ions that combine with hydrogen ions. Scientists us a pH scale to
determine whether a liquid is an acid or a base. PH refers to hydrogen
ion concentration, which is measured by a scale. The scale goes from
0-14, where liquids having a pH level of 0-7 are acids, and 7-14 are
bases. Any substance with a pH level of 7 is considered neutral.

IMPORTANT QUESTIONS:

How are all acids/bases similar?

similar, and discovered bases are similar. We will use our discoveries

when diluted.

Chapter 5                                    Chemical
reactions
               Ionic compounds and
EXTRA WORKSHEET 2:

precipitation reactions
Ionic compounds form crystal lattices of cations and anions. Below in Table 1
is a list of some common cations and anions that make up ionic compounds.

Table 1

        Positive ions (cations)                                 Negative ions (anions)
    Chemical name               Symbol                      Chemical name                        Symbol
Hydrogen ion            H+                            Fluoride                             F–
Lithium ion             Li+                           Chloride                             Cl–
Sodium ion              Na+                           Bromide                              Br–
Potassium ion           K+                            Iodide                               I–
Copper(I) ion           Cu+                           Hydroxide                            OH–
Calcium ion             Ca2+                          Nitrate                              NO3–
Magnesium ion           Mg2+                          Oxide                                O2–
Barium ion              Ba2+                          Sulfide                              S2–
Copper(II) ion          Cu2+                          Sulfate                              SO42–
Iron(II) ion            Fe2+                          Carbonate                            CO32–
Iron(III) ion           Fe3+                          Nitride                              N3–
Aluminium ion           Al3+                          Phosphate                            PO43–


Naming ionic compounds
Naming ionic compounds is relatively simple. The naming conventions follow
just two rules:

1    The chemical name is made up of the name of the cation followed by the
     name of the anion.
     Example: an ionic compound made up of potassium cations and fluoride
     anions is known as potassium fluoride.


2    Ions from the same atom but with a different charge are distinguished by
     roman numerals that show the charge of the ion. These roman numerals
     are included in the chemical name.




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
     Example: Iron atoms form two ions – iron(II), Fe2+ and iron(III), Fe3+. These
    both form oxides known as iron(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide.

    _____________________________________________________________

    a   lithium carbonate __________________________________________


    b   aluminium bromide _________________________________________


    c   copper(II) nitrate ___________________________________________


    d   sodium chloride ___________________________________________


    e   calcium iodide _____________________________________________


           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 2
     f      ammonium hydroxide _______________________________________


    g      lithium nitride _____________________________________________


Predicting precipitation reactions
Some ionic compounds are soluble in water (dissolve) and some ionic
compounds are insoluble in water (do not dissolve). This means that when
two aqueous solutions of soluble ionic compounds are mixed, the ions may
exchange to form an insoluble compound. When this occurs, the insoluble
compound comes out of solution as a solid.

This type of chemical reaction is known as a precipitation reaction and the
insoluble solid is known as the precipitate. Scientists can predict if mixing two
solutions will result in a precipitate by using solubility rules.

Some solubility rules are shown in Table 2. These rules tell you which
combinations of anions and cations are soluble and which combinations are
insoluble.

searchText:
Making Salts
 Aim: to make and name salts by neutralisation reaction.

Equipment:
                                                        Safety Information
• Sodium hydroxide solution
                                                        Acid – corrosive to skin and eyes
• Beaker
                                                        Wear goggles, clean spills
• 50 cm3 measuring cylinder                             immediately.

• Hydrochloric acid                                     Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.

• Dropping pipette                                      Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
                                                        immediately.
• Stirring rod or capillary tube
                                                        Bunsen burner – risk of burns.
• Universal indicator paper
                                                        Place under cold running water for ten
• Evaporating basin
                                                        minutes. Inform teacher.
• Bunsen burner

• Gauze

• Tripod

• Heat proof mat




Method (series circuit):
Step 1: You must wear goggles at all times. Measure 25cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution into a beaker.

Step 2: Drop by drop, add hydrochloric acid to the sodium hydroxide.

Step 3: After every few drops, take a small sample on the stirring rod or capillary tube and test the pH.
Keep adding acid until you have obtained a neutral pH result (pH 7 – green).

Step 4: Once you have a neutral solution, pour it into an evaporating basin.

Step 5: Using a tripod, mat, gauze and Bunsen burner set-up as shown above, heat the solution, until
about 1/3 remains. This is a saturated solution.

Step 6: Once the equipment is cool, move the evaporating basin to a warm place in the room, and leave
to evaporate completely overnight.


                                                Page 1 of 2
                                                                                    Making Salts

Questions
 1. What is meant by neutralisation?

 2. What is a saturated solution?

 3. What is the name of the salt produced in the reaction?

 4. Write a word equation for the neutralisation reaction in your investigation.

 5. Name the salt produced in these reaction:
    a. Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
    b. Sulphuric acid and calcium carbonate
    c. Nitric acid and calcium hydroxide




                                                Page 2 of 2
 Answers
1. What is meant by neutralisation?
   An acid and a alkali react together and produce a salt and water with neutral pH.

2. What is a saturated solution?
   A saturated solution cannot dissolve anymore solute. In this example no more salt can be
   dissolved.

3. What is the name of the salt produced in the reaction?
   Sodium chloride

4. Write a word equation for the neutralisation reaction in your investigation.
   hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide  sodium chloride + water

5. Name the salt produced in these reaction:
   a. Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
   Potassium chloride
   b. Sulphuric acid and calcium carbonate
   Calcium sulphate
   c. Nitric acid and calcium hydroxide
   Calcium nitrate

    Aim: To observe the different reactivities of different metals and acids.

  magnesium and zinc                                           Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher

Method:
It might be useful to stand your test tube rack over plain white paper or a mini whiteboard to help you
with labelling and identifying the contents.

Step 1: Place six test tubes in the test-tube rack.

Step 2: Add a 2–3cm depth of dilute hydrochloric acid to the first three tubes.

Step 3: Add a 2–3cm depth of dilute sulphuric acid to the remaining three tubes.

Step 4: Add a small piece of a different metal to each of the tubes with
hydrochloric acid in them. Record which metal you add to each tube.

Step 5: Add a small piece of the same metals to each of the tubes with sulphuric
acid in them. Record which metal you add to each tube.

Step 6: Observe any reactions and make a note of your observations in your
table of results.

Step 7: From your observations, choose one of the metals that reacts rapidly
with the acids. Collect and test the gas produced. Your teacher will show you
how to test the gas being produced in these reactions.

                                                                                  Metal and Acid Reactions

Choose another of the metals that reacts rapidly with the acids. In a clean test tube, add a piece of
this metal to a 2–3cm depth of one of the acids. This time, however, place a cork loosely in the top
of the test tube so that any gas produced escapes slowly. Light a wood splint, remove the cork and
immediately hold the flame to the mouth of the tube. If nothing happens, you may need to try again.

    a. hydrochloric acid + magnesium 

    b. hydrochloric acid + copper 

    c. sulphuric acid + iron 

    d. sulphuric acid + zinc 

 6. Complete the symbol equation for the reaction between sulphuric acid and magnesium.

    a. H2SO4 + Mg

Answers
1. Write down the metals you tested in order of the most reactive to the least reactive.
   magnesium – zinc – iron - copper

2. What gas was produced by the reaction?
   hydrogen

3. When a metal and an acid react, they always produce the gas you found and a salt. Show this as a
   word equation.
   metal + acid   salt + hydrogen

4. Describe how you tested for the gas, and the observations you made if the gas was present.
   Capture the gas produced with a loosely fitting bung placed in the neck of the test tube, and test
