searchText:
Treating heart disease
Task

Look at the information sheets about different methods for treating heart disease. Use the information to fill in the table.

           Method                     Description                         Advantages                        Disadvantages




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016                                  27263                                                         Page 1 of 7
                                                                      Treating heart disease

Information sheets


  Artificial valves - what are they?
  It’s a device implanted in the heart of a
  patient to replace their faulty valve.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Artificial valves - advantages
        No rejection

  Artificial valves: disadvantages
        Can damage red blood cells, so
         patients need to take anti-clotting
         drugs.


  Biological valves – what are they?
  They are based on valves taken from
  animals, such as pigs or cattle. They are
  treated with chemicals to stop your body
  rejecting them.
  By Stif Komar (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0
  (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia
  Commons


  Biological valves – advantages
        No need for blood thinning drugs as
         they don’t damage red blood cells.

  Biological valves – disadvantages
        Valves can harden and need replacing.



  Stents – what are they?
  Stents are used to treat narrow coronary
  arteries. The stent is pushed into position
  using an x-ray, the balloon is inflated,
  expanding the stent, and then removed,
  leaving the stent to open up the artery.

  Stents – advantages
        Lowers risk of infection as major
         surgery
         not required.

  Stents – disadvantages


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016                              27263                Page 2 of 7
                                                  Treating heart disease

       Fatty deposits can build up again.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016          27263                Page 3 of 7
                                                     Treating heart disease


  Bypass surgery – what is it?
  A surgical procedure used to treat coronary
  heart disease.
  It transplants a vein from the leg to divert
  blood around narrowed or clogged parts of
  the major arteries to improve blood flow and
  oxygen supply to the heart.
  Around 20,000 coronary artery bypass
  grafts are carried out in England every year.

  Bypass surgery – advantages
       No rejection risks.
       Very effective treatment.

  Bypass surgery – disadvantages
       Major surgery, so involves risks.




  Statins – what are they?
  These are drugs which lower cholesterol
  levels by stopping the liver producing as
  much.
  Patients can also change their diet to help
  reduce cholesterol.

  Statins – advantages
       They reduce cholesterol which helps
        slow down the build-up of fatty layers
        in the arteries.

  Statins – disadvantages
       They have possible side effects, e.g.
        liver damage.
       Patient has to remember to take them
        regularly.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016             27263                Page 4 of 7
                                                   Treating heart disease


  Artificial pacemakers - what are
  they?
  Some people can’t control their heart rate.
  Artificial pacemakers can be fitted under the
  skin. A wire is passed from a vein to the
  right atrium. This sends electrical impulses
  to the heart to control the heartbeat.

  Artificial pacemakers – advantages
       Major surgery not required, so not very
        risky.

  Artificial pacemakers –
  disadvantages
       The immune system can reject the
        pacemaker and it will need replacing.
       The pacemaker may sometimes
        malfunction.


  Heart transplants – what are they?
  A heart transplant is an operation to
  replace a damaged or failing heart with a
  healthy human heart from a donor who
  has recently died.
  Heart transplants are rarely performed in
  the UK, mainly due to a lack of suitable
  donors.
  There were 197 heart transplants
  performed in the UK between 2012 and
  2013.

  Heart transplants – advantages
       A better quality of life (improved
        strength, energy & stamina).
       More normal lifestyle day to day
       An improved chance of a longer life.

  Heart transplants – disadvantages
       Major surgery (anaesthetic risks,
        bleeding, clotting, infection)
       Anti-rejection drugs needed for life
       A shortage of donors.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016           27263                Page 5 of 7
                                           Treating heart disease




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2016   27263                Page 6 of 7
                                                                                   Treating heart disease
Teaching notes

Copy the information sheets, cut them up and spread round the room. Ask students to
find the information to fill in the table with.

Ideas for differentiation

For students who need more support:

      the table could be partially filled in
      don’t cut the information sheets up
      students could work in groups and find information for just two methods each.

For more challenge ask students to:

      create their own table
      research the advantages and disadvantages themselves
      remove the headings from the information sheets.

searchText:
Where Do Bacteria Live?
 Aim: to take bacterial swabs and determine conditions for bacterial growth.


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Petri dish with nutrient agar
                                                         Cultures – possible bacterial
• Sterile cotton swabs                                   infection risk

• Coloured permanent marker pens                         Handle sealed Petri dishes only.
                                                         Dispose of in biohazard marked bags. Wash
• Ruler
                                                         hands after handling.
• Clear sticky tape
                                                         Glassware – risk of cuts if broken
• Incubator
                                                         Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
• Location class list                                    immediately.


Method:
Step 1: Your teacher will assign you a location from where to collect your sample.

Step 2: Without removing the lid, turn your Petri dish upside down and label the perimeter with your
name and the date.

Step 3: Using a ruler, carefully draw a line across the middle of the Petri dish to divide it into two
halves. On one half, write the name of the location from where you will collect your sample, and label
the other half as ‘control’.

Step 4: Remove the swab from the packaging, taking care not to touch the end. Gently rub the swab on
the assigned location.

Step 5: Quickly but carefully open the lid of the
Petri dish – just wide enough to fit the swab in –
and rub the swab over the agar in a zig-zag pattern
in the half labelled with your location. Take care
not to mark the agar, or to rub onto the half marked
as control.

Step 6: Replace the petri dish lid and secure on four
sides with sticky tape. Leave some gaps to prevent
anaerobic bacteria growing.

Step 7: Place your Petri dish, upside down, into
the incubator. This helps to prevent condensation
occurring, and allows easier identification of the
plates when checking them.


                                                 Page 1 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?

Step 8: Examine your Petri dish again after one day, two days and then five days. Record all observations
on your result sheet.

Step 9: Your teacher may also conduct a control* investigation to measure bacteria from the air.


 This could be done by simply leaving a Petri dish of agar open and exposed for a specified time
 length e.g. one hour, then sealing and incubating with the other Petri dishes.




                                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                                     Where Do Bacteria Live?
Location Class List
Teacher note: Suggested are several locations and space to add in your own. You may decide for students
to investigate a location each or to work in pairs, depending on your class size. We recommend assigning
the students to a location and them displaying the list to the class.

Results
Draw the bacterial colonies (if any) which have grown on your agar plate.




                After 1 day                   After 2 days                     After 5 days

Count the bacterial colonies that have grown on the agar and complete the table below.
Tips for counting the colonies:
•   Dot each colony with a coloured marker as you count.
•   Use a different colour each time you examine to count the additional colonies only. Add this amount
    to the previous count.
•   Place the Petri dish on a piece of graph paper and count the colonies row by row.
•   If there are many colonies to count, divide the area into 2 using a marker pen, count the colonies in
    ½ then multiply by 2 to find the total.



    Location:

                              Day                                    Number of colonies




Compare your results with the other locations. Your teacher may ask you to add your results to a
collective data table.
You may be given the opportunity to take photographs as a means of recording and comparing the
bacterial growth from difference locations.
                                                                                  Where Do Bacteria Live?

Questions


1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?
                                                                                   Where Do Bacteria Live?

Answers

1. Which location has the most number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

2. Which location has the least number of colonies on day 5? Is this the location you expected?
   This will depend on the locations used and the results the students have obtained.

3. Why is it important to use sterile nutrient agar for the investigation?
   It ensures that the culture(s) which grow on the agar after incubation, are only the ones from the
   swab, and therefore ensure that the investigation is valid.

4. Describe the common environmental conditions where the highest bacterial growth was found.
   (Think about temperature, light, moisture etc.)
   Bacteria are likely to be found in abundance in areas which are moist, and contain traces of food
   for nutrition. Also high traffic items or locations, e.g. mobile phones and door handles may also
   show high levels of bacteria.

5. What does the control Petri dish show? Explain why.
   The control dish will likely show some growth of bacterial cultures. These cultures will have
   come from the air around the Petri dish whilst it was left open.

6. What measures can you take to reduce your exposure to bacteria?

    • Wash your handles before and after eating or preparing foods, suing hot water and soap.

    • Bleaching and disinfecting worktops and surfaces regularly.

    • Ensuring that mouths and noses are covered, and then hands are washed after coughing
    and sneezing.

    • Drying and removing excess moisture from areas such as the bath tub, shower head and
    kitchen sink.

    • Other sensible suggestions.

searchText:
Flame Tests

What is the flame test?

The flame test is used to visually determine the identity of an
unknown metal of an ionic salt based on the characteristic colour
the salt turns the flame of a Bunsen burner.

What are the limitations of this test?

The value of the flame test is limited by interference from other
brighter colours and by ambiguities where certain different metals
cause the same flame colour.

What is happening?

When the salt is placed into the flame, the electrons from the metal
become excited and jump up energy levels. When they fall back to
their ground state they emit the energy they absorbed as photons of
light. Often these photons are in the visible spectrum and a colour
unique to that ion can be seen in the flame.


Method

  1. Light your Bunsen burners so that a hot flame is produced
  2. Collect a pop stick and dip it in distilled water. Place it in the
     blue flame, and then remove it. Observe the colour of the
     flame and record it in your table.
  3. Next using a fresh popstick, dip the stick into the distilled
     water and then into the Barium chloride. Record the colour in
     your table.
  4. Repeat for all of the metal chlorides, using a fresh popstick
     each time.

Atomic Theory

                                  Part One: Flame Tests
                                Part Two: Atomic Spectra
                      Part Three: Applications of Spectra (optional)

                                              C12-2-02 &03




This activity will focus on the visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum.


Background Information:
About 300 years ago, Sir Isaac Newton saw a beam of sunlight through a glass prism. He discovered
that light is made up of a spectrum of seven distinct visible colors. This spectrum of colors always
appears in the same order. You can see this color spectrum (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo,
Violet and all the colors in between) when you look through a diffraction grating. There are two color
ranges that are not visible to our eyes in this spectrum: below red is infra-red and above violet is ultra-
violet. In a rainbow after a rainstorm this same color spectrum appears in the same order. Rainbows are
created when sunlight passes through rain drops that act as millions of tiny prisms.

The color of a solid object depends on the colors of light that it reflects. A red object looks red because it
reflects red light and absorbs all other colors. A blue object looks blue because it reflects blue light and
absorbs all other colors. A white object reflects all colors of light equally and appears white. A black
object absorbs all colors and reflects no visible light and appears black. Just like when you color with too
many colors in one area with crayons or markers, all colors are absorbed, none are reflected and it
appears black!


Explanation of visible light at the electronic level:

What do fireworks, lasers, and neon signs have in common? In each case, we see the brilliant colors because the
atoms and molecules are emitting energy in the form of visible light. The chemistry of an element strongly
depends on the arrangement of the electrons. Electrons in an atom are normally found in the lowest energy level
called the ground state. However, they can be "excited" to a higher energy level if given the right amount of
energy, usually in the form of heat or electricity. Once the electron is excited to a higher energy level, it quickly
 loses the energy and "relaxes" back to a more stable, lower energy level. If the energy released is the same
amount as the energy that makes up visible light, the element produces a color. The visible spectrum, showing the
wavelengths corresponding to each color, is shown below:




Note: [1 Å = 0.1 nm]


Is light a particle or a wave?

Is light composed of waves or of particles? If light is waves, then one can always reduce the amount of
light by making the waves weaker, while if light is particles, there is a minimum amount of light you can
have - a single ``particle'' of light. In 1905, Einstein found the answer: Light is both! In some situations it
behaves like waves, while in others it behaves like particles.

This may seem odd. How can light act like both a wave and a particle at the same time? Consider a
duck-billed platypus. It has some duck-like properties and some beaver-like properties, but it is neither.
Similarly, light has some wavelike properties and some particle like properties, but it is neither a pure
wave nor a pure particle.




A wave of light has a wavelength, defined as the distance from one crest of the wave to the next, and
written using the symbol . The wavelengths of visible light are quite small: between 400 mm and
650 nm, where 1 nm = 10-9 m is a ``nanometer'' - one billionth of a meter. Red light has long
wavelengths, while blue light has short wavelengths.

A particle of light, known as a photon, has an energy E. The energy of a single photon of visible light is
tiny, barely enough to disturb one atom; we use units of “electron-volts”, abbreviated as eV, to measure
the energy of photons. Photons of red light have low energies, while photons of blue light have high
energies.

The energy E of a photon is proportional to the wave frequency f,
                                  E=hf
where the constant of proportionality h is the Planck's Constant, h = 6.626 x 10-34 J s.

Also, the relationship between frequency and wavelength can be defined as:

                                 f=c
                                   λ

where c is the speed of light (3×108 metres per second).


So photons still have a wavelength. A famous result of quantum mechanics is that the wavelength
relates to the energy of the photon. The longer the wavelength, the smaller the energy. For instance,
ultraviolet photons have shorter wavelengths than visible photons, and thus more energy. This is why
they can give you sunburn, while ordinary light cannot.


Spectra can be simplified to one of three basic types. Simple examples in the visible wavebands are
shown below:

This investigation is a simulation of radioactive decay. Radioactive decay is a random

searchText:
Chapter 6                          Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Available nitrogen

The nitrogen cycle
Nitrogen (N) is an essential component of the molecules that carry genetic
information, and of proteins, the building blocks of life. All organisms require
nitrogen to live and grow. Seventy-eight per cent of air is nitrogen in the form
of N2 molecules. The two atoms of nitrogen are held together strongly making
the molecule relatively chemically inactive and therefore unavailable to living
things. For plants and animals to be able to use nitrogen, it must be in a
chemically available form such as ammonium (NH4+) or nitrate ions (NO3–), or
the compound urea (NH3)2CO. Nitrogen is often in short supply in natural
ecosystems and is a limiting factor for plant growth.

There are five main processes in the nitrogen cycle (see Figure 1):
   •   nitrogen fixing
   •   nitrification
   •   nitrogen uptake by plants
   •   decomposition
   •   denitrification.




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 Figure 1 The nitrogen cycle.


Nitrogen fixation
Some bacteria, for example those of the genus Rhizobium, can fix nitrogen
(convert nitrogen into a usable form) through metabolic processes. Many
nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in a symbiotic (depending on each other for
survival) relationship with host plants, especially leguminous plants. Other
nitrogen fixing bacteria are free-living in soils and in water.

Small, but significant amounts of nitrogen are fixed from the air by high-
energy natural events such as lightning, forest fires, and even hot lava flows.
The high energy involved in these natural occurrences breaks the bonds
between the nitrogen atoms in the N2 molecule, making individual atoms
available for nitrogen-fixing chemical reactions.


Human alteration of the nitrogen cycle
Early in the 20th century Fritz Haber, a German scientist, developed a way of
fixing nitrogen in a chemical reaction at high temperatures and pressures. He
created nitrogen-rich chemical fertilisers that could be applied directly to the
soil. By using nitrogen-rich fertilisers, the yield of crops has improved and
productivity of agricultural land has increased. The protein content of the
crops and the food value of the crops have also increased. This has helped
feed the rapidly increasing human population.

Burning fossil fuels, using chemical nitrogen-rich fertilisers and cultivation
(growing) of legumes all add fixed nitrogen to the biosphere. Within the last
century, through these activities, humans are greatly increasing the amount of
nitrogen cycling between the living world and the soil, water and atmosphere.
We have more than doubled the rate of nitrogen entering the land-based
nitrogen cycle.

searchText:
Chapter 6                         Sustainability
EXTRA WORKSHEET 2: The phosphorus cycle

The phosphorus cycle
Phosphorus is an essential element of DNA, cell membranes, bones and
molecules important to the processes that release and use energy in the
body.

Phosphorus is like carbon and nitrogen in that it cycles through natural
ecosystems. However, unlike these other elements, phosphorus is not
present in the air. Phosphorus is found in sedimentary rocks. The
phosphorous cycle begins with phosphate ions (PO4) in sedimentary rocks
such as limestone.

Water percolating through the soil dissolves phosphate ions from the rock and
distributes them through the soil. Some of the phosphate ions remain in the
soil; others move into the ground water and into rivers and streams.

Phosphate ions in the soil are absorbed by plant roots and used and stored
within the plant. Animals then eat the plants and so the phosphorous passes
up the food chain. When dead plants and animals and their wastes are
decomposed, phosphorus is returned to the soil.

Once it gets into the soil the phosphorus is available to be taken up by plants
once again and so the cycle continues. However, some of the phosphorus
may move through the soil dissolved in rain water. It may be carried into rivers
and into oceans hundreds or thousands of kilometres away from where the
phosphorus was released. The phosphorus may circulate in the ocean,
entering the ocean food webs through algae. Alternatively, the phosphorus
may settle in the sediments at the bottom of a lake or the ocean. There it
becomes part of sedimentary rocks, such as limestone, and is lost to the
cycling process for hundreds of thousands or millions of years. The
phosphorous cycle is shown in Figure 1.




           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 Figure 1 The phosphorus cycle.


In natural ecosystems, phosphorus is added to the soil when rocks are
weathered and when plant and animal wastes are decomposed. In urban
environments, phosphorus from sewage treatment plants goes out to the
ocean. In agricultural (farm) ecosystems, the plants and animals are taken to
market. The phosphorus is added to the urban ecosystem instead of being
recycled. The soils in agricultural ecosystem are therefore running out of
phosphorus. To maintain healthy crops, farmers have to add phosphorus to
soils through using fertilisers.

7 RESOURCE DISCUSSION ep
Resources
Natural resources can be classified as either non-renewable or renewable.

Non-renewable resources cannot be replaced — once they are consumed they are gone
for ever. Resources such as coal, iron, natural gas, uranium, and crude oil are all non-
renewable. Some of these resources, such as coal and gas, can re-form. However, they
take millions of years to do so, and as such cannot be renewed in a suitable timeframe
to be considered renewable.

Renewable resources can be used, and within a few years or a few decades, they can be
replaced. Resources such as trees, oxygen, and fresh water are renewable resources.
Living things are often thought of as renewable resources because they reproduce.
They will continually be replaced, as long as we don’t over use them.

Energy
Natural resources are also used to provide energy.

Some non-renewable energy sources are called fossil fuels. Fossil fuels include coal,
crude oil and natural gas.

Fossil fuels are made from the remains of plant matter that died millions of years ago.
Swamps once covered large areas of the Earth and thick layers of dead plant material
built up and were buried and compressed. These layers eventually turned into coal,
crude oil or natural gas.

Renewable sources of energy, sometimes called alternative sources of energy, include
solar, tidal power, wind power and geothermal power.

searchText: right 0 GM back in the spotlight The West Australian Friday, 15 December 2017 7:35AM PGA grains committee chairman Gary McGill.Picture : Astrid Volzke WA farm lobby groups are concerned an inquiry into compensation for non-GM farmers will explode into a broader campaign against the gene technology. A new Senate committee parliamentary inquiry will examine potential compensation schemes for farmers who claim economic loss because of genetically modified material. The landmark inquiry was sparked by a 900-signature petition from European consumer rights organisation FOODwatch , tabled by Greens MLC Diane Evers earlier this year. It called for “farmer protection legislation to compensate any non-GM farmers who suffers economic loss form GM contamination”. But supporters of the technology this week flagged concerns about the inquiry. Both the Pastoralists and Graziers Association of WA and WAFarmers agreed there was “no need” for the examination and common law should cover what PGA labelled “very rare” instances of farm-to-farm contamination. PGA grains committee chairman Gary McGill said the inquiry was a “tactic by the anti-GM movement” designed to “intimidate the cautious GM farmer”. “If someone, through some incursion, suffers economic loss, for example through a crop over-spray... our public liability program looks after these things,” he said. “We will argue there is no need for any special legislation... common law, discussions over the fence - most people are reasonable - they have a yarn and work it out.” WA Agriculture Minister Alannah MacTiernan said she supported the inquiry, which comes almost two years after the Marsh versus Baxter case, in which Kojonup farmer Steve Marsh unsuccessfully sued his neighbour Michael Baxter over GM canola contamination. “We need to ensure that GM and non-GM farming can co-exist,” she said. “Growing GM crops makes financial sense for some, but if neighbouring farmers growing organic crops lose money as a result of contamination, we need to look at whether that financial burden should be shared.” “We will await the outcome of the committee’s inquiry and encourage stakeholders to make a submission.” Ms Evers said the rights of non-GM farmers were not sufficiently protected by law. “It is apparent from the case of Kojonup farmer Steve Marsh that the rights of non-GM farmers in WA, who outnumber farmers growing GM, are not sufficiently protected by law,” she said. “For as long as farmers want to meet demand from consumers for non-GM products, the risk of their fields being contaminated and them experiencing economic loss will remain. “WA farmers should not lose their right to sell non-GM crops at a higher price, due to the actions of another grower. This is an issue that cannot be ignored.” Hundreds of thousands of hectares of GM canola is grown in WA each year after the Barnett Government changed regulations in 2010. Previously, WA was classed a GM crops-free zone with just two exceptions, GM canola grown Statewide and GM cotton in the Kimberley’s Ord irrigation area. Study raises health concerns over GM crops Rebecca Dollery Updated 23 Sep 2012, 8:36am PHOTO: In 2010 the WA Government lifted a ban on GM crops.(User supplied) RELATED STORY: Cancer in rats reignites GM food debate The second study this month to link genetically modified crops with serious health problems has prompted calls for the WA government to ensure the State's GM crops are safe. The latest study, published in the journal of Food and Chemical Toxicology, shows rats fed a GM corn diet over their two year lifespan, suffered mammary tumours and severe liver and kidney damage. The corn, produced by the American multinational Monsanto, had been sprayed with the company's weedkiller, Roundup. The State Government controversially lifted a ban on GM crops in 2010. At least 10 per cent of WA's canola crop is now genetically modified and GM wheat trials have been conducted at locations around the State. The decision to lift the ban has since been the subject of international attention. Earlier this year a Kojonup farmer took his neighbour to the Supreme Court for allegedly allowing a GM canola crop to contaminate his organic farm. Anti-GM campaigners say the State Government could put farmers and consumers at risk if it doesn't instigate an urgent assessment of the use of GM and Roundup in WA. The director of Australia's Safe Food Foundation, Scott Kinnear, says the WA Government has a responsibility to pay attention to the latest study on rats. "The Government would be wise to have a look at this research and a lot of the other indicator research," he said. "There is now a plethora of research that is building to show harm from GM." Mr Kinnear said he did not think banning GM products altogether was the answer. "It's too early to call for a ban on GM, but what we should call for is a change in the way we regulate GM." Full confidence In a statement the WA Minister for Agriculture Terry Redman said the Government has full confidence in the Australian regulatory system for GM products. "Which includes both Food Standards Australia New Zealand and the Office of Gene Technology Regulator," he said.

searchText:
Moles Galore: Quantitative Chemistry
Goals

       Establish a solid understanding of moles and Avogadro’s number
       Practice estimation skills
       Introduction to common ions used in chemical reactions
       Have fun and get to know your fellow students

Background

       Atoms, molecules, and ions: The atom is the smallest unit that can be
        identified as a specific element (e.g. a copper atom, containing one copper
        nucleus surrounded by electrons). Molecules contain many atoms bonded
        together. Ions are charge species, and can be either atoms or molecules.

       The mole is a unit that helps us answer the question "How much?" It makes
        numbers much more manageable. Just like donuts are measured in dozens,
        and paper is measured in reams, atoms and molecules are measured in
        moles. Mole is abbreviated "mol".

       Avogadro's number: NA= 6.022142 x 1023 mole-1 refers to the number of
        items in a collection containing 1 mole of that item. It is derived from the
        number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12 (e.g. a 60-carat diamond,
        or a 1.8 cm cube of graphite). For some interesting history and controversy
        regarding Avogadro's Number, read An Exact Value for Avogadro's
        Number.

       The mole in reactions:
        The mole is the common language in a chemical reaction. For example, for
        the reaction:

                                 Pb+2(aq) + 2OH¯(aq) → Pb(OH)2(s)

        You could say:
        1 Pb+2 ion reacts with 2 OH¯ ions to form 1 lead(II) hydroxide molecule, or
        1 mole of Pb+2 reacts with 2 moles of OH¯ to form 1 mole of lead(II)
        hydroxide

        However:
        1 gram of Pb+2 and 2 grams of OH¯ do NOT form 1 gram of lead(II)
        hydroxide
       Atomic/molar mass: Each cell in the periodic table contains a non-integer
       number. This represents the average mass of one atom of this element (in
       amu). It also represents the mass of one mole of an average sample of this
       element (a.k.a. "molar mass", in grams/mole). The molar mass of a
       compound is the sum of the molar masses of each atom in the compound.

      Converting grams to moles:
       Use dimensional analysis (i.e. set up the problem using just units):
         grams * (moles/gram) = moles
         grams / (grams/mole) = grams / (molar mass) = moles

      Converting molarity to moles for solutions:
       The unit M = moles/liter is used to refer to the concentration, or "molarity"
       or a solution. To convert from molarity to moles, you must know
       concentration and volume of a solution. Use dimensional analysis (i.e. set up
       the problem using just units):
          L * (moles/L) = moles

title: Kinship- indig society
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Kinship is at the heart of Indigenous society . A person’s position in the kinship system establishes their relationship to others and to the universe, prescribing their responsibilities towards other people, the land and natural resources. Traditional kinship structures remain important in many Indigenous communities today. [1] There are over 500 Indigenous nations across Australia. Indigenous nations cover wide geographical areas, and have distinct borders. Within these nations there are clan groups, and within the clan groups there are family groups. Clan groups share a common language and kinship system, which is based on either patrilineal or matrilineal lines of descent. [2] There are three levels of kinship in Indigenous society: Moiety, Totem and Skin Names. Moiety The first level of kinship is Moiety. Moiety is a latin word meaning ‘half’. In Moiety systems, everything, including people and the environment, are split into two halves. Each half is a mirror of the other, and to understand the whole universe these two halves must come together. A person's Moiety can be determined by their mother's side (matrilineal) or their father's side (patrilineal). Moieties can also alternate between each generation (people of alternate generations are grouped together). [3] People who share the same Moiety are considered siblings, meaning they are forbidden to marry. They also have a reciprocal responsibility to support each other. [4] Each nation and language has its own term for Moiety. For example, the Yolngu people of north-eastern Arnhem Land are either Dhuwa or Yirritja . In the Yolngu worldview, ancestral beings assigned everything in the universe to either the Dhuwa or the Yirritja Moiety. For example, the black cockatoo is Dhuwa , while the white cockatoo is Yirritja . The two Moieties complement and balance each other in ceremonies, marriage, and daily life. Totems The second level of kinship is Totem. Each person has at least four Totems which represent their nation, clan and family group, as well as a personal Totem. Nation, clan and family Totems are preordained, whereas personal Totems recognise an individual’s strengths and weaknesses. Totems link a person to the universe - to land, air, water and geographical features. People don’t ‘own’ their Totems, rather they are accountable for them. Each person has a responsibility to ensure that their Totems are protected and passed on to the next generation. Totems are split between Moieties to create a balance of use and protection. For example, while members of one Moiety protect and conserve the animal, members of the other Moiety may eat and use the animal. [5] Skin Names The third level of kinship is the Skin Name. Similar to a surname, a Skin Name indicates a person’s blood line. It also conveys information about how generations are linked and how they should interact. Unlike surnames, husbands and wives don’t share the same Skin Name, and children don’t share their parents’ name. Rather, it is a sequential system, so Skin Names are given based on the preceding name (the mother’s name in a matrilineal system or the father’s name in a patrilineal system) and its level in the naming cycle. Each nation has its own Skin Names and each name has a prefix or suffix to indicate gender. There are 16-32 sets of names in each cycle. For example, in a matrilineal nation, if a woman with the first name in the cycle (One) has a baby, the child’s Skin Name will be the second name in the cycle (Two). All other ‘Twos’ in that community are now considered the sibling of that child, and all ‘Ones’ are considered their parents. When that child grows up and has children of their own, those children will be Threes. This sequential naming continues until the end of the number cycle is reached, then it begins again at One. [6]
